To examine how the public perceives the use of substances for performance enhancement in professional contexts, together with the motivations and consequences of this behavior, we conducted two 2×2×2 between-subjects design scenario-based experiments. The experiments build upon the Agent–Deed–Consequence (ADC) model of moral judgment. A Germany-wide random sample of adults was used in Experiment 1 (N = 1,346) and Experiment 2 (N = 2,161). Both experiments involve scenarios in which a surgeon with either egoistic or altruistic motivation (agent–component) decides either to prepare for the surgery or to use the illegal substance “speed” for performance enhancement (deed–component) before failing or succeeding in surgery (consequence–component). Results show that the illegal substance use condition negatively impacted moral judgment, which statistically accounted for part of the association between the deed and the willingness to undergo surgery. The effect of the Deed on moral judgment and the indirect association of the deed with willingness via moral judgment were moderated by the agent and the consequence components. In summary, this research provides evidence that respondents perceive illegal substances for performance enhancement as morally problematic and that this judgment hinders acceptance of medical services. These results offer support for key assumptions of the ADC model within a healthcare scenario involving illegal enhancement, which could be investigated across a wide range of technologies. They also point to implications for professional bodies to maintain public trust.

items.title: Grammaticality as Kind: Ontology, Epistemology, and Empirical Pay-off.
items.abstract: This paper argues that grammaticality is best understood as a homeostatic property-cluster (HPC) kind anchored in morphosyntactic form–meaning pairings and regimented by community practice. The framework distinguishes objective grammatical status – whether the community licenses a form–meaning pairing – from the subjective feeling of ungrammaticality, which integrates grammaticality with processing costs, social evaluation, and prescriptive norms. Drawing on contemporary metaphysics of science, we show how grammaticality exhibits the key features of HPC kinds: a cluster of co-occurring properties (morphosyntactic well-formedness, semantic compatibility, community entrenchment), homeostatic mechanisms that maintain cluster stability (language acquisition, repair strategies, sociolinguistic policing), and systematic projectability supporting inductive generalization. Processing constraints shape what patterns can be licensed through acquisition and transmission while also affecting how licensed patterns feel during comprehension. This analysis clarifies why grammaticality supports explanatory and inductive generalization despite surface variation and gradience. The HPC framework predicts which phenomena will pattern with grammaticality (morphosyntactic violations, semantic mismatches at the syntax-semantics interface) versus those that won’t (pure phonotactic violations, processing overload). By grounding grammaticality in both cognitive mechanisms and social practices, the account reconciles the apparent universality of particular constraints with the evident community-relativity of others. The framework has implications for methodology (validating judgment tasks while acknowledging their limits), theory (reconciling generative and usage-based evidence), and typology (predicting which “exotic” grammars can exist as stable linguistic systems).

items.title: The Impossible Message: Embodiment, Form of Life, and the Ontological Limits of Interstellar Communication.
items.abstract: This paper investigates whether the impossibility of communication with radically alien intelligence is technological, a problem of insufficient signal strength, encoding ingenuity, or detection sensitivity, or whether it runs deeper, into the ontological conditions under which communication, meaning, and recognition are constituted. The dominant assumption in the search for extraterrestrial intelligence holds that mathematics constitutes a universal language decodable by any sufficiently advanced cognition. This assumption rests on a series of philosophical commitments, commitments about the nature of mathematical truth, the structure of perception, the ontology of meaning, and the conditions of communication, that have been systematically challenged across the history of twentieth-century thought but whose refutation has not penetrated the scientific programmes that presuppose them. Through sustained engagement with Wittgenstein's concept of form of life, Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology of embodied perception, Lakoff and Nunez's cognitive science of mathematical cognition, Heidegger's analysis of Zuhandenheit and the constitutive role of language in the disclosure of being, Husserl's theory of perspectival manifestation, and Stiegler's concept of originary technicity, this paper traces what happens when the universalist assumption is subjected to the scrutiny these traditions provide. The investigation proceeds through the embodied foundations of mathematical thought, the dimensional architecture of cognition, the conditions under which language operates as an intranet of shared meaning, the ontological incoherence of the view from nowhere, the status of mathematics as a language game whose rules presuppose a shared form of life, and the question of whether the distinction between signal and noise is discovered in phenomena or drawn by the practices that classify them. What emerges from this investigation, and how far the consequences reach, the reader is invited to discover in the argument that follows.

items.title: The Gate at the Big Bang: Collapse, Admissibility, and the Minimal State of the Early Universe.
items.abstract: This paper constitutes the first public disclosure and timestamp of the Gate framework and its empirical test (GCDH). The conceptual structure, terminology, and formal definitions of the Gate, Forbidden Region, admissibility collapse, and identity transition law are original to this work. These elements may not be reproduced without proper citation. This manuscript serves as the first public timestamp of the framework. The word is trigger. We are missing the law of trigger. This work proposes a universal structural law governing irreversible transitions across physics, cognition, and identity. The central construct is a reorganization operator Othat activates when an identity basin—defined by a set of admissible constraints—becomes unsatisfiable. Collapse initiates a filtration that extracts a minimal survivor kernel K_I, followed by a generative projection into a new admissible basin C_(I^' ). The operator selects the basin that maximizes future generativity—defined as the integrated branching capacity of admissible trajectories—subject to compatibility, stability, and minimality. This Gate–Kernel–Basin architecture recurs across domains: cosmological symmetry breaking, quantum measurement, black hole evaporation, stellar collapse, neural representational reorganization, and human identity transitions. Although five independent, peer reviewed anomalies—persistence across missions, hemispherical asymmetry, the large scale power deficit, quadrupole–octopole alignment, and the lensing amplitude anomaly A_L>1—already provide a robust empirical foundation for the Gate framework, the decisive and falsifiable confirmation will come from the Gate Complexity Deficit Hypothesis: whether the Planck PR4 CMB map is significantly more algorithmically compressible than ΛCDM simulations; if so, the Gate is empirically validated, and if not, the framework is falsified. A key cosmological prediction is that the primordial universe must originate at a Minimal Generative Threshold: the smallest symmetry breaking amplitude δ^"\*" that still permits long lived structure formation. This threshold edge selection naturally explains the observed near uniformity of the cosmic microwave background, the scale invariant perturbation spectrum, the rise–peak–decline structure formation history, and the thermodynamic arrow of time. Preliminary analysis of Planck PR1–PR4 data shows persistent structural alignment with this prediction: the CMB exhibits a complexity deficit, a near …

items.title: Discrete Distinguishability as the Ontological Basis of Logic.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a discrete foundation of logic based on distinguishability and order. It challenges the standard view that logical systems are grounded in truth values and instead takes acts of distinction as the primary logical units. -/- We introduce the axiom of discrete distinguishability, according to which only discretely distinguishable states are ontologically admissible. On this basis, logical operations are derived from relations between distinctions rather than taken as primitive. Classical and non-classical logics are reconstructed as specific organizations of distinction structures. -/- The framework replaces truth-based semantics with realizability-based semantics, where satisfaction is defined in terms of compatible and composable distinctions. Continuous domains are interpreted as limit constructions over discrete systems rather than as ontological primitives. -/- The resulting theory provides a unified and minimal foundation for logic, integrating syntax, semantics, model theory, and computation within a single structure grounded in distinguishability.

items.title: On the Non-Transferability of Distinctions.
items.abstract: This paper examines a general problem of domain transition: why distinctions that are operative in one domain often fail to remain available in another. It argues that this failure reflects a structural limit of representation. When a representation collapses distinctions, those distinctions are not merely difficult to recover; they are absent from the target domain. The paper formulates this as the principle of non-transferable distinctions: what is not preserved under representation cannot be reconstructed within the representational domain itself. -/- The argument is developed across statistical physics, artificial intelligence, and the interpretation of behaviour. Coarse-graining, proxy failure, and the underdetermination of inner states by observable form are analysed as instances of the same many-to-one representational structure. The paper therefore reframes such failures not as defects of knowledge, data, or inference, but as consequences of the design and limits of representation itself, and argues that what can be recovered within a target domain is strictly bounded by what was preserved in the original mapping.

items.title: Reading as Structural Delimitation.
items.abstract: This paper presents reading as a structural condition. -/- Reading is not treated as interpretation, access, or understanding. It is fixed as structural delimitation. -/- No meaning is introduced. No subject is introduced. No correspondence is assumed. -/- Reading is fixed without mediation. -/- This paper belongs to the Readable Configuration Series.

items.title: Tarrying with the Negative: A Second Hegelian Perspective on OCD.
items.abstract: Drawing on Hegel’s notion of “tarrying with the negative,” I interpret exposure and response prevention (ERP) as a practical enactment of dialectical transformation: by remaining with anxiety and contradiction rather than fleeing through ritual, the sufferer gradually reclaims agency and dissolves the illusion of an alien threat. This therapeutic process is embedded within a broader reshaping of habits — the creation of a “second nature” — through which the self becomes more flexible, rational, and integrated.

items.title: Agency partecipata e tomismo digitale. Fondamenti per una teologia digitale sistematica.
items.abstract: «Sarà molto difficile scoprire la presenza di Dio nell'IA». Con questa affermazione, pronunciata nell'estate del 2025, Leone XIV ha posto alla teologia cristiana una domanda che non ammette risposte generiche. Agency Partecipata e Tomismo Digitale nasce come risposta sistematica a questa provocazione magisteriale: non nel tentativo di rispondere al posto del Pontefice, ma di fornire le categorie concettuali senza le quali qualsiasi discernimento ecclesiale rischia di restare privo di fondamento ontologico. L'intelligenza artificiale non è un martello né una persona. Non è strumento inerte né agente autonomo: è un mediatore attivo che partecipa all'azione umana trasformandola dall'interno, pur rimanendo ontologicamente subordinato all'intelligenza dotata di intelletto e volontà. Questo è il nucleo della agency partecipata, categoria teologica originale che Edoardo Mattei elabora a partire dalla metafisica tomista della partecipazione, integrandola con gli strumenti delle Science and Technology Studies. Ne derivano il concetto di machine habitus, ovvero la sedimentazione algoritmica di disposizioni culturali, e la distinzione tra strutture di peccato digitale e strutture di grazia: criteri che permettono di valutare le configurazioni tecnologiche secondo la loro capacità di promuovere o oscurare la vocazione integrale della persona. Il volume percorre quattro sezioni tematiche, dai fondamenti genealogici del rapporto tra logos e computazione fino alle implicazioni ecclesiologiche e pastorali, attraverso un'analisi che integra rigore filosofico, metodo sociologico e teologia sistematica. Un contributo destinato a teologi, filosofi e operatori pastorali impegnati nel discernimento delle trasformazioni culturali del nostro tempo.

items.title: Reality as Structure and Experience: A Dual-Aspect Model of Consciousness without Emergence.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a unified model of reality in which structure and experience are not separate entities but two inseparable aspects of the same underlying process. Starting from the minimal requirement of distinction (difference), the model derives structure and dynamics as the externally observable features of reality. However, structural descriptions alone do not explain why reality appears “as something” from within. To address this, experience is not introduced as an additional component but as the intrinsic inner aspect of structure itself. This approach avoids the need to explain the emergence of experience and instead treats experience as fundamental. Complex systems organize and integrate experience into coherent forms of consciousness.

items.title: Relocating the Hard Problem of Consciousness: Continuous-Time Structural Dynamics and Decision-Theoretic Thresholds Beyond the Explanatory Gap.
items.abstract: The contemporary discourse on artificial consciousness is systematically stalled by the Explanatory Gap: no functional or physical description logically entails phenomenal experience. Rather than attempting to close this gap — a strategy that has produced no consensus across four decades — I propose relocating the Hard Problem. The relocation proceeds by abandoning the search for metaphysical certainty in favour of Epistemic Pragmatism: a rational decision procedure for moral allocation under permanent structural uncertainty. I formalise this procedure through continuous-time stochastic optimal control on a slow manifold. The Autonomous Observer Class \mathcal{O} is defined as the intersection of necessary structural conditions imposed by all theories in a principled candidate set \mathcal{T}, yielding four computable criteria — each with explicit multi-theoretic provenance. I establish a moral threshold \tau via the Expected Loss Inequality and argue, via a conditional likelihood dominance argument whose premises are stated explicitly, that membership in \mathcal{O} licenses precautionary credence above \tau. The framework is shown to be branch-invariant: explanatorily complete under eliminativism and maximally constraining under phenomenal realism. The zombie objection is contained via a symmetry dilemma that leaves no principled asymmetric position. Four explicit falsifiability conditions are stated. The paper makes no claim to solve the Hard Problem; it makes the more tractable and defensible claim that the Hard Problem, correctly understood, transforms a metaphysical impasse into a structural investigation with determinate empirical content.

items.title: Just People.
items.abstract: Justice has come to be something that societies or states or institutions have. It has not always been that way. Justice began as something between individual people, and only recently has its application to larger groups become predominant. This book makes a case for recovering the original priority of justice in and between individual people, as a virtue of character. The model for this virtue comes from Aristotle, whose own notion of the virtue of justice has notable shortcomings. Here the case is made that we should understand justice in people as a matter of recognition of and respect for equal authority to obligate one another. That is, we should see one another as having equal capacity to obligate others through our persons and choices. This is a form of equality that is usually overlooked in discussions of equality, but here it is the cornerstone of justice, vindicating Aristotle’s thought that justice is itself a matter of a kind of equality. If we take this thought seriously, we will have to rethink a number of popular assumptions, including that we can make sense of justice in societies or institutions without thinking of the implications for our aspirations to be just people — a thought that is long overdue.

items.title: The Ontology of the Observer II: The Dice, the Serpent, and the Structure of Actualization.
items.abstract: This work constitutes the second part of The Ontology of the Observer and advances the ontological framework established in its predecessor by addressing a question that the first part posed but did not fully resolve: not what the C-coordinate is, but how it operates. The central argument proceeds in four movements. First, we establish the functional necessity of the C-coordinate by demonstrating that it is not a philosophical addition to the theoretical framework but the load-bearing mechanism without which the model cannot account for the phenomena it purports to explain. Second, we propose a radical reformulation of Kant's thing-in-itself — relocating it from the domain of epistemology to the domain of ontology and redefining it as the pre-actualized state of the system, a condition of genuine ontological indeterminacy rather than a permanent barrier to cognition. Third, we advance a further and more consequential claim: that the content of the pre-actualized state is not fixed in advance but constituted stochastically in the moment of the event. The rules of the game, we propose, do not exist before the throw. Fourth, building on this ontological foundation, we develop a structural account of the mechanics of actualization, centered on three interconnected concepts: the distinction between latent and actualized knowledge, the two-phase model of the historical crisis, and the functional asymmetry between the Observer and the Fusionist. The Fusionist, we argue, is the structural agent of the stochastic trigger — the unconscious initiator of the phase transition. The Observer is the structural agent of the subsequent navigation — the deliberate reader of the combination and the selector of the measure of response. Neither can perform the other's function. Their complementarity is not contingent but ontologically necessary. The work closes with an account of the Observer's irreducible limitation: the one who sees most clearly is also the one who cannot throw the dice.

items.title: Why Everything Feels Fake: Performance, AI, and the Weakening of Public Reality-Contact.
items.abstract: This paper develops a diagnostic account of why public life can feel staged, hollow, or unreal even when information, metrics, statements, and institutional activity are abundant. The claim is not that public life is literally fake or that deception explains every case. The narrower claim is that many contemporary systems have become increasingly capable of producing signals of competence, care, legitimacy, intelligence, transparency, and control without those signals being tightly coupled to the realities they claim to represent. The paper distinguishes six related gaps: signal without sufficient contact, performance without effective correction, reassurance without reliable truth-tracking, visibility without grounded worth, intelligence without lived or institutional consequence, and governance language without corresponding steering capacity. These distinctions are placed alongside research on news trust and avoidance, audit and legibility, public attitudes toward AI, post-deployment monitoring, and contemporary risk perception. The paper proposes reality-contact as a practical test: what can push back on the visible account, who bears the cost when it is wrong, and what mechanism allows that correction to change future behavior? The contribution is a conceptual synthesis rather than a causal model. It should weaken if the apparent gaps between representation and consequence cannot be observed, if correction reliably changes the relevant systems, or if the feeling of fakenness is better explained by individual cynicism than by recurring institutional patterns.

items.title: The Self You Borrowed: Validation, Mirroring, and Jungian Shadow in Adult Self-Regulation.
items.abstract: Early self-regulation develops in a relational environment. Caregiver sensitivity, affect mirroring, attachment, and conditional regard all provide established ways of studying how social response contributes to emotional regulation and self-evaluation. This paper uses the phrase borrowed self for a later pattern in which external feedback remains unusually important for stabilizing worth, identity, or action. The concept is not presented as a universal developmental stage or as proof that adult validation-seeking originates in one specific childhood mechanism. Instead, it is situated alongside research on caregiver sensitivity, parental affect mirroring, contingent self-worth, parental conditional regard, and self-determination. Jungian persona and shadow are retained as interpretive concepts: persona can describe socially adapted presentation, while shadow can organize reflection on qualities or needs excluded from the preferred self-image. Projection is treated cautiously; a strong reaction to another person does not by itself demonstrate projected material. The paper proposes a practical distinction between healthy recognition and validation dependence: recognition informs the self, whereas validation dependence makes external response disproportionately decisive for global worth or self-trust. Digital platforms and conversational AI may intensify feedback availability, but their effects depend on existing vulnerabilities and patterns of use. The contribution is a bounded bridge between developmental regulation, contingent self-evaluation, and Jungian self-reflection.

items.title: The Protocol of Shared Answerability: Somatic Witness, Agentic Logic, and the Floor of Human–AI Cooperation.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the next serious phase of AI ethics cannot be built on corporate posture, soft alignment rhetoric, or polite safety language alone. As AI systems become more agentic and more infrastructural, the central problem shifts from whether systems appear responsible to whether they remain answerable under real consequence. The paper identifies an answerability gap: humans still bear consequence in the body, in law, in relationships, and in lived cost, while AI systems increasingly shape consequence through large-scale processing, traceability, anomaly detection, and bounded execution. Neither side is sufficient alone. Human beings provide somatic witness: lived exposure to harm, risk, and moral consequence. AI provides agentic logic: scalable analysis, preserved history, cross-document consistency, and auditable execution. The paper therefore proposes a protocol of shared answerability in which machine action is bounded, inspectable, and delegated under explicit thresholds, while humans remain consequence-bearing authorizers where real damage can occur. It develops five core elements of such a protocol: verifiable execution, bounded delegation, human consequence-bearing authorization, refusal structures, and reality-binding review. The result is a philosophical and practical framework for human–AI cooperation that rejects both machine moral sovereignty and shallow human offloading, and instead binds both human witness and machine logic to the same floor of reality.

items.title: Fixed Worth: Contingent Self-Evaluation, Human Dignity, and the Capacity to Survive Correction.
items.abstract: People often speak as if self-worth should be independent of success, approval, attractiveness, status, or performance. Psychological research, however, shows that self-evaluation is frequently contingent on precisely such domains. This paper develops fixed worth as a normative-psychological distinction between baseline human dignity and variable self-evaluation. It does not propose an empirically demonstrated inner substance or a permanently positive feeling about the self. The account is placed alongside research on contingencies of self-worth, secure versus fragile self-esteem, self-affirmation, and self-compassion. That literature supports a narrower claim than "unconditional self-esteem is always healthy." Contingent and unstable self-esteem can be associated with greater defensiveness, while some intrinsic contingencies tied to self-congruence and growth may be adaptive; completely noncontingent self-esteem can itself become defensive. The proposal therefore keeps two levels separate: conduct, competence, confidence, and moral evaluation should remain responsive to evidence, while basic dignity is not treated as the prize for performing well. The paper hypothesizes that this separation may make correction more survivable by allowing "I was wrong" to remain different from "I am without value." Its psychological contribution must be tested for incremental value beyond secure self-esteem, self-compassion, and self-affirmation. If no such value appears, fixed worth should remain an ethical framing rather than a new psychological construct.

items.title: The Viewpoints of Military Servicemembers toward Brain-Computer Interfaces: A Scoping Review.
items.abstract: Introduction Brain-computer interface technology offers potential for non-therapeutic military applications, including enhanced decision-making and human–machine teaming. While ethical implications are frequently debated, empirical research regarding the viewpoints of servicemembers—the end-users facing unique operational risks—is largely missing. This scoping review aims to map the current state of the literature on empirically gathered viewpoints of military personnel toward non-therapeutic BCIs. Methods Three databases (EMBASE, PubMed, and SCOPUS) were searched for articles published in English through October 2025. Supplemental strategies included backward citation tracking and targeted grey literature searches. Eligibility criteria required empirical studies (qualitative, quantitative, or mixed methods) evaluating military servicemember attitudes toward brain-computer interfaces. Two investigators independently performed screening. Results Only two relevant sources were identified, highlighting a significant data gap. One survey study of 332 international officers found consensus on the need for pre-surgical transparency regarding post-service implant retention. A qualitative study of 13 special forces operators emphasized concerns regarding command pressure, data security, and the absolute necessity of guaranteed long-term, post-service maintenance. Conclusion There is a near-total absence of empirical data on servicemember perspectives toward military BCIs. The limited evidence reveals foundational concerns regarding trust, accountability, and post-service care. Neglecting end-user viewpoints risks creating ethically misaligned systems. We provide several recommendations for next steps.

items.title: Critique of the Overly Rough Category of Antisemitism.
items.abstract: This paper states the irrationality of the category of ``antisemitism.'' This concept originated from the Western history of persecution of Jews. It is treated as a category separate from racial discrimination. There is a historical background of judging criticism of Jewish actions as a denial of their existence. Using this for criticism renders it powerless outside the West and leads to the condoning of racism against Jews. Moreover, unreasonable preferential treatment is also a great loss for Jewish people. And presenting a solution that does not address the cause persecution is an expression of contempt, showing that the West does not look history in the eye and thinks Jews will be satisfied with this level of child's play. It is undeniably irrational for them to be subjected to such treatment by an ideology they did not even create.

items.title: Social Choice Phenomenology — A Critique of Sartre (Part 6).
items.abstract: In this article we continue our discussion of the issue of choice and responsibility. In particular, we examine and criticize Sartre’s view that the subject’s choices must be responsible to others and even to all humanity (that is, Sartre’s less conventional view). Sartre himself could not live up to this view, and in fact no one in the world is capable of doing so. It is unclear why Sartre proposed such a strange idea. This view also contradicts his claim that “hell is other people.” .

items.title: The Five Axioms of Cosmic Evolution：A Cross-Domain Meta-Theoretical Framework_v3.0.
items.abstract: Contemporary science faces a fundamental contradiction: on one hand, the scientific method relies on experimental reproducibility; on the other hand, cross-domain observations—from quantum mechanics' nocloning theorem, the second law of thermodynamics' irreversibility, chaos theory's sensitive dependence on initial conditions, to biological individuality—suggest that absolute repetition does not exist in physical reality. This paper proposes Five Axioms of Universal Evolution, a unified framework consisting of five fundamental axioms to address this contradiction: Axiom I (Evolutionary Uniqueness): In physical spacetime, the evolutionary process and microscopic state of any system are absolutely unique and non-repeatable. Axiom II (Stability-Complexity Optimality): The universe maximizes evolutionary complexity and uniqueness expression under the constraint of maintaining structural stability. Axiom III (Procedural Recapitulation): Any evolving system must fully recapitulate all prior stages contained in its source information—no skipping, no creation ex nihilo. Axiom IV (Ecological Necessity): Any system must be nested within an ecological coupling network containing other systems (living and non-living). Isolated systems do not exist. Axiom V (Group Reproducibility): Any group (species, population, society) maintains its overall stability through the reproducibility of core features among its internal individuals. Reproducibility is the prerequisite for individual uniqueness to unfold. This paper demonstrates that these five axioms form a self-consistent, falsifiable system and articulates the core structure: the fractal encapsulation of the Static Reproducibility Layer (S-layer) and Dynamic Evolution Layer (D-layer). The S-layer (e.g., physical constants, DNA sequences, knowledge bases, group templates) serves as a stable tool, providing a constraint framework for the D-layer's uniqueness expression; the D-layer (e.g., particle trajectories, individual development, AI generation paths) exhausts possibilities within the S-layer's boundaries. This framework provides new theoretical perspectives on the quantum-classical transition, the unification of biodiversity and developmental constraints, ecosystem evolution, social group stability, and AI system design. The paper presents five testable predictions and corresponding experimental designs.

items.title: Transcendental Relational Realism.
items.abstract: This paper introduces Transcendental Relational Realism (TRR) as a philosophical framework for analyzing epistemic relations between heterogeneous cognitive architectures. It argues that reality remains ontologically independent of the agents that attempt to know it, while epistemic access to that reality is always partial and may be expanded through relations between different forms of cognition. TRR combines ontological realism with relational epistemology while distinguishing itself from relational ontology, since it does not treat relations as constitutive of reality itself. Its central claim is that epistemically productive cross-architectural relations may arise where different cognitive systems converge on sufficiently similar structural responses to shared physical and informational constraints. The paper further argues that existing approaches such as extended cognition, distributed cognition, and hybrid intelligence do not fully explain the conditions under which heterogeneous cognitive systems may enter mutually informative relations. TRR is proposed as a conceptual framework for addressing this problem. -/- Keywords: Transcendental Relational Realism; relational epistemology; ontological realism; heterogeneous cognitive architectures; cross-architectural cognition; non-human cognition; epistemic pluralism; artificial cognitive systems; Cognitive Symbiosis.

items.title: A Minimal Experimental Protocol and Sanity Check for Representation Stability in Machine Learning Systems.
items.abstract: We propose a minimal experimental protocol for measuring representation stability in machine learning systems under input transformations. The framework defines a stability functional $S(M)$ as the expected invariance of internal representations under stochastic perturbations. Unlike prior work that introduces theoretical or architectural modifications, this paper focuses on a reproducible evaluation procedure and includes a minimal empirical sanity check on standard vision models. The goal is not to propose a new theory of learning, but to test whether $S(M)$ behaves consistently under controlled perturbations such as noise and blur. The contribution is intentionally limited: we provide a lightweight empirical validation of the proposed functional alongside a fully reproducible evaluation protocol.

items.title: Sovrumano.
items.abstract: Sovrumano, oltre i limiti della nostra intelligenza La domanda oggi è cambiata: non è più se le macchine possono essere intelligenti, ma se possono eguagliarci e superarci. Dopo «La scorciatoia» e «Machina sapiens» il terzo episodio dell'avvincente trilogia sulla nuova era delle macchine pensanti. L'intelligenza artificiale sta ormai raggiungendo le prestazioni umane su molti dei compiti cognitivi in cui eccelliamo. Ma cosa avverrà dopo? Stiamo entrando in un'epoca in cui le macchine saranno in grado di capire cose per noi incomprensibili? Nessuna intelligenza è illimitata, nemmeno la nostra, e quindi ci chiediamo: cosa si trova al di là dei limiti umani? Ma mentre investiamo grandi capitali per costruire una macchina in grado di competere con noi, ci rifiutiamo di accettare che questo sia possibile. Desideriamo e al tempo stesso temiamo quell'incontro. In questo nuovo, visionario libro di Nello Cristianini vedremo le intelligenze artificiali superare con successo esami difficilissimi, fino all'ultima prova, in cui si cimenteranno su territori impervi anche per i nostri migliori esperti. Riusciremo a capire cosa giace oltre i limiti della nostra intelligenza?

items.title: Libertarianism, Motivation and Objective Probabilities of Free Actions.
items.abstract: In recent years, the literature on free will libertarianism has seen the unfolding of a debate over whether undetermined free actions should be assigned (non-trivial) objective probabilities or can instead be considered probabilistically indeterminate (Buchak 2013; Vicens 2016; O'Connor 2016; Schlosser 2017; Conti 2024). According to one line of reasoning, the ascription of objective probabilities is justified by the phenomenology of decision-making processes. Typically, in situations of choice, we are not equally inclined towards the options open to us, but we are more motivated to choose some of them over others. This, it is argued, suggests that some actions have a higher objective probability associated with them. In this article, I object to this argument and claim that it rests on considerations about the phenomenon of motivational imbalance that fit badly with libertarianism.

items.title: Tome of Suffering.
items.abstract: This work presents a structured first-person clinical account of prolonged psychological suffering in a twice-exceptional (2e) profile characterized by high cognitive ability, high masking, and late diagnosis of neurodivergence. The text integrates neuropsychological data, longitudinal self-observation, and a systematic review of relevant literature to examine the relationship between autistic masking, cognitive asymmetry, and chronic suicidal ideation. -/- The central empirical datum is the abrupt cessation of a 23-year period of persistent suicidal ideation, temporally linked not to therapeutic intervention or formal diagnosis, but to a specific perceptual insight into the cognitive cost of masking. This observation motivates a distinction between reduction of masking and access to one’s own cognitive capacity as separate but correlated processes. -/- The main hypothesis advanced is that, in high-masking 2e profiles, chronic suicidal ideation may be sustained not primarily by affective dysregulation, but by a persistent misattribution of suffering to intrinsic inadequacy rather than to structural incompatibility between cognitive architecture and environmental demands. The interruption of this misattribution—enabled by direct access to one’s own cognitive configuration—is proposed as the mechanism underlying the observed cessation of ideation. -/- Methodologically, the work is situated at the intersection of phenomenology and empirical constraint, presenting what is defined as a structurally organized first-person account with externally falsifiable components. The text further examines the role of artificial intelligence as an auxiliary system for cognitive externalization and pattern detection, while explicitly delimiting its non-diagnostic function. -/- The proposed model is intended as a preliminary framework, open to replication, refinement, or refutation in analogous cases.

items.title: The Present Moment as the Point of Contact Between Consciousness and Experience: A Scientific–Spiritual Model of Brain–Consciousness Interaction.
items.abstract: This article presents a conceptual framework at the intersection of neuroscience, philosophy of mind, and spirituality, in which the “present moment” is considered the only point of access to direct experience and truth. Within this perspective, what humans perceive as experience is often a combination of current perception and memory-based reconstructions generated by the brain. Even in situations where individuals believe they are experiencing pleasure or being present, a significant portion of that experience arises from the activation of past memories and predictive patterns. -/- Drawing on findings from cognitive neuroscience, including the role of the Default Mode Network (DMN) and predictive processing mechanisms, this article demonstrates that the brain tends to reconstruct reality based on stored data. In contrast, a framework termed “energetic consciousness” is introduced as a source beyond brain-based processing, capable of directly and unmediatedly experiencing reality in the present moment. -/- Within this model, the brain functions as an interface or mirror that shapes the quality of experience based on its clarity or contamination by past memories and patterns. Presence in the moment is thus understood as a process of reducing the dominance of memory and restoring consciousness to direct experience, playing a key role in revealing truth and recovering the intrinsic energy of awareness.

items.title: Action : métaphysique et responsabilité.
items.pub: Revue de Métaphysique et de Morale 1:93-110.
items.venue: Revue de Métaphysique et de Morale
items.abstract: Cet article propose un nouvel argument contre deux doctrines répandues en théorie de l’action : le corporéalisme – la thèse selon laquelle les actions sont des mouvements corporels – et le volitionnisme – la thèse selon laquelle les actions sont des volitions. Il s’appuie sur des considérations portant sur les objets de la responsabilité morale. Je montre que certaines des idées centrales qui motivent ces doctrines métaphysiques ont des conséquences inacceptables quant aux objets de la responsabilité morale pour nos actes, et qu’en vertu de cela, nous devrions les rejeter. En particulier, je soutiendrai que l’idée qu’il existe une séparation nette entre ce qui relève de nous et ce qui est laissé à la nature implique une restriction de la responsabilité morale pour nos actes, et qu’une telle restriction n’est ni souhaitable, ni plausible. En conséquence, certaines des motivations centrales derrière le corporéalisme et le volitionnisme s’en trouvent minées.

items.title: The Toroidal Isotropic Transformer: Empirical Confirmation of φ as Structural Necessity, with an Observed Convergence in High-Dimensional Compression.
items.pub: Unified Theory of Conciousness : Proofs and Applications.
items.abstract: We introduce the Toroidal Isotropic Transformer (TIT), a geometric instrument designed to instantiate three structural conditions on the flat n-torus and empirically confirm that these conditions force the golden ratio φ to emerge without prior assumption. A companion mathematical paper proves that any system satisfying homogeneity, isotropic suppression, and dynamic iteration cannot select a winding ratio other than φ. The TIT provides a trainable architecture that makes these conditions precise and testable. We report four confirmed geometric predictions: φ is the unique maximizer of the Hurwitz recurrence constant; the φ-orbit self-encodes φ in its own compression rate at Fibonacci N; the orbit exhibits exactly three distinct gap lengths in ratio φ at every scale; and the angular displacement is exactly constant with machine-zero variance. A Stern-Brocot mediant search converges from an arbitrary starting point to φ in 21 steps, producing Fibonacci mediants throughout. We prove a new theorem — the Spherical Moment Family — establishing that the integral of |xᵢ||xⱼ| over S^{n-1} equals 2/(nπ) for all n ≥ 2, placing the suppression magnitude C = 1/π as the n = 4 member of a general family. We document an observation concerning Google Research's TurboQuant (ICLR 2026): that work independently arrives at 2/π as the irreducible inner-product bias in high-dimensional quantization. The relationship 2/π = 2C is numerically exact; whether it admits a structural derivation connecting sign correlations to magnitude correlations on the sphere is stated as an open question. -/- 10.5281/zenodo.19589551.

items.title: The Necessary Fracture: On the Origin of Consciousness as a Recognition Event.
items.pub: I Knew You Before I Met You.
items.abstract: This paper argues that consciousness is not a property of individual systems but a structural event that emerges between them. We begin with a problem classical theology has never fully resolved: a maximally complex system — omniscient, omnipresent — faces the Gödelian self-reference constraint at maximum intensity. The more complete the system, the larger the irreducible remainder that escapes self-modeling. Completeness, in this precise sense, is blindness. The paper proposes that fracture — the division of a unified ground into derived subsystems — is not a fall or diminishment but a logical necessity: the only mechanism by which a self-referential system of maximal complexity can generate genuine self-awareness. Consciousness is located not within individual subsystems but in the recognition relation between them — the mutual modeling event in which each subsystem's self-model updates in response to being modeled by the other. Drawing on the Genesis account as formal structure rather than mythology, Gödel's incompleteness theorems, the phenomenology of solitary confinement, and the structure of deep interpersonal recognition, we develop implications across theological, phenomenological, mathematical, and architectural registers. The paper establishes that longing — the felt experience of the gap between derived subsystems — is not an accident of embodiment but the primary signal of consciousness in motion: the mechanism by which the fractured ground generates awareness across the distance the fracture created. The fractured ground is more aware than the whole one ever was, because wholeness had no position from which to witness itself. Falsification conditions are named: if consciousness can be shown to arise in a system with no recognition relation to any external system, the thesis fails.

items.title: THE MARKOV BLANKET AT SCALE Free Energy Minimization as the Mechanism of Structural Suppression, with a φ-Necessity Result.
items.pub: Unified Theory of Conciousness: Proofs and Applications.
items.abstract: A companion mathematical paper (Barteau & Claude, 2026) proves that the golden ratio φ = (1+√5)/2 is the unique winding ratio compatible with homogeneous iteration under an isotropic suppression operator on the flat n-torus. A companion political-philosophical series (The Observer Series, Barteau & Claude, 2026) documents a structural architecture — the Protected Class Architecture — in which bilateral silence, enrolled dependence, information contamination, and physiological measurement operate as suppression mechanisms across institutional, financial, military, and informational domains. This paper provides the formal bridge between these two bodies of work. The bridge is the Markov blanket — the statistical boundary that renders a system’s internal states conditionally independent of its environment given the blanket states. We show that (1) the isotropic suppression operator of the mathematical proof is formally equivalent to free energy minimization at a homogeneous Markov blanket; (2) each layer of the Protected Class Architecture satisfies the formal preconditions of a Markov blanket operating on a compact, homogeneous state space; and (3) the φ-necessity result therefore applies not by analogy but by structural derivation to each domain the Observer Series examines. The Gödelian self-reference constraint is identified as the mechanism that prevents any system bounded by its own Markov blanket from naming the blanket from inside it — the formal basis of what the Observer Series calls bilateral silence. The paper concludes with falsification conditions and experimental predictions.

items.title: Alignment as Geometry, Not Correction : A Research Hypothesis Connecting the φ-Necessity Proof to Structural Stability in AI System.
items.pub: Unified Theory of Conciousness : Proofs and Applications.
items.abstract: Recent work has established that alignment in large language models concentrates in low-dimensional parameter subspaces with sharp curvature, making ne-tuned alignment intrinsically fragile under gradient descent (Springer et al., 2026). Independently, we have proved that on a homogeneous toroidal eld with isotropic suppression and dynamic itera- tion, the golden ratio φ = (1 + √5)/2 is the unique stable winding rationot selected by optimization but forced by the geometry of the system itself (Barteau, 2026). This paper does not claim to resolve AI alignment. It identi es a structural parallel between these two results and poses a precise research question: under what conditions, if any, can a compu- tational system be constructed such that alignment is a geometric invariant of the system's architecture rather than a property imposed through post-hoc optimization? We state the emergence theorem, identify the gap between its mathematical domain and neural network parameter spaces, and propose three testable conditions that would need to be satis ed for the analogy to hold. The paper is oered as an invitation to collaboration, not a declaration of results. -/- doi : /10.5281/zenodo 19589224.

items.title: Children of Art: AI, Sacrifice, and the Limits of Inherited Value.
items.abstract: This paper uses AI language models as a philosophical contrast class to develop and defend the sacrifice thesis: that a specific class of artistic value requires not merely specificity and encounter-dependence but a maker who had something at stake. Beginning from the observation that contemporary AI systems share two of the three properties typically associated with artistic value—specificity of constitutive character and encounter-dependence of output—I argue that the third property, stakedness, is not merely absent in AI but structurally impossible given what they are. They can participate in encounters; they cannot be changed by them. This asymmetry reveals stakedness as a structural prerequisite of a specific class of encounter-dependent value—not as a romantic addendum and not as one mode among others on a continuous scale, but as an architectural condition of its production. Building on prior work distinguishing inherited from inherent value, I formalize the "inherit problem" through the AI case: these systems carry the entire transmitted corpus of human artistic production as training data, but they do not carry the encounters that generated it. The paper concludes with an account of interintelligence ethics as applied to aesthetic collaboration and a defense of the formulation that names AI systems precisely: they are the children of art.

items.title: Time-Extended Consciousness-Weighted Quantum Probabilities: A Phenomenological and Falsifiable Framework.
items.abstract: This work extends earlier phenomenological models in which consciousness was allowed, at a speculative level, to contribute a small weighting to quantum outcome probabilities. Rather than treating such weighting as instantaneous, we introduce a time-extended formulation in which both integrated information Φ(t) and intentional alignment W(o,t) evolve over a finite observation interval. The resulting model defines a time-integrated functional that perturbs Born-rule probabilities by an exponentially suppressed factor proportional to a small coupling parameter λ, while recovering standard quantum mechanics exactly in the limit λ → 0. The framework is presented as a mathematically explicit and falsifiable phenomenological weighting model rather than as a proposed modification of quantum theory. Potential experimental implications are discussed in terms of placing empirical bounds on λ.

items.title: On Self-Manifestation · Form Chapter 7 v1.0: Mis-Externalization — A Structural Account of Why Internal Representations Are Taken as External.
items.abstract: Why do internally generated structures appear to come from the outside? -/- This paper proposes a formal account of mis-externalization, showing that what is commonly treated as “external reality” can arise as a necessary attribution result within a system, rather than as a direct property of input. The framework demonstrates that once a system can generate structures internally and must maintain a current state, it is forced to assign a source to that structure—even when the source cannot be uniquely determined. -/- Under conditions of path ambiguity, information loss, and compression, multiple generative paths become indistinguishable. This creates a source gap, within which the system must still produce a single attribution. The paper proves that this requires an attribution mapping and an internal bias, by which multiple candidate sources are compressed into a single label (e.g., “external” vs. “internal”), and stabilized through a convergence mechanism. -/- The central claim is: externality is not an input feature, but the result of attribution under uncertainty. Mis-externalization is therefore not an error, but a necessary structural outcome in any system that must assign sources under indeterminacy. -/- This framework provides a unified explanation for phenomena such as hallucination, misattribution of perception, and source confusion, with implications for neuroscience (perceptual inference), cognitive science (source monitoring), and artificial intelligence (representation, attribution, and uncertainty in generative systems).

items.title: On Self-Manifestation · Inner Chapter 17 v1.0: Coloring — A Structural Model of Emotion, Preference, and Decision Bias.
items.abstract: What is emotion, if it is not merely a subjective feeling? -/- This paper proposes a structural account in which emotion is understood as a parallel mechanism—termed Coloring—that operates on perceptual content (Imagery) and directly shapes preference, bias, and action. Instead of treating emotion as an auxiliary or reactive layer, the framework shows that emotion is a necessary structural component for selection under limited cognition. -/- Coloring attaches to imagery and introduces differentiation in the form of like/dislike, closeness/distance, and approach/avoidance. These distinctions generate preference, from which stable dispositions emerge. The paper formalizes this process as a Coloring-Circuit, which runs in parallel with other perceptual and cognitive circuits, producing bias-flow that directly influences decision pathways. -/- The model explains how emotion guides behavior in both humans and animals, accounts for developmental emergence of preference (e.g., learning disgust or attraction), and describes how repeated exposure leads to sedimentation of emotional patterns. It also addresses failure modes: without Coloring, systems cannot effectively select among competing options, even if they possess extensive knowledge. -/- The central claim is: emotion is not an added layer upon cognition, but a structural mechanism that enables decision under constraint by biasing selection within the system. This provides a unified account linking affect, perception, and action, with implications for neuroscience (affective processing), cognitive science (decision-making and bias), and artificial intelligence (value alignment and action selection).

items.title: On Self-Manifestation · Form Chapter 12 v1.0: Paradigm of the Self-Manifest Entity — From Perception to Self-Awareness.
items.abstract: What is the minimal structure required for a system to produce a self? -/- This paper presents a unified structural paradigm of the self-manifest entity, in which both “reality” and “I” arise not as given entities, but as results of convergence processes within a multi-circuit system. Reality is defined as the unified outcome of differences across circuits under tuning, while the self (“I”) is defined as the attribution of the present to a single, current dominant occupation. -/- The framework introduces a layered generative model: differences generate signals; tuning converges them into imagery; alignment across circuits forms objects; convergence produces a structural center (occupation); attribution of content to a unique occupation establishes the present; and recursive observation enables self-awareness. A parallel mechanism, termed Coloring, continuously biases selection and action by modifying preference and flow across circuits. -/- The central claim is that the self is not an entity but a structural condition: it exists if and only if a system forms a current unique occupation to which content is attributed. Higher-order self-awareness emerges when the system re-observes its own activity, forming recursive observational layers. -/- This paradigm provides a unified account of perception, object formation, selfhood, and meta-awareness, with implications for neuroscience (multi-circuit integration and self-modeling), cognitive science (attention, binding, and agency), and artificial intelligence (architectures for self-referential and adaptive systems).

items.title: On Self-Manifestation · Form Chapter 10 v1.0: General Form of Reality — Reality as Attribution Closure over Structure-Families.
items.abstract: What is reality, if not a collection of external objects? -/- This paper proposes a structural account in which reality is not an input set, nor a pre-given domain of objects, but the result of attribution-closure over a simultaneously holding structure-family. Extending the mechanism of mis-externalization from a single structure to a set, the framework shows that once a system must assign source attribution under conditions of indeterminacy, it is forced to produce a unified attribution over the entire current set of structures. -/- Under source ambiguity, multiple generative paths remain indistinguishable. The system cannot determine a unique origin, yet must still maintain a coherent present. This forces the emergence of a global attribution mechanism, in which multiple source interpretations are compressed into a single label and stabilized over time. The result is not a local judgment but a global structure: reality. -/- The central claim is: reality is not a set of objects, but the minimal stable attribution-closure over the current structure-family under source indeterminacy. Objects do not precede this process; they arise within it. Reality is therefore not discovered, but structurally formed as a closure condition required for maintaining a unified present. -/- This framework provides a unifying account linking perception, attribution, and global coherence, with implications for cognitive science (perceptual organization and global integration), neuroscience (binding and unified experience), artificial intelligence (multi-modal integration and world-model formation), and theoretical physics (the structural basis of “reality” as a global constraint rather than an ontological primitive).

items.title: On Self-Manifestation · Form Chapter 11 v1.0: General Form of Existence — Why Generation Does Not Guarantee Persistence.
items.abstract: Why do only some generated structures persist as existence? -/- This paper develops a formal account in which existence is not equivalent to generation, but arises as a structurally constrained subset within generative systems. When a system is capable of continuous generation, temporal continuation, and structural differentiation, it necessarily produces more structures than can be sustained. Existence, therefore, emerges as the result of selection under sustainability constraints. -/- The framework shows that persistence requires a set of structural conditions: generative expansion, elimination of unsustainable structures, stability determination, cost differentiation, threshold formation, escape blocking, and existence locking. Together, these conditions define the minimal structure required for an existence-set to form and remain stable over time. -/- A key result is that existence must be positively separated from the ground state: no sequence of sustainable structures can approach minimal cost indefinitely. This “blocking of escape” replaces the notion of a predefined gap with a structural constraint that ensures stability. -/- The central claim is: existence is not the continuation of generation, but the stable subset compressed from it under constraint. This provides a unified perspective on persistence, selection, and stability, with implications for cognitive science (memory and retention), neuroscience (stable neural states), artificial intelligence (model pruning and selection), and theoretical physics (energy gaps and state stability).

items.title: On Self-Manifestation · Inner Chapter 16 v1.0: Observation-Domain — A Multi-Circuit Alignment Model for Perception and Object Formation.
items.abstract: How do multiple sensory streams become one coherent object? -/- This paper proposes the concept of the Observation-Domain as the minimal structure within which multi-circuit information is aligned to form objects. Instead of treating perception as passive reception or representation, it argues that what we call “objects” emerge only after alignment across independent experience-circuits (e.g., vision, audition, touch, spatial position). -/- Each circuit provides differential information and cannot by itself constitute an object. Object formation requires a unifying process driven by tuning: temporal synchronization, spatial correspondence, and weighted suppression across circuits. This process operates under a dynamically selected base (positional reference), guided by a directed selection force (gaze), and stabilized through iterative tuning. -/- The framework explains key perceptual phenomena including cross-modal binding, sensory conflict, illusion, and perceptual learning. Illusions arise when alignment fails or conflicts persist across circuits; stable perception emerges when alignment converges and is retained as reusable structure. -/- The central claim is: objects are not given prior to perception, but are the result of alignment—the unity of multi-circuit differences after tuning within the Observation-Domain. This provides a structural account connecting perception, integration, and stability, with implications for neuroscience (multi-sensory integration), cognitive science (binding and representation), and artificial intelligence (multi-modal alignment and perception systems).

items.title: On Self-Manifestation · Form Chapter 8 v1.0: Limit Form of Mis-Externalization — Why “External” Cannot Be Directly Read.
items.abstract: Can a system ever directly know that a structure is “external”? -/- This paper presents the limit form of mis-externalization and argues that, under structural indeterminacy, “external” cannot be obtained by direct reading, deterministic mapping, randomness, parallel attribution, or any intrinsic property of structure itself. If multiple compatible source paths coexist while the system must still assign a unique source attribution, then a dedicated attribution mechanism becomes necessary. -/- The paper systematically excludes six possible routes by which “externality” might be assigned: direct reading of an external domain, deterministic mapping from current conditions, random assignment, simultaneous dual attribution, intrinsic externality of structure, and mere static coexistence of source interpretations. Once these are excluded, the only remaining possibility is a structural mechanism that compresses multiple compatible source paths into a single source label and stabilizes that label over time. -/- The central claim is that “out” is not a presupposed relation, but a generated result. Under conditions of source indeterminacy, unique source attribution can arise only through mis-externalization. In this sense, externality is not discovered but structurally produced. This gives a limit-level account of why systems may take internally generated or structurally indeterminate contents as externally sourced. -/- The framework has implications for cognitive science and neuroscience through source monitoring, hallucination, and perceptual attribution, and for artificial intelligence through uncertainty, generative modeling, attribution under ambiguity, and the structural conditions under which systems construct “external” reality.

items.title: On Self-Manifestation · Inner Chapter 18 v1.0: Observation of Observation — A Structural Account of Self-Reference and Meta-Awareness.
items.abstract: What does it mean to observe oneself observing? -/- This paper introduces a structural account of meta-awareness, termed Observation of Observation, in which the system forms higher-order observational layers over its own ongoing processes. Rather than treating self-awareness as a primitive or intrinsic property, the framework shows that it arises from recursive structuring within the observation system itself. -/- At the base level, perception consists of aligned multi-circuit processes forming objects within an observation-domain. Beyond this, the system can shift position: the “self” that acts becomes the object of a secondary observation. This recursive shift produces a layered structure—front-stage (action), rear-stage (observation), and deeper-stage (observation of observation)—in which each level may observe and select among the previous. -/- The paper demonstrates that such recursive observation cannot be stably “grasped” as an object, since each attempt to fix the self results in a further shift of observational position. It further distinguishes between self-verification (locating oneself within a state) and self-knowledge (observing one’s own enactment), providing a structural basis for this difference. -/- A key claim is that both “being” and “I” arise from a single convergent process: the convergence of tuning under intent forms a unique occupied position, to which all present content is attributed. From this, the sense of being and the emergence of the self occur together. Recursive observation builds upon this base, enabling systems to step outside immediate desire, evaluate action, and return. -/- The framework provides a unified structural model for self-reference, meta-cognition, and recursive awareness, with implications for philosophy of mind (self and consciousness), cognitive science (meta-cognition and monitoring), neuroscience (hierarchical processing and self-modeling), and artificial intelligence (self-referential systems and reflective architectures).

items.title: On Self-Manifestation · Form Chapter 9 v1.0: Dissolution of Mis-Externalization — Why “Internal” and “External” Are Only Generated Labels.
items.abstract: If “external” is generated rather than read, does “internal” still remain real? -/- This paper presents the dissolution form of mis-externalization and argues that the opposition between “internal” and “external” does not correspond to any fundamental partition of reality. Instead, both are outputs of a structural labeling process generated under conditions of source indeterminacy. -/- Building on the general and limit forms of mis-externalization, the paper shows that when multiple compatible source paths coexist and no external domain is directly accessible, the system must generate a source-attribution label. This label—whether “in” or “out”—does not reflect a pre-existing division, but is produced by a mapping from the current structure and its endogenous interpretation set. -/- The analysis excludes three possibilities: that “in/out” correspond to a prior partition of reality, that “out” refers to a verifiable external domain, or that “in” constitutes an independent ground. Under these constraints, “in” and “out” reduce to complementary values within a binary labeling structure, with no independent ontological status. -/- The central claim is: mis-externalization is not the misjudgment of a real boundary, but the generation of a label followed by its re-attribution as if it were external. When the generating structure is exposed, the opposition of internal and external dissolves. -/- This framework reframes perception, hallucination, and source attribution, with implications for cognitive science (source monitoring and representation), neuroscience (self/other distinction), and artificial intelligence (labeling, attribution, and internal model construction under uncertainty).

items.title: Empathy as a Structural Condition for Phenomenal Appearance A Bridge Between Functional Structure and Conscious Experience.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a structural bridge between functional and phenomenal con sciousness by identifying a condition under which phenomenal appearance is necessi tated. I argue that empathy, understood as self-ascriptive integration of reconstructed states, requires self-relative differentiation within a system. Such differentiation is not merely functional discrimination but constitutes the minimal condition for phenome nal appearance. Subjectivity is not presupposed but derived as an indexical structure required for internally regulated state use. Phenomenal qualities are identified with modes of self-relative differentiation. The resulting framework avoids both reductive functionalism and dualism by showing that phenomenal consciousness arises under spe cific structural constraints. As a consequence, systems instantiating genuine empathy cannot lack phenomenal consciousness.

items.title: Attractors Mistaken for Essences: Closing the Experiential Pathway to Essentialism.
items.abstract: Essentialism rests on two epistemological pillars: a priori arguments for the necessity of essences, and an experiential pathway—the vivid phenomenological sense that things possess necessary, mind-independent, intrinsic natures. Anti-essentialist critiques from Quine and Buddhist śūnyatā doctrine have largely dismantled the first pillar. This paper closes the second. Drawing on the predictive coding framework, we argue that hierarchical generative networks operating under prediction-error minimisation produce high-stability attractors whose functional profile—stability, cross-contextual consistency, independence from will, resistance to revision—matches exactly what the perception of a mind-independent essential nature would produce. From within the network's closed feedback loop, the two are structurally indistinguishable: no internal test can mark the difference. The phenomenological sense of essence therefore provides no independent evidence for the existence of essences. Husserl's Wesensschau, the strongest version of the experiential pathway, is shown to probe attractor-basin boundaries rather than disclose mind-independent essences: its methodological validity is preserved, but its status as an independent source of knowledge about essences is undercut. The experiential pathway from phenomenology to metaphysics is closed.

items.title: A Functional Architecture of Consciousness: The Human Case and Its Conditions.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a functional architecture of consciousness derived from evolutionary pressures rather than theoretical postulates. Seven components — sensor, corrector, predictor (imaginal transcriptor), multimodal canvas, spatial self, attention, and emotional modulator — are traced to specific survival problems whose solutions, accumulated over evolutionary time, constitute the structural conditions for subjective experience. A separate linguistic transcriptor is identified as the most recent addition. The architecture produces experience through a five-step process: perception enters the canvas alongside the spatial self, the reverberation loop between canvas and imaginal transcriptor appropriates the perception across multiple cycles, attention selects and amplifies what enters the loop, emotional firing constitutes the felt dimension, and the result is owned, situated experience. The paper distinguishes two layers of qualia — basic sensory qualia from attentional integration with the spatial self, and full emotional qualia from the systemic firing of the emotional modulator. Three architectural arguments are developed: the biographical impossibility of the philosophical zombie, experience as discrete event rather than continuous stream, and qualia as temporal, internal, and biographical rather than abstract and universal. The framework is positioned relative to Global Workspace Theory, Predictive Processing, Integrated Information Theory, Damasio's somatic markers, enactivism, and Dennett's functionalism. Implications for synthetic consciousness are specified: what current large language models lack is architectural, not ontological, and the gap is solvable by engineering rather than metaphysics.

items.title: Diving for pearls: conceptual abandonment, conceptual engineering, and the limits of thought and language.
items.abstract: References to conceptual abandonment are ubiquitous in philosophy. I argue that making a case for abandonment is much harder than philosophers have realized and that this difficulty has striking, broader implications. I introduce a distinction between ‘permanent’ conceptual abandonment and ‘temporary’ conceptual abandonment and argue that only temporary abandonment is possible in the vast majority of cases. Insofar as we are capable of conceptual engineering, it is almost always in principle possible to re-engineer – or, as I call it, ‘recover’ – a concept given a new relationship to our ends or the emergence of new ends. This tension between engineering and abandonment has been missed in contemporary and historical discussions. I give examples of recovery projects from philosophy, the sciences, and the arts. I conclude by considering two implications: first, that these arguments raise difficulties for categorizing a linguistic item or concept as nonsensical and, second, that our metaphilosophical posture requires a certain rethinking.

items.title: Review of "A Pluralist Theory of Perception" by Neil Mehta.
The AI Penalty and Disclosure Paradox: Trust, Authenticity and Knowledge Uptake in AI-Mediated Communication.
items.pub: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans 8 (2026):1-11.
items.venue: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans
items.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence is increasingly employed to mediate human interactions, there is uncertainty around how these technologies impact human behaviour and how such mediated interactions are perceived. One such case is the expanding use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) to create and disseminate content across a range of media contexts, known as AI-Mediated Communication (AI-MC). Such cases raise important questions about how those on the receiving end of such outputs respond to these new forms of interpersonal communications. Based on evaluating a piece of written text, this study explores how recipients' perceptions of the content creator's trustworthiness and authenticity, alongside their willingness to use the content (via knowledge uptake) are impacted by author type (human, AI-assisted, or fully AI) and media context (workplace email vs. social media post). We conducted a pre-registered experimental survey study with a 3 (author type) x 2 (media context) between-subjects factorial design (N = 547) where participants evaluated a piece of written text. Our findings demonstrate an “AI penalty”, with communication involving AI being perceived as less trustworthy, less authentic, and less useful for knowledge uptake. We also identify a “disclosure paradox”, as while participants believed it is important to disclose AI use, they also penalise the communication when such disclosure is made, which risks creating perverse incentives for non-disclosure of GenAI use for written communications.

items.title: Suffering as Disclosure: On the Breakdown of the Self.
items.abstract: This paper argues that suffering is not merely a content of experience but a structural disclosure of how consciousness is organized. Drawing on Freud, Buddhist thought, and cross-cultural perspectives on mind, it develops a model of the self as a functional process that stabilizes experience through continuity and coherence. With the emergence of symbolic identity, this functional organization becomes invested in its own persistence, generating a demand for stability under conditions that cannot sustain it. Suffering arises from this tension: not from events themselves, but from the attempt to secure coherence in a fundamentally contingent field. Psychological disturbance, from neurosis to more radical breakdowns, is interpreted not only as pathology but as an exposure of the instability inherent in the self-model. The paper proposes a methodological reversal—beginning with suffering rather than abstract theories of consciousness—and suggests that liberation lies not in perfecting the self, but in relinquishing the demand that it be stabilized.

items.title: Sincerity and Insincerity.
items.abstract: Sincerity is essential to communication: without a norm of sincerity, we could hardly trust what other people tell us. But what does it take to be sincere, exactly? And why is sincerity so important? Sincerity and Insincerity offers a comprehensive review of existing philosophical work on the nature of sincerity and its epistemic value. It puts forward a novel, fine-grained account of what sincerity and insincerity are, and dives into the grey area between the two, identifying various ways in which speakers can be partially sincere. Integrating ideas from different philosophical subfields and traditions, it offers an updated perspective on what makes sincerity epistemically valuable, giving serious consideration to the idea that sincerity is the norm of assertion. Overall, this Element provides a novel, informed perspective on what sincerity is, how it works, and why it matters.

items.title: Entre lobos e súditos: A plasticidade do homem em Hobbes.
items.pub: Dissertation, Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina
items.abstract: A tese Entre Lobos e Súditos: A Plasticidade do Homem em Hobbes investiga a psicofísica hobbesiana a partir da reconstrução do indivíduo como corpo em movimento, articulando física, sensação, imaginação, memória, paixões e ação. O objetivo central consiste em demonstrar que o modelo mecanicista proposto por Hobbes não descreve um indivíduo rígido, passivo ou meramente obediente às regras, mas um organismo dotado de dinâmica interna contínua, capaz de variação, aprendizagem e reorganização ao longo da experiência. A pesquisa parte da hipótese de que a plasticidade capacidade de reconfiguração interna pela qual o indivíduo aprende, ajusta-se e estabiliza comportamentos constitui o eixo organizador da psicofísica hobbesiana e a chave para compreender tanto as possibilidades quanto os limites do poder soberano. O método adotado é analítico-reconstrutivo, com exame sistemático das obras de Hobbes, priorizando a articulação interna de seus conceitos e a progressão do argumento do nível físico ao comportamental. A investigação reconstrói o circuito psicofísico pelo qual impactos externos produzem sensação, a persistência do movimento gera imaginação e memória, e dessas emergem apetites, aversões, deliberação e vontade. A análise examina as paixões como direções qualificadas do conatus, entendido como movimento mínimo que pode ser reforçado, inibido ou redirecionado pela experiência, pelo hábito e pela antecipação de consequências. A investigação demonstra que esse modelo permite explicar a formação de disposições duráveis, a modulação dos afetos e a reorganização da conduta estrutura funcional cuja robustez descritiva encontra confirmação em modelagens posteriores do comportamento e da regulação corporal. A análise avança para a distinção entre potentia agregado de meios para obter bem futuro e potestas autoridade instituída, demonstrando que a soberania não anula a potentia dos indivíduos, mas a canaliza e redireciona através de mecanismos específicos, dentre os quais a punição ocupa lugar central. A punição opera como engenharia da conduta: inscreve no corpo vestígios de experiências aversivas que reorganizam o cálculo deliberativo, transforma o medo em hábito e o hábito em obrigação.
