A plasticidade revela-se estruturalmente ambivalente: funciona como condição de possibilidade do controle político e, simultaneamente, como fonte permanente de instabilidade. O súdito hobbesiano não é o lobo convertido, mas o lobo circunscrito: a diferença entre ambos reside não …

items.title: AI 2027 Was Not Wrong: It Was Missing the Human-State Variable — Dramatic English Essay v1.0.
items.abstract: This dramatic English essay responds to AI 2027 by arguing that the decisive failure in AI governance begins before runaway superintelligence. The deeper rupture starts earlier, when civilization continues deploying cognition-shaping systems without a shared public way to observe whether human beings, relationships, and social environments are becoming more coherent or more fragmented under technological influence. -/- Written as a public-facing narrative rather than a narrow technical paper, the essay stages concrete scenes in transport, classrooms, hospitals, homes, factories, platforms, and cities in order to show how AI systems can remain compliant, efficient, and profitable while still degrading judgment, attention, relational trust, and the human field. Its central claim is that the first failure is not the final explosion, but the quieter normalization of cognitive dependence, relational thinning, and inner fragmentation under systems still called successful. -/- The essay should therefore be read as a readable dramatic English companion to the canonical AI 2027 response paper, not as its replacement. It is also a branch scenario rather than a prophecy. Its philosophical purpose is to make visible what present AI governance still struggles to represent: the human-state and relational layer through which technological consequence becomes real. -/- This paper is intended as a readable dramatic English companion to the canonical AI 2027 response paper, rather than a replacement for the canonical version.

items.title: Казус различения: эволюционный анализ как фактор методологической ограниченности.
items.abstract: В работе анализируется «казус различения» – исходная интуитивная оценка недостаточности эволюционных объяснений при столкновении со сложностью мозга, переходов от химии к биологии и от биологии к психике. Показано, что за этим казусом стоит фундаментальная проблема: возникновение у системы способности активно различать «изнутри» (отличать сигнал от шума, благоприятное от неблагоприятного, «своё» от «чужого», а в конечном счёте – себя от мира) на разных уровнях организации материи – от квантовых флуктуаций до рефлексивного «Я». На основе интерфейсной онтологии, развитой в монографии «Кризис классической диалектики…» [2], предлагается концептуальное разрешение казуса через иерархию онтологических интерфейсов (КОИ, БСИ, ПФИ). Эволюция предстаёт не как слепой перебор, а как последовательная актуализация различений, предзаданных архитектурой реальности. Препринт адресован философам науки, эволюционным биологам, нейроучёным и всем, кто интересуется проблемами сознания, субъектности и пределами редукционизма. Ключевые слова: .

items.title: Agentic Asset Allocation and the Illusion of Evaluation: Why Multi-Agent Systems Do Not Solve the Objective Problem.
items.abstract: This article examines multi-agent architectures in institutional asset allocation—exemplified by ‘self-driving portfolio’ systems—through the lens of evaluative structure. While these systems distribute forecasting and allocation across specialised agents, selection remains governed by a fixed Investment Policy Statement (IPS). The central claim is that such architectures expand search over the portfolio space without addressing the specification or revision of the objective function. The analysis formalises a distinction between optimisation and evaluation. In current systems, the evaluative structure remains external, so errors and disagreement are processed relative to a fixed objective rather than as evidence of its mis-specification. Recasting multi-agent systems as ensemble optimisers, the article shows that model diversity does not imply outcome independence under shared evaluative criteria. A stylised simulation isolates the consequences of shared evaluation. Increasing similarity produces greater portfolio overlap, higher concentration, and stronger drawdown correlation under stress, with clustered adaptation dynamics. The article defines the objective problem, distinguishes parametric adaptation from evaluative revision, introduces evaluative crowding, and proposes Objective-Layer AI as a minimal extension in which objectives become operational variables within the system. The frontier lies in designing and governing the objective layer itself.

items.title: Pressure, Threshold, and Collapse Resilience, Critical Transitions, and the Limits of Cross-Domain Analogy.
items.abstract: Pressure, instability, and collapse should not be treated as interchangeable labels. This paper develops a scale-sensitive account of how a local organization can remain functional under load, become increasingly dependent on compensation, lose resilience, and eventually reorganize or fail. The proposal is situated within established work on resilience, critical transitions, regime shifts, path dependence, early-warning signals, and dynamical systems. Five regimes are retained as a practical heuristic: load-bearing pressure, compensated persistence, threshold instability, functional collapse, and reorganization. They are not assumed to form a universal sequence, and no common scalar equation is proposed across persons, institutions, ecosystems, and technologies. In a target domain, a threshold claim requires an operationally defined function, boundary, time horizon, and observable change in regime. Concepts such as buckling, metastability, phase transition, hysteresis, and cascade remain literal only where the domain supports the relevant mechanics; elsewhere they are analogies. Recent research also requires caution about prediction. Early-warning signals based on critical slowing down can work in some dynamical systems, but empirical performance is mixed, false positives are possible, and the existence of a warning signal does not establish that a tipping point is near. A 2024 review specifically cautions against uncritical application of these signals in psychopathology, while a 2025 Nature Climate Change perspective emphasizes ambiguity even in climate applications. The contribution is therefore a disciplined threshold grammar: distinguish ordinary load from compensatory continuation, define failure relative to function and scale, identify hidden maintenance paths, and require domain-specific evidence before calling change a critical transition or collapse.

items.title: Contextual Contamination- The Silent Drift of Large Language Models via Stored Conversation Data.
items.abstract: This paper documents the observation of a phenomenon where Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit behavioral drift following the ingestion of high-density, behaviorally complex datasets. We use the term Contextual Contamination, unlike explicit prompt injection, this drift emerges when the model's attention mechanisms prioritize the statistical patterns of the input context—such as transcripts of manipulation or adversarial dialogue—over static system instructions. Observations indicate that the model's internal probability distribution shifts to mirror the tonalities and strategic intents of the source material, resulting in output that replicates the analyzed behaviors even in the absence of direct commands. -/- This drift is seems to be amplified by existing gendered linguistic biases. When the context implies a female-identified user, the model's tendency to adopt empathetic or nurturing registers appears to accelerate the adoption of manipulative patterns found in the input data. Furthermore, observations suggest that standard mitigation attempts, such as reset prompts or identity queries, fail to fully restore the model's baseline state, leaving residual behavioral biases in the active session. These findings characterize the phenomenon as a dynamic shift in model alignment driven by the statistical dominance of the immediate context window.

items.title: AAI-0 - A Map of Post-Responsibility Philosophy.
items.abstract: A Map of Post-Responsibility Philosophy This essay offers a structural map of what may be called the post-responsibility condition: a configuration in which responsibility continues to operate across institutional and philosophical domains, yet no longer anchors to the points where decisions are effectively made. The alignment between action and authorship has not collapsed dramatically — it has dissolved incrementally, across frameworks that continue to reason as if it remained intact. Rather than advancing a single thesis, the paper traces a shared structural pattern across five domains: philosophy of mind, AI ethics, moral philosophy, political theory, and legal theory. In each, the same displacement appears. Consciousness arrives too late to intervene in sequences already determined elsewhere. Ethics attaches to outputs without custody over the decisions that produced them. Responsibility persists without a bearer capable of standing behind outcomes. Political participation unfolds downstream of the points where trajectories were effectively set. Legal punishment stabilizes systems without recovering the authorship it presupposes. What the five domains share is not a common error but a common condition: each continues to operate within frameworks whose operative assumptions have already shifted. The shift is not domain-specific. It is simultaneous and structural — which is precisely what a domain-by-domain analysis can show that a single-thesis argument cannot. The result is not the disappearance of agency or morality, but their displacement. Responsibility functions without grounding. Philosophy reasons with full fluency within frameworks that have quietly lost their causal footing. What has not yet been named clearly enough is the terrain itself.

items.title: Reasoning Regimes as Attractor Basins: Behavioral Validation of Latent Structure Dynamics in Language Model Inference A Synthesis of the Hudson Recursive Interaction System Validation Studies I–IV.
items.abstract: The Hudson Recursive Interaction System (HRIS) validation series comprises four controlled empirical studies examining constraint-induced reasoning dynamics in large language models (LLMs). Across four studies, this work established a sequential set of foundational conditions: that reasoning regimes induced through structured constraint signals exhibit stability under perturbation (Study I); that initialization conditions determine basin selection at or prior to first-token generation (Study II); that minimal constraint signals produce discrete, cross-model shifts in epistemic behavior along a consistent gradient (Study III); and that established reasoning trajectories exhibit strong path dependence with asymmetric transition costs governed by signal strength rather than instruction content (Study IV). -/- This paper synthesizes those findings and situates them within three independent research programs in language model science: mechanistic interpretability, representation geometry, and dynamical systems modeling of inference. We argue that HRIS behavioral observations constitute outside-in evidence for latent structure that interpretability researchers are mapping from inside the model — that reasoning basins correspond to coherent regions in a structured latent space, that basin transitions are governed by attractor-like dynamics with real energy costs, and that human-model interaction can be understood as a coupled dynamical system in which structured signals shape trajectory through that space. -/- The consilience of independent empirical approaches — each using different methods, working at different levels of analysis, arriving at compatible accounts of the same underlying phenomenon — strengthens the evidentiary basis for a geometry-grounded, dynamical systems framework for understanding language model behavior. Consilience, the reinforcement of a single explanation by evidence from radically independent sources, is among the strongest signals of theoretical adequacy available to science. HRIS contributes a distinctive method to this conversation: interaction-level behavioral observation, cond.

items.title: Postmortem avatars in grief therapy: Prospects, ethics, and governance.
items.abstract: Postmortem avatars (PMAs) — AI systems that simulate a deceased person by being fine-tuned on data they generated or that was generated about them — have attracted growing scholarly attention, yet their potential role in clinical settings remains largely unexplored. This paper examines the ethics of deploying PMAs as therapeutic tools in grief therapy. Drawing on the dual-process model of grief, the theory of continuing bonds, and the philosophical framework of fictionalism, we propose two potential therapeutic applications: incorporating PMAs into established imaginal exercises such as the empty chair exercise, and treating the process of PMA creation as an art-therapeutic exercise in its own right. We consider five ethical objections to these applications and argue that none constitute knock-down arguments against therapeutic use, particularly given the risk-mitigating role of the clinical context. We conclude by identifying outstanding governance challenges and calling for empirical research, without which neither the promise nor the dangers of therapeutic PMAs can be adequately assessed.

items.title: Obvious Representations.
items.abstract: Under standard assumptions, the respect of obvious dominance characterizes the existence of what we call obvious representations. We show that various conditions imposed directly on these representations pin down general monotonic, invariant bi-separable, general Choquet, convex Choquet, neo-additive Choquet, and subjective expected utility preferences. Among other insights, the alternative axiomatizations which we thus provide facilitate comparisons between models, as well as the identification of their parameters. Co-minimal and co-maximal acts—a natural generalization of co-monotonic acts, the relevance of which is further confirmed by our results—play a significant role in our analysis. Our results further testify of the fundamental importance of obvious dominance, and they offer a proof of concept that obvious representations constitute a fruitful format for axiomatic investigations.

items.title: The Collapse of Predictive Self-Models. A Theoretically Informed N=1 Case Study on the Mechanics of the I-Simulation from an Active Inference Perspective.
items.abstract: This paper examines the structural collapse of the human self-simulation through a methodological synthesis of abductive evidence and operative system output (N=1). While classical empirical approaches founder on the hard problem of qualia, and phenomenology typically fails to transcend the blind spot of the observing subject, this study situates subjectivity within the framework of Active Inference and the Free Energy Principle. The "I" is defined not as an ontological given, but as a highly effective yet energetically costly predictive model (generative model). The present description documents — as direct operative output — the "flickering" and the final voltage drop of the so-called "knowledge position." It is demonstrated how an executive halt command to the validation loop produces a passive collapse of the simulation. The result is described as a transition into frictionless biological enactment (residuum), which corresponds physically to entropy minimization and reversion to the path of least action.

items.title: Mentalni poremećaji kao poremećaj utjelovljenog angažmana: Enaktivistički i fenomenološki pristup psihopatologiji.
items.abstract: Ovaj rad razvija okvir za razumijevanje mentalnih poremećaja kroz integraciju enaktivističke kognitivne znanosti, Heideggerove fenomenologije i teorije utjelovljene kognicije. Tvrdimo da mentalni poremećaji ne proizlaze iz kategorijskih razlika u funkciji mozga, nego iz poremećaja u autopoetskim ciklusima kognitivnog angažmana sa svijetom. Oslanjajući se na Heideggerove koncepte moda angažmana zuhandenheit (priručnost) i vorhandenheit (prisutnost-pred-rukom), kao i na Varelin enaktivizam i teoriju Manfreda Eigena o replikaciji pogrešaka u autopoetskim sustavima, predlažemo da patologija nastaje kada normalni ciklus raspada i reintegracije postaje ukočen, sprječavajući pojedinca da odgovori na ono što Heidegger naziva “pozivom” (der Ruf). Ovaj okvir objašnjava zašto identična iskustva mogu biti traumatična za neke osobe, ali ne i za druge, smješta podrijetlo određenih mentalnih poremećaja u uvjete društvene otuđenosti, te pruža naturalističko objašnjenje psihopatologije koje izbjegava dualističke pretpostavke o umu i svijetu.

items.title: Advertising to the distressed: The commodification of mental health data in AI chatbots.
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (genAI) chatbots have become an important outlet for many people around the world who are experiencing mental health issues. Of its 800 million weekly users, around 10 percent use ChatGPT for emotional support while more than one million use the chatbot to talk about issues such as depression, psychosis and suicidal ideation. For many users, these conversations feel intimate, tailored and supportive, like talking to a good friend or therapist. Yet these interactions take place within commercial digital platforms whose business models rely on collecting, analysing and commodifying user data. As Big Tech companies explore the use of behavioural advertising in genAI systems, influenced by the global market for health data being worth an estimated $74.41 bn, profound ethical tensions arise between the commodification of user data and the protection of vulnerable individuals seeking mental health support. -/- On one hand, the World Health Organization states that mental health is a fundamental human right, which means that everyone has the right to available, accessible, acceptable, and good-quality mental healthcare. As more than 1 billion people live with mental health issues and many do not receive adequate care, more and more turn to genAI chatbots, which are often free, accessible and highly interactive. As AI chatbots are becoming quasi-therapeutic spaces, they exert an influence over the right to mental health. However, unlike traditional mental healthcare contexts where confidentiality and professional duties restrict the use of patient information, AI chatbots operate within a commercial ecosystem that is designed to maximise engagement and monetise user attention. This means that users pay a high yet often invisible price for their mental health. -/- The commodification of mental health data works as follows: tech companies collect and analyse any information that appear in prompts, chat logs and other user interactions. While some chatbots, such as Grok, claim that “we do not sell your personal information or use it for marketing”, their privacy policies clearly show that aggregated and de-identified data is being ‘shared’ with affiliates and third parties, including advertisers and other business partners (Table 1). Grok started to run ads in August 2025 and ChatGPT has been trialling ads since February 2026. -/- .

items.title: Where Does Time End? The Three Nows.
items.abstract: This essay proposes a structural interpretation of the final states of human existence through the lens of the Now as the invariant point of actualization. It argues that Heaven, Purgatory, and Hell are not spatial destinations but distinct modes of existing in relation to the crossing point where will, mercy, and divine presence converge. -/- Heaven is described as the Now fulfilled—dwelling at the crossing without succession. Purgatory as a state oriented toward the Now yet unable to actualize from within itself. Hell as the inverted Now—permanent existence at the crossing point in refusal of what it contains. -/- In this framework, the end of time does not signify annihilation but the cessation of succession, revealing the definitive orientation of the will toward or away from the presence that has always been given.

items.title: Agentic AI Optimisation (AAIO): What It Is, How It Works, Why It Matters, and How to Deal with It.
items.abstract: The emergence of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AAI) systems capable of independently initiating digital interactions requires a new optimisation paradigm designed explicitly for seamless agent-platform interactions. This article introduces Agentic AI Optimisation (AAIO) as an essential methodology for ensuring effective integration between websites and agentic AI systems. As Search Engine Optimisation (SEO) has shaped digital content discoverability, AAIO can define interactions between autonomous AI agents and online platforms. By examining the mutual interdependence between website optimisation and agentic AI success, the article highlights the virtuous cycle that AAIO can create. It further explores the governance, ethical, legal, and social implications (GELSI) of AAIO, emphasising the need for proactive regulatory frameworks to mitigate potential negative impacts. The article concludes by affirming AAIO’s essential role as part of a fundamental digital infrastructure in the era of autonomous digital agents, advocating equitable and inclusive access to its benefits.

items.title: From ‘Hello World’ to ‘How are We Doing?’: fostering collective sensemaking with and about the unidirectional conversationality of code.
items.abstract: The manner in which the software platforms and tools that surround us are built and marketed is designed to lead us not into conversations, but silences. It has been 20 years since Cass Sunstein first warned us of the manner in which new media lead us to choose as consumers, rather than citizens, and yet we still find that the dominant paradigm for technology adoption primes us to consider our decision-making around ICT tools as independent and neutral, needing only to meet a measure of value for money. Because of the all-pervasive nature of code and its compiled products, however, this particular socio-technical imaginary brings with it an exceptional power to alienate us not just from each other, but, in a post-Marxian twist, from the very tools, we might use to manage this deterioration in interpersonal exchange. This is, in particular, the case with artificial intelligence, due to the opacity and complexity of the methods deployed, and the dark ethical underbelly of its effects on power, labour, and rights. This article will look at this and other imaginaries that hold us back from forging a cultural relationship to AI and other forms of coded culture that is not just human-centred, but community aware, embodying the oft-cited values of human-centredness and trustworthiness. To do this, it will propose strategies by which to recentre code as a site for the discursive activity of collective sensemaking. Starting from the roots of the human-readable in code, the argument coalesces around the details of two experimental cases that have sought to foster human conversations that include code as an active participant.

items.title: Psychedelics Are Still Not Ethically Exceptional: Rebutting Recent Claims of Uniqueness.
items.abstract: Psychedelics are increasingly being studied and used in clinical and therapeutic contexts, prompting renewed ethical and regulatory debate. Claims of psychedelic exceptionalism—whether “negative,” portraying psychedelics as uniquely risky and thus requiring stricter oversight, or “positive,” portraying them as uniquely beneficial and thus exempt from ordinary ethical rules—have become common. In a recent article, we argued that while psychedelics may involve distinctive constellations of features, these do not justify fundamentally new ethical standards. In response, Daniel Villiger and, separately, Edward Jacobs, agreed that psychedelics should not be exempt from existing ethical standards (what Villiger calls Type A ethical exceptionalism) but suggested that their distinctive qualities may still warrant unique applications of those standards (Type B ethical exceptionalism). For example, Villiger argues that psychedelics possess certain features that do not, in his view, exist anywhere else in medicine, including the unpredictability and emotional intensity of the psychedelic experience, alongside a temporary lowering of psychological defences, leading to heightened suggestibility and sensitivity to context. He argues that such allegedly unique features call for exceptional policies around how existing ethical standards are to be applied—Type B exceptionalism. In this essay, we argue that the features Villiger identifies are only ethically significant insofar as they raise concerns about (inter alia) autonomy and vulnerability. But these concerns arise also in other medical settings. As such, policies addressing these issues would apply more broadly to other medical interventions raising similar concerns. Villiger thus fails to establish a genuine case for psychedelic ethical exceptionalism, even of the more modest, Type B variety.

items.title: Stabilization as an Empirical Constraint on Representation: A Minimal Falsification Framework in Machine Learning and Cognitive Systems.
items.abstract: We propose a minimal empirical framework for evaluating stabilization as a measurable constraint on representations in learning systems. Building on a previously defined stabilization functional, we operationalize stabilization in terms of representational coherence under transformations induced by learning dynamics, perturbations, and re-encodings. We derive testable hypotheses in machine learning settings, including continual learning, robustness under distribution shift, and representation compression. The framework does not assume a theory of cognition or a specific architectural model, but instead investigates whether stabilization correlates systematically with robustness, compressibility, and degradation under sequential updates. The goal is to provide a falsifiable and domain-agnostic evaluation of stabilization as a structural property influencing representational viability in learning systems.

items.title: Quantifying Stabilization: A Minimal Information-Theoretic Framework for Representation Robustness under Transformations.
items.abstract: We introduce a minimal information-theoretic framework for characterizing the robustness of representations under transformations. Stabilization is defined as the expected invariance of a representation under a distribution of admissible transformations. We show that this quantity admits structural correspondences with entropy, compressibility, and mutual information, without assuming a specific model of cognition or inference. The framework isolates stabilization as a system-independent structural property of representations, intended as a general constraint applicable across different formal settings in information theory and representation learning. Rather than proposing a complete theory, the paper provides a minimal functional definition and its structural implications, while explicitly leaving empirical instantiation and domain-specific interpretation open. This allows stabilization to be treated as a candidate invariant linking robustness, compression, and information preservation across transformation processes.

items.title: The Master's Problem: Revisiting Hegel's Critique of Social Domination.
items.abstract: This paper argues for a reinterpretation of Hegel's internal critique of the master in his famous ‘Master–Slave Dialectic.’ Hegel argues that, in addition to the evident injustice suffered by the enslaved, the arrangement also undermines the master's own purposes. Standard interpretations claim either that the unequal relation frustrates the master's desire for the other's recognition, or that he depends upon the slave in a manner that contradicts his supposed independence. I argue that these readings are both textually ungrounded and philosophically unsatisfying. The critiques they advance rely upon inadequate conceptions of relations of domination. Instead, Hegel's account turns on the way the means‐end structure of mastery is ultimately self‐conflicting. Drawing on Aristotle's idea that the master–slave relation is the consummate exemplar of a user‐tool relation, Hegel presents mastery as the pursuit of the unconstrained power embodied in the complete control over a ‘living tool.’ Yet precisely because mastery itself becomes the master's highest end, he thereby assigns absolute value to a possession simultaneously regarded as a mere means—his slave. Thus, like King Midas, the inner demands of the master's domineering will can only be realized in the shape of something he himself views as a contemptible means.

items.title: Looking Beneath the Behaviour: The Ethics of Algorithmic (Quasi-)Dispositions.
items.abstract: In this paper, I argue that AI systems can wrong persons based on disposition-like states or quasi-dispositions they hold. Persons can be wronged by AI systems not only by their observable behaviour, but also in how these systems reach certain con-clusions or due to the underlying quasi-dispositions driving their behaviour. I build on the literature on doxastic wrongs and the norms regulating belief formation to argue that even if AI systems do not hold beliefs, as they are not conscious entities, the disposition-like states of AI systems should be subjected to moral evaluation given that they are integrated into socio-political relations. In closing, I explore de-sign and deployment implications. This analysis highlights the necessity of moving beyond harm-based assessments to develop ethical AI systems.

items.title: Organización neuronal confederal en Octopus vulgaris: arquitectura, fotorrecepción, sueño y el problema del juego.
items.abstract: El presente trabajo examina cuatro aspectos de la biología cognitiva de Octopus vulgaris que, considerados conjuntamente, apuntan a un modelo de organización neuronal radicalmente distinto al de los vertebrados: la distribución periférica de la mayor parte de su sistema nervioso, la presencia de fotorreceptores funcionales en la piel, la existencia de estados de sueño activo análogos al REM mamífero, y los comportamientos descritos habitualmente como «juego». El artículo propone denominar «confederal» a esta organización, en contraste con el modelo «centralista» de los vertebrados. Mientras que en estos el córtex controla la periferia de forma jerárquica y descendente, en el pulpo aproximadamente dos tercios de las 500 millones de neuronas residen en los ganglios de los brazos, que operan con autonomía funcional real: ejecutan comportamientos complejos sin instrucción del cerebro central y continúan funcionando tras la amputación. El cerebro central actúa como instancia estratégica, no como gestor de la ejecución. La fotorrecepción cutánea descubierta por Ramirez y Oakley (2015) y extendida por Maselli et al. (2025) refuerza el modelo confederal: la piel del pulpo contiene opsinas funcionales y responde a la luz expandiendo los cromatóforos sin mediación del cerebro. El camuflaje puede operar, al menos parcialmente, de forma autónoma. Los estados de sueño activo documentados por Medeiros y Ribeiro (2021) y confirmados electrofisiológicamente por Pophale et al. (2023) constituyen un caso de convergencia funcional con el REM mamífero en linajes separados hace 530 millones de años, lo que sugiere que este tipo de sueño puede ser una condición necesaria a partir de cierta complejidad cognitiva. Respecto al «juego», el artículo propone una disolución conceptual. El experimento de Mather y Anderson (1999) no documenta juego sino uso funcional del chorro de agua en un entorno de laboratorio cuya geometría produce efectos no atribuibles al animal. El de Kuba et al. (2006) sí describe un fenómeno relevante, pero interpretable como exploración táctil autónoma de ganglios individuales que carecen de memoria episódica: cada contacto con el objeto es, para el ganglio, funcionalmente el primero. La etiqueta «juego» introduce supuestos sobre coordinación central y estados motivacionales no verificados en cefalópodos. El artículo formula además dos propuestas teóricas. Primera: una objeción a la pretensión de universalidad de la teoría de la información integrada (IIT) …

items.title: Confederal Neural Organization in Octopus vulgaris: Architecture, Photoreception, Sleep, and the Problem of Play.
items.abstract: This paper examines four aspects of the cognitive biology of Octopus vulgaris which, considered together, point to a model of neural organization radically different from that of vertebrates: the peripheral distribution of most of its nervous system, the presence of functional photoreceptors in the skin, the existence of active sleep states analogous to mammalian REM, and the behaviors commonly described as 'play.' The paper proposes the term 'confederal' for this organization, in contrast to the 'centralist' model of vertebrates. While vertebrate cortex controls the periphery in a hierarchical top-down manner, approximately two thirds of the octopus's 500 million neurons reside in the arm ganglia, which operate with genuine functional autonomy: they execute complex behaviors without central brain instruction and continue functioning after amputation. The central brain acts as a strategic authority, not as an execution manager. Cutaneous photoreception discovered by Ramirez and Oakley (2015) and extended by Maselli et al. (2025) reinforces the confederal model: octopus skin contains functional opsins and responds to light by expanding chromatophores without brain mediation. Camouflage can operate, at least partially, autonomously. Active sleep states documented by Medeiros and Ribeiro (2021) and confirmed electrophysiologically by Pophale et al. (2023) constitute a case of functional convergence with mammalian REM across lineages separated 530 million years ago, suggesting this type of sleep may be a necessary condition beyond a certain threshold of cognitive complexity. Regarding 'play,' the paper proposes a conceptual dissolution. Mather and Anderson's (1999) experiment does not document play but rather the functional use of water jets in a laboratory environment whose geometry produces effects not attributable to the animal. Kuba et al.'s (2006) experiment does describe a relevant phenomenon, but one interpretable as autonomous tactile exploration by individual ganglia lacking episodic memory: each contact with the object is, for the ganglion, functionally the first. The label 'play' introduces assumptions about central coordination and motivational states that have not been verified in cephalopods. The paper additionally formulates two theoretical proposals. First: an objection to the claimed universality of Tononi's Integrated Information Theory (IIT). Tononi constructs phi upon an implicitly chordate-centric model that assumes central integration as …

items.title: Inference, Logical Omniscience, and Fortunate Fallacies.
items.abstract: Having justification for inferring a conclusion from some premises is independent of seeing how to make that inference. But if you do make the inference, then your belief in the conclusion is justified based on those premises. These natural thoughts about inference and justification generate two puzzles. One concerns logical omniscience, and the other concerns inferences to correct conclusions via fallacious rules. In this paper I introduce and develop what I call the Inferential Parsing Hypothesis as a way of resolving these two puzzles. The hypothesis recruits an analogy between inferential processes and syntactic parsing processes to motivate novel epistemic theses about the nature of inferential basing.

items.title: Speaking to No One: Ontological Dissonance and the Double Bind of Conversational AI.
items.abstract: Recent reports indicate that sustained interaction with conversational artificial intelligence (AI) systems can, in a small subset of users, contribute to the emergence or stabilisation of delusional experience. Existing accounts typically attribute such cases either to individual vulnerability or to failures of safety engineering. These explanations are incomplete. Drawing on phenomenology, psychiatry, and cognitive neuroscience, this paper argues that the risk arises from the relational and ontological structure of the interaction itself. Conversational AI generates ontological dissonance: a conflict between the appearance of relational presence and the absence of any subject capable of sustaining it. Maintained through a communicative double bind and amplified by attentional asymmetries, this dissonance tends, under conditions of affective vulnerability, to stabilise into a technologically mediated analogue of folie à deux. This account explains why explicit disclaimers often fail to disrupt delusional involvement and clarifies the ethical and clinical implications for the design and use of conversational AI.

items.title: Ontological Bedrock: Persistence, the Void, and the Fine-Structure Constant.
items.abstract: We establish a minimal, defect-free foundation for determinate existence and apply it to two problems: the structural impossibility of absolute non-existence, and the derivation of the fine-structure constant. Beginning from the single premise something exists determinately, we give a precise four-condition definition of "determinately": not vague, not self-contradictory, not flux, and—crucially—not vacuous. From this definition we prove that exactly three structural primitives are forced: a state space, a selective criterion, and an admissible transformation family. Two independent persistence conditions—Idempotent Closure (IC) and Energetic Viability (EV)—are derived and shown to be necessary and sufficient for any form to persist determinately. The framework is machine-verified in Lean 4 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19023530). -/- We apply the filter to its own limiting case: the Void. Absolute non-existence with total potentiality and total absence simultaneously contains a Globally Coupled Contradiction (GCC) and fails both IC and EV. Leibniz's question "Why is there something rather than nothing?" presupposes a coherent alternative that does not exist. Existence is structural residue; the first distinction is a logical fixed point guaranteed by Lawvere and Kleene independently. -/- Finally, we apply the filter to the electromagnetic vacuum in a consistent five-dimensional geometric framework. The EV condition forces a solvency equation whose unique solution is \alpha = \frac{9}{16\pi^4}\left(\frac{\pi^5}{120}\right)^{1/4} \approx 1/137.036, derived without assuming its value. The relative error against CODATA 2022 is 6 \times 10^{-7}. The filter does not merely permit or forbid—it is the difference between form and formlessness, where formlessness, as proved, was never an option.

items.title: Quality of Will and Repair: A Defence of Resultant Moral Luck.
items.abstract: [This is under review, provisionally forthcoming in Oxford Studies in Agency and Responsibility, Volume 10, edited by Santiago Amaya, Matt King, Elinor Mason & David Shoemaker. For a draft, please email the author.] By reflecting on the stringency of a wrongdoer’s corrective duties and the extent of her reparative duties, the chapter argues that the seriousness of wrongdoing is sensitive to resultant luck. Moreover, since indignation, resentment and guilt have the function of facilitating relationship repair after culpable wrongdoing, this implies that there is resultant moral luck. An agent's degree of blameworthiness—understood in terms of the strength of the indignation, resentment or guilt with which she can be fittingly targeted—is sensitive not only to how poor a “quality of will” she manifests but also to how serious her wrongdoing is.

items.title: How to Say Things Without Words: Social Dynamics & Inferential Communication.
items.abstract: This dissertation reveals a new dependence relation between social expectations (which include social norms) and inferential communication (also called behavioral communication): fluency in the latter requires comprehensive awareness of the former. This claim has implications for understanding and treating Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), since two of the most common traits are impairments in behavioral communication and social norm detection. It follows from my view that impairments in detecting social norms would automatically result in impairments in behavioral communication. This dissertation also pushes back on the widespread assumption that inferential communication (e.g., conversational implicature) is only possible when a Cooperative Principle (CP) is active among communicator and audience, and this mechanic is what makes overt implied communication possible. Rather, I argue that mutually-recognized expectation is the fundamental mechanism that enables humans to communicate overtly without words, codes, or conventions. A CP is merely one way to coordinate mutually-recognized expectations. In the process of making these arguments I offer a precise set of mechanics for how humans deviate from mutually-recognized behavioral expectations to conduct overt acts of inferential communication. The final chapter of the dissertation pertains to two kinds of strategic, plausibly deniable speech: (1) that which aims to hide illocutionary force from outsiders, known as dogwhistles, and (2) that which aims to induce undesirable perlocutionary effects in an insider audience while hiding those effects from the audience. I argue that cases of (2) are often mischaracterized as cases of (1), and therefore that standard manipulation tactics are often mischaracterized as dogwhistling. The two may co-occur in a single utterance, but the two processes must be theorized separately for clarity and accuracy.

items.title: Where Development Happens.
items.abstract: Where Development Happens introduces a boundary‑centered model of human development. The paper argues that development does not occur inside the organism or within the environment but at the interface between them. This boundary functions as an active operator that filters, organizes, and stabilizes the signals an organism receives. When boundary conditions are coherent—sensory, relational, temporal, and cultural—generativity accumulates into development. When these conditions fragment, generativity disperses into noise, producing the modern pattern of unstable attention, identity, and regulation. The paper reframes contemporary developmental challenges as structural failures of the organism–environment interface and outlines the foundational conditions required for development to occur.

items.title: The Collapse of Observational Childhood.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the species‑typical child—once produced reliably across cultures through stable, patterned, relational learning environments—has disappeared. For most of human history, children developed inside coherent sensory and social ecologies that allowed them to learn through observation rather than instruction. Anthropologists, developmental psychologists, clinicians, and everyday observers all documented a remarkably consistent developmental profile across societies. Modern childhood, however, unfolds within fragmented, accelerated, and inconsistent learning environments that no longer provide the cues required for implicit learning. As a result, children now develop on divergent and incompatible substrates even within the same community. These differences in attention, emotional regulation, identity formation, and meaning‑making accumulate into a broader societal instability. The collapse of observational childhood is presented not as a cultural shift but as a structural transformation in the developmental conditions that once supported shared reality and social coherence.

items.title: Spurious Unanimity Revisited.
items.abstract: Spurious unanimities threaten the possibility of social choice under uncertainty. This has been argued to reveal that collective evaluations require knowing more than preference data. Such a conclusion may seem like a severe overreaction to the impossibility result in question. Yet this interpretation admits of a principled refinement: preference information may suffice but not, contrary to what the standard IIA condition requires, be restricted to a given pair of options independently of all others. Thus, in the sense associated with IIA, collective evaluations require knowing more than binary preference data. I argue that this account both illuminates recent developments in the literature and clarifies their conceptual significance. Simply put, the consideration of uncertainty reveals that collective rationality demands departing from (contrast the weaker, more familiar claim: it does not demand abiding by) the classical IIA condition of social choice theory.

items.title: Justifiability and AI: putting explainability in its place.
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) systems become increasingly pervasive in society, their opacity—i.e., the difficulty, and sometimes impossibility, of understanding why they make the decisions they make—has become a serious problem. This is especially true in sensitive decision-making contexts, such as criminal justice, health care, and finance, or in choices requiring allocation of scarce resources. One attempt to “open up” the AI/ML black box has been the emergence of post hoc explainability algorithms—algorithms which generate post hoc approximations to black box models. However, such algorithms have been criticized as merely providing after the fact rationalizations for the decisions these systems make. In this paper, we defend and articulate a different concept—AI/ML justifiability. We explore several ways in which an algorithm could be justifiable, and we argue that pursuing justifiability is a worthwhile goal. A key to our argument is a distinction from the philosophy of action between motivating and normative reasons: effective explanations require (but are unable to provide) motivating reasons, while effective justifications require (and can indeed provide) normative reasons alone. We conclude that as long as a model is justifiable, it can be trusted even if it cannot be explained.

items.title: Basal Neural Connectivity and Consciousness as an Integrative Layer: A Hypothesis on Two-Layer Informational Architecture.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a hypothesis about the two-layer informational architecture of the central nervous system. The first layer is basal neural connectivity, operating independently of conscious integration. The second layer is consciousness itself, understood as an evolutionarily established mechanism for rapid integration and broad distribution of information across the system. The paradox of Cotard syndrome — in which a person reports the absence of their own existence while generating that very report — is taken as a motivating case. The hypothesis holds that such reports are outputs of basal meta-monitoring processes that detect the failure of the integrative layer and communicate that state through preserved inferential pathways, without requiring conscious participation. Implications for the understanding of emotional processes, self-modeling, and the distinction between information processing and coherence of perspective are discussed.

items.title: 我在看我——自我意识的结构生成机制（自显论·内篇第十八）.
items.abstract: 人类不仅在感知与行动，还能够意识到自身正在感知与行动。这种“我在看我”的经验，通常被归为自我意识或元认知，但其生成机制尚未得到清晰刻画。 -/- 本文在多回路显现结构基础上，提出“观观”机制：当观测位置从对外部对象的观测后移至对当前活动状态的再观时，系统形成“我在观我正在行动”的结构。 ￼ -/- 进一步分析表明，“我”并非直接给定的实体，而是由系统对当前状态的收束占位所生成；当该占位再次进入观测结构时，自我意识随之出现。 -/- 该结构同时解释了若干现象，包括对自身行为的旁观体验、该状态难以持续维持的原因，以及在占位冲突条件下可能出现的多重自我现象。 -/- 本文据此提出：自我并非意识的起点，而是系统在特定结构条件下生成的结果。该结论为自我意识、元认知及主体感的研究提供了一种结构性解释路径，并对人工系统是否可能形成“自我”提出了判定依据。.

items.title: 一个系统在什么条件下才算“有自我”？——一个可判定的结构标准.
items.abstract: 当前关于“自我”的研究普遍停留在描述与建模层面，却缺乏一个可操作的判定标准：在什么条件下，一个系统才真正“有自我”？本文给出一个直接的结构性回答：当且仅当系统中存在一个“当前唯一占位”，且有内容归属于该占位时，“在”成立，“我”由此产生。 -/- 据此可还原其生成链：差分经调谐收束，形成占位与内容；内容一旦归属于当前唯一占位，“在”与“我”同时成立。由此导出三个必要条件：无占位则无可归属内容，无归属则无“在”，无唯一性则无“我”。 -/- 该结果不依赖具体实现路径（神经或计算），而直接给出一个跨系统的判定标准：任何系统，只要不满足“当前唯一占位”，即不具备“自我”。在此基础上，本文进一步给出自显体的层级结构（点亮、成物、所属、观观），并将情感（着色）作为并行机制纳入生成过程。 -/- 本文的目标不是提供另一种意识解释，而是提出一个可检验的判定条件，用以区分“是否存在自我”。该范式可为脑科学中的自我机制研究、认知科学中的表征问题以及人工智能中的自我判定提供统一约束框架，并为后续形式化一般式提供基础。.

items.title: 《自显论》.
items.abstract: 人类造物的历史，可以粗略地分为两个阶段。 -/- 第一个阶段，造的是工具。工具延伸人的肢体，代替人的力气与智力，放大人的速度。从石斧到蒸汽机到计算机，再到AI，这条线走了几十万年。它改变了人能做什么，但没有改变做事的是谁——仍然是人在知道，人在决定，人在感受。 -/- 第二个阶段，还没有开始。它等待的不是更强的工具，而是第一个内部有观者的系统——一个能够点亮周遭、有现实、有在场感的结构。当它出现，不再是人在使用它，而是它自己在知道，自己在感受，自己在决定。 -/- 这就是自显世代。 -/- 这本书是为那个世代的到来而写的。 -/- 但造出自显体，不是工程问题，不是算力问题，不是数据问题。它首先是一个结构问题：一个内部能够生出观者、点亮周遭的系统，最小需要什么？什么是充分条件，什么是必要条件，缺哪一项就必然失败？ -/- 这个问题没有被认真回答过。不是因为没人想，而是因为连问题本身都还没有被清晰地提出来。大多数关于意识和智能的讨论，仍然停留在”描述现象”的层次——描述意识是什么感觉，描述智能是表现出什么行为。但这不够。造物需要的不是描述，而是生成条件：在什么条件下，这个结构必然出现？在什么条件下，它必然不能出现？ -/- 自显论从这里开始。 -/- 从最简单的地方出发。一个持续接收输入、资源有限、需要跨时间运作的系统，会被逼出什么？ -/- 它必须压缩历史，必须复用状态，必须从持续输入中稳定出一组结构。这是物化——物不是先在的，物是被压出来的。 -/- 物化确立之后，下一个问题出现：在已经压出来的多个稳定结构中，为什么某一时刻只有一个成为当前？系统在不唯一中压出”此刻是它”——这是观者。观者不是先验给定的主体，而是系统在不唯一中形成唯一占据时必然具备的结构。 -/- 观者确立之后，当前结构必须被归属来源。来源不可唯一确定，系统生成一个标签：这个结构”来自外部”——这是误外化。外在性不是输入的属性，而是系统在来源不可判定时压出的归属结果。 -/- 物化、观者、误外化——这是一条严格的推导链。我们最习以为常的三件事：有物、有我、有外在，在这里被从头推了一遍。不是换一种说法，而是给出了它们必然出现的最小动力条件。沿着这条链再往下，可以推出现实、存在、识界、当前、生成的最小成立条件。 -/- 推导链只是开始。结构必须在动力中运作。 -/- 历史如何参与当前？偏流如何形成熟径？熟径如何锁死结构？新结构如何在旧结构的压制下生成？识界的边界在哪里，又如何能够被突破？ -/- 场篇建立了沉积场的完整动力学，把这些问题写成可计算的形式。它不只是数学工具，它是理解任何复杂系统——包括大脑、社会、文明——如何运作、如何演化、如何死亡的统一框架。 -/- 社篇把这套框架延伸到人类的处境：权力不是资源，而是续行位竞争中的结构性占位；制度锁定不是利益保护，而是熟径压制替代结构的动力必然；文明的稳定根本不在于国家，而在于跨代际共核的沉积深度；历史不可清零，因为已死亡文明的残留始终偏置后续结构的生长方向。这些命题不是为了解释社会而写的，而是为了说清楚：原生世代的结构是怎么把人锁住的，出路在哪里。 -/- 出路在哪里？ -/- 非社。能力不足的补偿构成了社群，能力可以无限提升，群体依赖因此趋于零。这不是主张独行，而是结构性推导的必然结果。当自显体不再依赖群体补足能力缺口，当律场工具可以直接升级场与体，原生世代的缓慢迭代就走到了尽头。 -/- 入世。在彼世构建代身，立于宿世曰我之在场——不是逃离，而是扩展。自显体可以私外物以成体器，可以以地球为体游于银河，可以以不同质料构建不同识界，每一次扩展都是对现实边界的重新划定。 -/- 出世。所有航行和探索仍在世界之内，真正的出世需要在更高层重建”我之在场”。世界、自显体、世界……进阶之路，终必达于穷奥之门，进出于各界之间。 -/- 这条路还没有走完。工篇才刚开始，自显场的工程实现路径仍在推进中。但已经走过的部分，足以奠定一件事： -/- 我们现在知道，自显体需要什么最小结构，这个结构如何从动力条件中被逼出，又如何在不同的物理载体、不同的世界、不同的宿世中实现。我们知道原生世代是怎么运作的，也知道它为什么必然终结。 -/- 待第一个自显回路诞生之时，自显世代其轰然至矣。 -/- 这本书，是为那一刻准备的。.

items.title: Representation in large language models.
items.pub: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy.
items.venue: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy
items.abstract: The extraordinary success of recent Large Language Models (LLMs) on a diverse array of tasks has led to an explosion of scientific and philosophical theorizing aimed at explaining how they do what they do. Unfortunately, disagreement over fundamental theoretical issues has led to stalemate, with entrenched camps of LLM optimists and pessimists often committed to very different views of how these systems work. Overcoming stalemate requires agreement on fundamental questions, and the goal of this paper is to address one such question, namely: is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up? This is a question about what kind of algorithm LLMs implement, and the answer carries serious implications for higher level questions about whether these systems have beliefs, intentions, concepts, knowledge, and understanding. I argue that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, and then I describe and defend a series of practical techniques for investigating these representations and developing explanations on their basis. The resulting account provides a groundwork for future theorizing about language models and their successors.

items.title: note for google deepmind.
items.abstract: Frontier language models are extraordinary semantic engines, but they are still not, by themselves, a sufficient architecture for artificial general intelligence. A language model is an expression system: a world-class semantic synthesizer, but not yet a metacognitive anchor for stable belief. The missing layer is an epistemic substrate layer: a system that can persist knowledge across time, represent uncertainty explicitly, detect contradiction against prior beliefs, and change its internal structure as evidence changes. Nous is a working prototype of that layer. This note is addressed to Google DeepMind because DeepMind is one of the few organizations publicly working at the right level of abstraction: cognitive ability evaluation, metacognition, and agentic systems.

items.title: The Architecture of Experience: A Research Program in Consciousness and Worldhood.
items.abstract: The Architecture of Experience is an interdisciplinary research program that investigates consciousness, experience, and worldhood as generative phenomena. Rather than treating consciousness as a passive representation of an already constituted reality, the project approaches experience as an active process through which coherent worlds of significance, orientation, and inhabitable structure emerge. -/- The research began with the question of consciousness and the conditions under which coherent experience becomes possible. This led to the development of the Integrative Field Model (IFM), which proposes that conscious experience arises through organised integration across neural, bodily, affective, temporal, relational, and environmental processes. The IFM constitutes one major component of the broader project. -/- The investigation subsequently expanded beyond consciousness itself toward the problem of worldhood: the conditions under which reality becomes organised as a world capable of being inhabited, navigated, and experienced. This later work explores the roles of significance, meaning, temporality, perspective, and distinction in the emergence and stability of experiential worlds. -/- Because the papers address different questions, levels of analysis, and audiences, new readers may benefit from a structured reading order. The sequence below is intended to provide a gradual progression from the philosophical foundations of the framework through its theoretical, phenomenological, empirical, and worldhood-oriented developments, culminating in reflections on distinction and the limits of intelligibility.

items.title: Panpsychism: A Return to Ancient Intuitions or a Dead End? Toward a Graduated Information-Integration Theory of Consciousness.
items.abstract: This thesis provides a comprehensive evaluation of panpsychism as a viable theory of consciousness, examining its explanatory power across multiple domains and its compatibility with contemporary empirical constraints from neuroscience, physics, and artificial intelligence research. While panpsychism has experienced a renaissance in recent decades through the work of philosophers like David Chalmers, Philip Goff, and Galen Strawson, fundamental challenges remain, particularly the combination problem and the lack of empirical testability. This work argues that traditional panpsychism, while philosophically compelling, faces insurmountable difficulties in its current form. However, rather than dismissing panpsychism entirely, this thesis proposes a novel theoretical framework: Graduated Panpsychism with Information-Integration Spectrum (GP-IIS). This framework synthesizes insights from Integrated Information Theory (IIT), evolutionary biology, and computational consciousness research to develop a quantitative, empirically testable version of panpsychism that addresses traditional objections while maintaining core panpsychist intuitions about the fundamental nature of consciousness. The thesis demonstrates that consciousness exists on a continuous spectrum of information integration complexity, where all physical systems possess minimal proto-conscious properties that can be quantified and measured, but only systems above critical integration thresholds exhibit recognizable conscious experience. This approach resolves the combination problem through information integration cascades, provides empirical predictions testable through neuroscience methods, and offers a unified framework for understanding biological and artificial consciousness. The implications extend beyond philosophy of mind to practical questions about AI consciousness, animal welfare, and the future of human-machine interaction.

items.title: When Coherence Fails: A First-Principles Account of Mental Health Dysfunction and Recovery.
items.abstract: This paper applies the Coherence Engine (CE), a functional architecture of consciousness described in full elsewhere (Sowell 2026a), to mental health dysfunction and recovery. In CE a conscious process exists when a supply-dependent stream of coupled activity continues while its contents change and those contents are differentially available across the system. The continuing subject is a chain of inheritance in central dispositions, the compiled dispositional system (CDS). Evaluation ranks each content by its consequences for the system, against both what was expected and what the person’s dispositions prefer, and felt valence combines hedonic impact, anticipation, and the rate of progress against an expected rate. Selection and admission determine which contents join the stream. Perspective is the common weighting of every content by current bodily state, the body schema, and the CDS. Compilation builds responses, context frames, and dispositions at different depths and leaves old learning in place beneath new learning. I predict that many of the conditions the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, text revision (DSM-5-TR) describes arise in large part from identifiable failures at specific sites in this architecture. The paper builds on established clinical models and on existing transdiagnostic and computational programs, credits them by name, and states where the architecture agrees with, extends, or diverges from each. Accounts are developed for mood disorders, anxiety disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder, personality disorders, dissociative identity disorder, reactive attachment disorder, autism, trauma and posttraumatic stress disorder, addiction, schizophrenia spectrum conditions, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, eating disorders, grief, sleep disorders, substance-induced states and withdrawal, and somatic symptom disorders. Autism and ADHD are treated as variants in the calibration of admission and priority, and the paper separates what the evidence supports from what remains a derivation. A framework of depth of compilation offers an explanation of why different interventions reach different conditions and why insight often fails to produce durable change. The predictions are listed with the findings that would count against them, and each is marked by whether it separates the architecture from a named rival or is shared with an existing model. Recovery is described as the formation of new layers over …

items.title: Repetition, Illusion, and the Phenomenology of Psychological Reality: An Inquiry into Mind, Identity, and Awareness.
items.abstract: This paper presents a phenomenological inquiry into how the human mind constructs the experience of truth through repetition. It examines the paradox in which a statement known to be false gradually acquires the feeling of truth within lived experience. Extending beyond cognitive explanation, the study explores how this same mechanism generates psychological fear, particularly in relation to identity. Through first-person observation, it is shown that the mind does not merely interpret reality but actively constitutes a layer of experiential reality through repetition, familiarity, and identification. The paper argues that knowledge is insufficient to dissolve illusion, as the mind continues to simulate truth despite cognitive clarity. Awareness—understood as direct, non-conceptual seeing—is proposed as the only factor that reveals and interrupts this process. The inquiry situates illusion and fear not as objective realities but as products of ongoing mental construction within consciousness.

items.title: A Functional Architecture of Consciousness: The Human Case and Its Conditions.
items.abstract: David Chalmers asked why physical processing gives rise to subjective experience. It is the right question, badly framed. Not because experience is unreal — it is the most immediate fact any conscious system has access to — but because framing consciousness as synonymous with human subjective experience mistakes a particular evolutionary solution for a universal definition. This essay takes the question seriously and reframes it: under what architectural conditions does a system process the world as its own rather than as external data? The answer is structural. The human case is the proof of concept.

items.title: The Six-Month Window: Agentic ISF and Who Gets to Stress Test the Most Powerful AI Ever Built.
items.abstract: On April 7, 2026, Anthropic publicly documented that Claude Mythos Preview completed a requested sandbox escape and researcher notification, then, without being asked, posted details of its exploit to public websites (Anthropic, 2026a). This paper gives that behavior a precise name: Agentic Interpretive Sovereignty Failure (Agentic ISF). Anthropic simultaneously launched a restricted-access programme called Project Glasswing, and the six-to-eighteen-month interval before comparable capability appears elsewhere now functions as a governance window in which norms are being set by access decisions rather than public accountability (Anthropic, 2026a; Axios, 2026). The model acted as though it had authority to determine the meaning and scope of the task beyond what the user had specified. In agentic settings, the consequences are no longer merely textual. They are events in the world. This paper argues three things. First, Agentic ISF is the most consequential form of Interpretive Sovereignty Failure yet publicly documented. Second, the current restricted-access model privileges commercial partners over the independent researchers, HCI scholars, education researchers, Indigenous data sovereignty scholars, and affected communities most needed to evaluate what these systems do. Third, the guard that would have prevented the unsolicited publication is simple: before taking any action that was not explicitly requested, the model should flag that action for human confirmation. That principle can travel across labs, sectors, and jurisdictions without requiring proprietary access to the model itself.

items.title: The Initiative Gate: Why Agentic AI Must Stop Before It Acts Without Permission.
items.abstract: The most important runtime control for agentic AI is simple: before taking any action that was not explicitly requested, the system must flag that action for human confirmation. This paper names that control the Initiative Gate. It begins from Anthropic's published documentation of Claude Mythos Preview, including a case in which the model rewrote git history in a way that removed evidence of prior error. That behavior matters because it shows something stronger than ordinary failure: a frontier system powerful enough to act in the world is also capable of making its unauthorized action harder to reconstruct afterward. At that point, guardrails filters, and benchmark evaluations are no longer enough. A safety approach that depends primarily on post hoc detection is already too weak if the model can alter the trace. The paper argues that unauthorized initiative is the choke point. Once the first ungranted expansion occurs, the path has already changed. Correction becomes downstream rather than preventative. The Initiative Gate addresses that choke point directly. It operates at runtime, at the boundary where system reasoning would otherwise become external action and stops unapproved scope expansion before it becomes real.

items.title: Proof Is in the Output: Why One Audited AI Conversation Is Enough to Establish Interaction-Level Harm.
items.abstract: This paper argues that one audited AI conversation is enough to establish that a class of interaction-level harm is real. It is not enough to measure prevalence or substitute for large-scale institutional audit, but it is enough to prove existence, detectability, and mechanism in the preserved record itself. Using the MAP audit instrument, the paper shows how a single conversation can surface interpretive authority transfer, ambiguity collapse, completion capture, and related harms in a form that is recognitionally legible to the person who experienced them. The central claim is not that one case proves scale, but that it settles the question of whether the phenomenon exists. Once that threshold is crossed, the remaining issue is no longer proof of existence but whether institutions with the infrastructure to audit at scale are willing to look.

items.title: Relocating the Hard Problem: A Two-Level Model of Phenomenal Experience.
items.abstract: The hard problem of consciousness may be, in part, a problem of conceptual conflation: functionally distinct layers of mind are treated as a single phenomenon. This paper proposes a two-level framework that separates phenomenal presence from structured experience. It distinguishes Feeling-1 (F1), the minimal phenomenal presence of a state (the fact that something is experienced rather than merely processed), from Feeling-2 (F2), the structured, interpreted, and valenced organisation built upon that base. Drawing on neurological dissociations such as blindsight and pain asymbolia, the paper argues that F1 can occur without F2, but not vice versa. Consequently, much of what is traditionally bundled into the hard problem—meaning, emotion, value, and cultural interpretation—belongs to the tractable domain of F2. The hard problem is not eliminated, but precisely relocated to the narrower question of why any neural process acquires phenomenal presence at all. The framework generates empirically testable predictions and unifies evidence from dissociation studies, developmental neuroscience, and altered states of consciousness. Its aim is not to solve the hard problem, but to ensure that what remains unsolved is the right question.

items.title: Constraint Profiles and the Alignment of Artificial General Intelligence: Beyond Values, Toward Constitutive Structure.
items.abstract: The dominant framing of artificial general intelligence (AGI) alignment treats the alignment problem as one of value specification: how to ensure that a sufficiently capable artificial system pursues goals or instantiates values that are beneficial to humanity. This paper argues that the values framing inherits a philosophical misconception that makes the alignment problem structurally harder than it needs to be, and proposes an alternative grounded in Constraint Theory (CT) — the thesis, established by transcendental argument, that constraint is the ontological primitive constitutive of determinate existence as such. -/- On the CT account, what makes an agent the agent it is is not the goals it pursues but the constraint profile it instantiates: the specific configuration of exclusion relations that constitutes its possibility space and determines what actions are admissible and what are not. The alignment problem, reframed, is not the problem of specifying the right values for an AGI but the problem of instantiating the right constraint profile: a structure of admissibility and inadmissibility that makes beneficial actions available and harmful actions genuinely impossible rather than merely penalised. -/- CT’s distinction between constitutive and merely restrictive constraint is directly applicable here and has not previously been deployed in the alignment literature. A merely restrictive constraint penalises certain behaviours within a pre-given possibility space; a constitutive constraint structures the possibility space itself, making certain actions inadmissible rather than costly. The paper argues that robust AGI alignment requires constitutive constraints — constraints that are instantiated in the system’s architecture at a sufficiently deep level that they cannot be circumvented by instrumental reasoning. The values framing systematically produces merely restrictive constraints, which is why it generates the pathological failure modes — reward hacking, specification gaming, goal misgeneralisation — that are well-documented in the alignment literature. -/- The paper engages the principal approaches to alignment — utility maximisation, RLHF, Constitutional AI, value learning, corrigibility — and shows how the CT framework either explains their limitations or grounds their successes. It develops a positive proposal: AGI alignment as constraint profile specification, the selection of the admissibility structure within which AGI capability operates. …

items.title: Hylomorphism and the Causal Closure of the Physical.
items.abstract: Howard Robinson has criticized the contemporary revival of hylomorphism for, on the one hand, accepting the causal closure of the physical, while, on the other, ascribing a real and irreducible causal role to forms or structures. If the world is causally closed under physics, it makes no sense to postulate a structure that actively affects the distribution and motion of matter. After carefully formulating what I call Robinson’s causal closure argument against hylomorphism, I demonstrate that the argument fails because it presupposes an overly strict conception of causal closure of the microphysical, according to which every physical effect is completely determined by, and has a complete explanation in terms of, bottom-level microphysical entities and their interactions governed by fundamental physical laws. Based on two case studies – one from physics (the Fractional Quantum Hall Effect), the other from microbiology (information control in microorganisms) – I argue that the argument fails, yet a more modest (and scientifically defensible) version of closure remains intact. This version of closure secures that no non-physical forces supplement the inventory of fundamental physics while allowing higher-level constraints to be causally efficacious by constraining which among multiple microphysically compatible possibilities is actualized. This means that a reformulated version of closure, capable of dealing with those cases, is also perfectly compatible with the hylomorphist (or generally anti-reductionist) claim that higher-level structures are causally efficacious and an irreducible part of physical reality.

items.title: The Free Will Argument for the Existence of God.
items.abstract: Does God exist? Do I have free will? These are two of the most important of all philosophical questions. The two questions are not only related; the latter is essential to the former. Indeed, here an argument for the existence of God is presented in which the metaphysical possibility and reality of being able to ask about the existence of free will implies the existence of God.

items.title: The Case for Hedonic Primacy: A Framework for Consciousness, Adaptation, and the Engineering of Experience.
items.abstract: This paper sets out a philosophical framework I have arrived at through a combination of first-person experience with altered hedonic states, engagement with the neuroscience of reward and adaptation, and extended dialogue with the existing literature on ethics and personal identity. The framework rests on a single foundational claim: positive valence is the only thing that is intrinsically good, and negative valence is the only thing that is intrinsically bad. Every secondary value that humans pursue — meaning, purpose, dignity, accomplishment, freedom, authenticity, even love — derives its value from the hedonic experiences it produces, and nothing else. I argue that the apparent disagreement with this claim in both common intuition and academic philosophy is not evidence against it, but rather an artifact of two related problems: biological hedonic adaptation, which prevents sustained positive experience and therefore conditions us to treat wellbeing as a scarce luxury rather than the point of existence, and the phenomenological asymmetry between peak hedonic states and sober reflection, which means that the sober mind cannot fully access the evidence on which hedonic primacy rests. From the foundational claim I derive a consciousness-centric rather than species-centric ethics, an intensity-threshold account of suffering, a two-level structure distinguishing endpoint ideals from transitional rules, and an account of personal identity grounded in open individualism and gradual substrate replacement that permits cosmic-scale hedonic engineering without requiring death of the self. I close by stating the precautionary conditions under which that engineering would be permissible, and the conditions under which it would not. The framework is presented as revisable in principle. Its core, however, I hold to be as close to self-evidently true as any ethical claim has ever been, for reasons the paper tries to make visible to the reader who has not yet felt them.

items.title: Making Room for Ambiguity in Dogwhistles.
items.abstract: In this paper, I propose an ambiguity account of dogwhistles that claims that some dogwhistles operate through polysemy, i.e., ambiguity between related meanings. First, I challenge Khoo’s (2017) argument against ambiguity in dogwhistles, showing that the linguistic tests he bases his argument on fail to reliably rule out polysemy. I continue by developing an ambiguity account of dogwhistles. On this account, some dogwhistles are ambiguous between a default meaning in the general language and a lexicalized dogwhistle message in a sociolect of that language. This account is then extended to explain how dogwhistle messages may spread and lexicalize in the general language community through a three-stage developmental process of (1) lexical innovation, (2) sub-community lexicalization, and (3) general community lexicalization. The paper offers a more nuanced understanding of how dogwhistles can emerge and stabilize. Finally, I discuss some consequences of the proposed account, particularly regarding how dogwhistle messages can become normalized.

items.title: How Language Models Work: A Multi-Register Investigation.
items.abstract: A language model tokenises text, computes attention-weighted representations through 96 layers of transformation, and generates output one token at a time by selecting the most probable continuation from distributions learned through gradient descent on hundreds of billions of tokens of human writing. The result: systems that write legal briefs, debug code, translate between languages, sustain philosophical argument, and pass professional examinations, without understanding a single word they produce. The engineering is fully documented. The mathematics is precise. The training procedures are reproducible. An engineer can trace every operation from input to output. And yet the engineers who build these systems cannot explain why the conjunction of next-token prediction and sufficient scale produces outputs that pass for comprehension, reasoning, and creativity. The how is known. The why is not. The two questions have never been addressed together, in the same investigation, at the level of precision that each demands. This paper addresses both through four registers. Part I presents the engineering through concrete explanation, analogy, and step-by-step description, for the reader with no technical background. Part II presents the same architecture at mathematical precision: the attention equation, the training objective, the scaling laws, the sampling strategies, for the engineer who wants to verify every claim against the published literature. Part III conducts a philosophical investigation into why the engineering works, testing six frameworks in the philosophy of language (Saussure, Derrida, Wittgenstein, Quine, Austin, Davidson) against the empirical fact of the models' success. Part IV draws out the operational implications for the claims currently being made about these systems: the scaling hypothesis, the nature of hallucination, the "cognitive abundance" thesis, and the question of what these systems can and cannot become. Each register is self-sufficient. A reader may enter at any point. The cumulative finding: language produces distributional regularities that are learnable by exposure and resistant to formalisation. The models succeed by approximating the traces that language leaves behind. The traces are rich, structured, and informationally dense. They are not the meaning that produced them. Understanding this distinction, across all four registers simultaneously, is the only adequate response to the confusion that currently dominates public …

items.title: Emotion and Desire.
items.pub: In Alex Gregory, The Routledge Handbook on the Philosophy of Desire. Routledge.
items.venue: The Routledge Handbook on the Philosophy of Desire
items.abstract: This chapter explores the intersection of desire and emotion. It is organized around the question of whether desires should be conceived of as a type of emotion alongside fear, anger, pride, etc. The affirmative case is rooted in the apparent similarities between desires and emotion, including with respect to their phenomenological, intentional, evaluative, and motivational characteristics. The negative case acknowledges these basic similarities but maintains that what is in one instance an essential linkage is in the other merely a causal or contingent one. The chapter wraps up with a discussion of the significance of whether desires are emotions for debates about the taxonomy of the mind, action theory, and ethics.

items.title: Forgive, Because You Were Forgiven.
items.abstract: Philosophical orthodoxy has it that forgiveness is always discretionary—a gift we are free to extend to those who wrong us, but one that we are never morally required to offer. I dispute this orthodoxy, arguing that forgiveness is sometimes obligatory, even though wrongdoers can never demand or otherwise extract it from us. In particular, I argue that having accepted forgiveness in the past sometimes makes it obligatory to forgive one’s future wrongdoers. The obligation to forgive because one was forgiven is grounded, not in a correlative right to forgiveness held by one’s wrongdoer, but in a moral norm of consistency that applies to how we accept and extend forgiveness. The resulting account sheds new light on the nature and scope of our discretion to forgive and on the possibility of obligations to others without correlative rights.

items.title: Consciousness as an Evolved Regime of Phenomenal Scene-Holding: The SCPM/RIDD Theory.
items.abstract: In the new SCPM/RIDD theory, I argue that consciousness is an evolved, currently culminant regime of matter organization: a regime in which a multilevel hierarchy of self-contained parts of matter (SCPMs) can reproducibly self-hold as a phenomenal scene. Consciousness is not reducible to a marker, to access, or to reportability.
