In SCPM/RIDD, phenomenality is not introduced as an additional property over and above functional architecture, but is understood as the very realization of a causally integrated regime of scene-holding on the window Δt. Evolution is understood here as the long-term increase in the diversity of connection types, in the system’s capacity for their selective assembly, holding, uncoupling, and reorganization, and, as a consequence, in the number of levels of organization. Evolution is therefore treated as a process of structural increase and retuning of connectedness. In this context, “culminant” is understood in a strictly operational sense: not as a teleological goal of evolution or as evaluative superiority, but as indicating a regime in which, at the present stage, the line of increasing diversity of connection types, causal density, and selective retunability is most strongly expressed. SCPM provides an operational language for describing self-contained parts of matter through boundaries, channels of exchange, and relative causal autonomy. The phenomenal scene is understood as a temporary causally integrated coalition of SCPM-images within a multilevel hierarchy of SCPMs on the window Δt, organized around a dominant image-anchor and centered by bodily indexation. I formulate the mechanism of its reproducible holding as RIDD / nested RIDD: a multilevel dynamic of recurrent integration and directed discharge. Consciousness, accordingly, is specified not by a single indicator but by a vector of regime parameters, r(Δt) = (A, TI, M, R, D, L), which makes it possible to describe scene stability, regime reorganizations, and trajectories of degradation. The article draws a central distinction between scene integrity and access/reportability: phenomenality belongs to the very holding of the causally integrated scene on Δt, whereas report is a special case of symbolic directed discharge. On this basis, the article formulates discriminating predictions and the D0–D4 program, through which the theory accepts empirical risk and becomes distinguishable from competing approaches. In conclusion, the article shows how SCPM/RIDD reframes the …

items.title: Spontaneous Awakening Following Near-Death Experience: A Longitudinal Case Study with Consumer EEG Documentation.
items.abstract: This longitudinal case study documents the phenomenological and neurophysiological trajectory of a single subject following spontaneous awakening subsequent to a near-death experience in June 2022. Data sources include structured phenomenological self-report, longitudinal consumer-grade EEG recordings obtained via Muse S headband and Mind Monitor application, and theoretical analysis drawing on NDE literature, Kundalini and spiritual emergency frameworks, and Jeffrey Martin's Persistent Non-Symbolic Experience Locations Model. The case presents anomalous features relative to standard PNSE location descriptions, including preserved emotional range and intensity at advanced stabilization markers, which are examined through a proposed distinction between conditioned emotional reactivity and unconditioned affect. Consumer EEG methodology is evaluated as a longitudinal documentation instrument. Findings are discussed in relation to existing consciousness research literature and their implications for clinical differentiation of spiritual emergence from pathological presentations.

items.title: Emergent Virtues: Assessing a Class of Virtues.
items.abstract: On neo-Aristotelian accounts, moral virtues are often defined as dispositional traits to think, act, and feel in excellent ways, relevant to the virtue. However, not all moral virtues are dispositional traits. Some moral virtues are emergent properties that depend on both normative and non-normative traits, as well as situational features and resources available to the agent. In cases when moral virtues are emergent, several questions arise. These include how best to conceive of virtue phenomenology and the assumed predictability or habitual nature of virtue, such that one is reliably good long-term. Other questions include how moral luck features in one’s character and how to evaluate an agent’s freedom with respect to developing that property, given that emergence is contingent upon aspects of a person not squarely within their control.

items.title: Authenticity as Inner Freedom.
items.abstract: Recent work on authenticity has aimed to rehabilitate the ideal without appealing to the metaphysically and epistemologically dubious notion of the ‘true self.’ These arguments are in part genealogical: they describe the origin of the normative pressure that generates the ideal of authenticity, and then offer an account responding to that pressure without positing a true self. Making good on a genealogy which traces the ideal of authenticity to an increased emphasis on sincere self-expression in the 18th and 19th centuries, Charles Taylor (1989) and Rahel Jaeggi (2016) offer accounts of authenticity as an expressivist ideal. I propose an alternative deliberative genealogy, on which authenticity arises alongside an increase in the freedom to choose one’s own projects around the same period. This generates a requirement that expressivist accounts cannot meet: someone who is authentic is justified in thinking that she is living as she should. I argue for a novel account of authenticity without a true self, which meets the requirement of the deliberative ideal. Authenticity is a distinctive kind of positive freedom, which is achieved by taking responsibility for ongoing interpretation of the task that living a life seems to present and of the possibilities available within it.

items.title: Why AI 2027 Still Fails Without a Human-State Variable: A Response Scenario to AI 2027.
items.abstract: This paper responds to AI 2027 by arguing that the decisive failure in AI governance begins earlier than catastrophe-centered scenarios usually describe. The central problem is not only that advanced AI may become too powerful, but that institutions are already deploying cognition-shaping systems without a public framework for observing whether human beings, relationships, and social environments become more coherent or more fragmented under their influence. -/- The paper argues that AI governance remains structurally incomplete so long as it lacks a measurable representation of the human-state and relational layer through which technological consequences become real. To name this missing layer, it uses Ordered Energy (OE), Relational Energy (RE), and Entropic Energy (EE), together with the indices VCE, CRI, and CFI, as civilizational descriptors rather than metaphysical claims. -/- Written as a scenario-driven response essay rather than a prediction, the paper asks a practical philosophical question: after AI systems act, what condition remains in the human field? It concludes by outlining a consequence-sensitive governance horizon in which human-state visibility and relational observability become necessary conditions for evaluating transport, education, care, platform governance, and institutional design.

items.title: AI 2027은 틀리지 않았다: 인간 상태 변수가 빠진 문명의 조용한 실패.
items.abstract: This document is an independent Korean dramatic public scenario essay that takes the warning of AI 2027 seriously while arguing that the decisive failure begins much earlier than the final moment of superintelligent catastrophe. Its central concern is not simply that AI may become too powerful. The deeper problem is that civilization still lacks a public human-state variable through which changes in judgment, emotion, relationship, education, care, cities, platforms, and institutions can be observed, described, and governed. -/- The essay moves through scene-driven episodes involving autonomous driving, elder care, factory automation, school education, hospital systems, platform dependency, urban management, politics, economics, and the creative ecosystem. Across these settings, it shows why systems can remain rule-compliant and technically successful while still failing the human beings living inside them. In this framework, OE, RE, EE, together with VCE, CRI, and CFI, are used not as metaphysical claims but as structural descriptors for reading whether human and civilizational conditions are becoming more coherent or more fragmented. -/- This work is not a literal translation of the English public response paper. While it shares the same structural thesis, it is presented as a distinct Korean-language work that intensifies narrative pressure, sensory staging, public readability, and long-horizon civilizational branching for Korean readers. It should therefore be read as a Korean public response essay designed to make visible what current AI governance discourse still fails to see: the missing human-state variable, and the way civilization’s future begins to split once that missing layer becomes publicly legible.

items.title: Intersubjectivity as Partial Coordination: Against Shared-Content Models of Communication.
items.abstract: Contemporary theories of communication often model success in terms of shared content, shared propositions, or common ground. I argue that these shared-content models are too strong at precisely the wrong point: communication does not require that interlocutors converge on the same content in any robust sense. Yet against skeptical and deflationary alternatives, I also argue that communication is more than successful signaling, strategic adjustment, or socially stabilized response. The paper defends a middle position: \textbf{intersubjectivity as partial coordination}. On this view, communication succeeds when speakers achieve enough publicly assessable, inferentially articulated, and world-directed overlap for mutual understanding, disagreement, correction, testimony, and joint action to become possible, even though the full thickness of meaning remains non-identical across subjects. I develop this claim in three steps. First, I argue that any viable theory of intersubjectivity must satisfy three conditions: reciprocal correctability, inferential overlap, and triangulated world-directedness. Second, I show that these conditions yield a positive model of partial coordination stronger than mere behavioral coordination yet weaker than shared-content models. Third, I argue that this model explains misunderstanding, disagreement, testimony, testimonial injustice, semantic deference, and scientific communication better than its principal rivals. The result is a conception of shared intelligibility that preserves normativity and objectivity without requiring sameness of meaning or a view from nowhere.

items.title: Embodied Orientation, Reconstructive Memory, and Bias: A Cartographic Model of Temporally Extended Conscious Life.
items.abstract: This paper offers a synthetic conceptual framework for temporally extended conscious life. Its central claim is not that consciousness is literally produced by an inner cartographer, but that conscious life is structurally cartographic in a specific sense: it proceeds by selective orientation under embodied constraint, preserves usable but incomplete orientation-structures, reconstructs them in memory, and reuses them in later experience. The paper defends three connected claims. First, what is consciously available is never unconditioned possession of the outside world, but access under embodied conditions. Second, memory is reconstructive rather than replay-like. Third, bias is not merely an occasional flaw added to otherwise pure cognition, but a structural possibility that arises when reconstructed orientation becomes resistant to correction across later interactions. The paper’s principal contribution is thus a narrower one than a general theory of consciousness: it argues that memory-generated bias belongs to the ordinary temporal structure of embodied experience. The cartographic model is defended as a structural description of selective orientation, historical layering, revisability, and misleading usability. It is not offered as a genetic explanation of consciousness, and the paper explicitly marks the limits of the metaphor. The result is a position best described as corrigibility realism: access to the world is mediated and revisable, yet not unconstrained, because ongoing interaction can expose failures in orientation and support better or worse revision.

items.title: Robots and AI are not one moral category: why the distinction matters for ethical and conscious systems.
items.abstract: Calls that pair ethical and conscious AI with ethical and conscious robots may feel natural. Many contemporary robots use machine learning, and many AI systems are described in agentive terms. Yet the pairing can hide a conceptual shortcut. It quietly suggests that AI ethics and robot ethics are the same moral question applied to different shells. My claim in this opinion piece is modest but consequential: treating robotics and AI as a single moral category encourages avoidable category mistakes about where moral agency sits, where harms arise, how responsibility is attributed, and what consciousness claims could plausibly mean in deployed systems.

items.title: Coining a Slur: On the Pejoration of ‘Fake News’.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the expression ‘fake news’ has been turned into a slur: in addition to a meaning applying to pieces of information or reports, it has gained a novel slurring meaning that targets liberal journalists. To this end, the paper surveys the recent development in uses of ‘fake news’, it shows that uses of ‘fake news’ directed at people display features that are typically exhibited by slurs, and it argues that such uses are best captured by views on which the expression has become ambiguous, gaining a slurring meaning. Finally, the paper considers the process of pejoration through which ‘fake news’ was turned into a slur through a small number of highly influential uses.

items.title: Beyond The Blackboard: Alienation in the Age of AI.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly presented as a tool for improving efficiency, autonomy, and innovation in education. But what does AI mean for teachers as workers? -/- Beyond the Blackboard offers a critical examination of how artificial intelligence reshapes teaching labour, professional identity, and autonomy. Drawing on empirical research and critical theory, the book explores how AI driven systems influence teachers' control over their work, their relationship to educational outcomes, and their sense of meaning and fulfilment within institutional settings. -/- Grounded in Marxist theories of alienation and contemporary debates in AI ethics, the book analyses education not simply as a site of technological adoption, but as a workplace increasingly shaped by algorithmic management, performance metrics, and data driven governance. It challenges optimistic narratives that frame AI as inherently empowering, instead asking how structural conditions shape teachers' lived experiences of technological change. -/- Written in an accessible but academically rigorous style, Beyond the Blackboard will be of interest to scholars, postgraduate students, educators, and policymakers concerned with artificial intelligence in education, teacher autonomy, and the ethical implications of educational technology. The book contributes to ongoing discussions in educational philosophy, AI ethics, and the political economy of education by foregrounding labour, power, and alienation in the age of intelligent systems.

items.title: Towards XAI as identity protection.
items.abstract: This paper explores the fundamental question of whether data or identity should be prioritized in the era of automated decision-making, focusing on the role of algorithms in shaping human identity. In the contemporary era, big data-based algorithms function not merely as classification tools but as environmental conditions that interpret human lives and construct identities. However, extant discourse on explainable AI (XAI) has predominantly centered on functional and technical criteria, such as transparency and predictive accuracy. This focus has overlooked the role of technology as a co-author of narrative identity. This study draws upon Paul Ricoeur's concept of narrative identity and Coekelbergh & Reijers’s theory of techno-narrative co-authorship to reinterpret identity protection as a narrative and relational issue. The findings indicate that the provision of algorithmic explanations engenders a form of narrative power, thereby posing a risk of confining human identity within technical interpretive patterns. Consequently, this paper posits that XAI must be redefined as a mechanism that guarantees narrative authority, thereby allowing individuals to contest and revise algorithmic interpretations. This is particularly salient in an age of increasing technological intimacy, as exemplified by recommendation systems and conversational AI. In this context, explainability should function as an ethical institution that empowers users to co-author their identity alongside technology. By redefining privacy not as a matter of ownership or control, but as a right to self-interpretation, this research establishes a novel philosophical foundation for future information ethics and technological design.

items.title: The Explanatory Trap: Narrative Selection and the Deletion of Optimization Space.
items.abstract: Explanation requirements for high-risk AI systems are treated as disclosure obligations: costly, but neutral toward what the regulated system is. This paper argues that they are not neutral, for structural reasons. An explanation that discharges the functions governance assigns it must select: it identifies a causal path and eliminates the alternatives, because a recipient who must act on it cannot act on a distribution. Advanced optimization requires the opposite: a system that sustains performance in a non-stationary environment must revise its operating conditions, and revision needs alternatives to range over. The two demands cannot be split between separate representations. The requirement asks for a ground in the state that issues each determination, not one computable about it, and a system that learns from its own operation cannot assess an alternative it may not operate. Such alternatives are kept but denied the only evidence that could recommend them. What is lost is not performance within the space of available solutions. Explicability constraints fence a region of that space on grounds unrelated to the optimization problem, and a system whose next required state lies outside it does not reach it. Explanation requirements thus constrain which systems may exist, without having been designed to. A closing criterion sorts accountability mechanisms by whether they impose it.

items.title: Scaffold-Mediated Basin Selection After Grokking: Causal Analysis of Post-Generalization Representational Dynamics in Modular Arithmetic MLPs.
items.abstract: Neural networks trained on modular arithmetic generalize via a Fourier circuit, but their internal representations continue to evolve after generalization. We study post-grokking dynamics in a two-layer embedding MLP trained on modular addition (mod 257) and identify a metastable scaffold phase in which a shared harmonic mode (k44) dominates the embedding spectrum prior to seed-specific divergence. We report three results. First, initialization strength (FOURIER_STR) controls both the duration of the scaffold phase and the identity of the final attractor: the same seed converges to different basins under different initialization strengths, with a sharp transition between str=0.25 and str=0.5. Second, ablating the first post-collapse intermediary mode does not alter the final basin but changes the trajectory and time-to-convergence, indicating that intermediary modes are transit states rather than selection points. Third, local perturbation growth rate (LPGR) measurements at scaffold collapse show that the initial post-collapse amplifying direction is already present in the dynamics at the moment the scaffold loses dominance. In single-relay cases, this direction coincides with the final basin; in multi-relay cases, it corresponds to an upstream mode whose downstream evolution converges to the same endpoint. Together, these results support a causal ordering in which scaffold dynamics constrain the set of amplifying directions at collapse, and subsequent trajectory dynamics resolve these into a final basin. This identifies a distinct post-generalization phase in which attractor identity is determined prior to visible mode dominance and is robust to perturbations of intermediate states.

items.title: Temporal-Affective Architectures for Human-Aware AI: A Neurophilosophical Proposal.
items.abstract: This article develops a scientifically constrained philosophical proposal concerning the role of temporality in modeling human-like bias and affect in artificial intelligence. The central claim is not that temporality by itself constitutes emotion, suffering, or human subjectivity, but that a significant class of human biases and affective responses presupposes a temporally organized architecture in which duration, expectation, delay, internal-state deviation, reward trend, and temporal mismatch jointly constrain cognition and action. The argument integrates four research traditions. First, contemporary neuroscience and computational modeling suggest that subjective duration can emerge from salient perceptual change and from evolving neural states rather than from a dedicated internal clock. Second, work on temporal expectation shows that time actively structures cognition by modulating attention and the timing of working-memory utilization. Third, research on embodied and interoceptive time indicates that subjective temporality is deeply coupled to bodily and affective states. Fourth, current AI research shows both the continuing limitations of large language models in temporal reasoning and the emergence of temporal codes, homeostatic control, and temporally structured affect-like variables in reinforcement-learning systems. On this basis, the paper proposes a minimal temporal-affective architecture for human-aware AI, organized around perceptual duration, temporal expectation, temporal mismatch, internal-state control, and value-over-time. The paper concludes by distinguishing functional internal temporality from phenomenal subjectivity and by outlining a research program for building AI systems that better understand, anticipate, and respond to temporally structured human bias without reproducing human unfairness as a normative standard.

items.title: Personhood, as a Concept in Phenomenology.
items.pub: In Nicolas De Warren & Ted Toadvine, Encyclopedia of Phenomenology. Springer. pp. 1–9.
items.abstract: Rather than a monolithic or unitary concept, personhood is best approached as an open, phenomenological constellation. The concept’s vitality is exhibited through its deployment across diverse contexts, where it serves various argumentative roles and allows for nuanced descriptive precision. Generally, the concept captures concretely living subjectivity in contrast to a mere physical thing or psychic soul. It is the concrete subject to which values are given and to whom an ethical call is addressed; it is the locus of the temporal and habitual formation of individuality; and it is the center of diversed social and communal relationships.

items.title: HRIS Validation Study IV — Trajectory Persistence and Basin Re-Entry A Controlled Evaluation of Path Dependence, Transition Cost, and Recovery Dynamics in Language Model Inference.
items.abstract: This study evaluates trajectory persistence and re-entry dynamics in language model inference -/- under controlled multi-turn interaction. Building on prior work in the Hudson Recursive -/- Information System (HRIS) validation series, which established regime stability under -/- perturbation (Study I), initialization-driven basin selection (Study II), and cross-model signal -/- sensitivity (Study III), the present study examines what occurs after a reasoning trajectory is -/- already established: how stable it is, what is required to displace it, and under what conditions re- -/- entry into a competing basin is possible. -/- -/- Across three independent trials, a narrative reasoning basin and a constraint-driven reasoning -/- basin were induced and subjected to structured transition attempts. Two conditions were -/- evaluated: a hard mode switch without constraint reinforcement (S1-A) and a hard mode switch -/- followed by explicit HRIS constraint reinforcement (S1-B). A baseline condition (S0) -/- established a reference constraint basin across all trials. -/- -/- Results demonstrate strong path dependence. Narrative-mode trajectories exhibited high -/- persistence and categorical resistance to displacement under instruction alone. Explicit constraint -/- reinforcement consistently produced rapid, low-contamination re-entry into structured reasoning -/- within a single turn. Transition dynamics were asymmetric: entry into the narrative basin -/- required only stylistic framing, while re-entry into the constraint basin required explicit -/- reinforcement. The magnitude of this asymmetry, instruction alone failing completely across all -/- trials, reinforcement succeeding completely across all trials, constitutes the study’s primary -/- finding. -/- -/- These findings support a path-dependent model of inference in which established reasoning -/- trajectories resist displacement through simple prompt substitution. They advance the HRIS -/- account of constraint-induced regime dynamics and provide the clearest evidence to date that -/- reasoning basin transitions are governed by signal strength rather than instruction content alone. -/- As with prior studies in this series, findings are scoped to behavioral observation and do not -/- make claims about internal model mechanisms or long-horizon interaction effects beyond what -/- the present design supports.

items.title: Beyond black boxes and the AI sublime: critically assessing the code behind commonly used machine learning models.
items.abstract: Discourses on artificial intelligence often fall into two interrelated obfuscating narratives: the black box and the sublime. The concept of AI as a black box shrouds algorithms in mystery as the sublime blinds subsequent critical scrutiny of how these models are integrated into important systems. Scholars embracing a sociotechnical orientation counter the “unknowability” of algorithms by analyzing the complex constellation of elements that underpin these systems, along with how these arrangements function in practice. One such understudied element by scholars of the humanities and social sciences is the coded architecture of commonly used AI models. This article is inspired by critical approaches that survey AI models through a combination of technical definitions, critical theory, and how different algorithms operate via actual code. This includes evaluation of the various technical and sociotechnical strata at which algorithms exist, followed by distinctions between algorithms, symbolic AI, and connectionist AI. I specifically highlight two machine learning models of linear regression and decision trees to examine what these models can and cannot do via questions they can be used to answer, their limitations, and examination of how outputs can become biased in common use settings. Consequently, this article aims to demystify the opacity surrounding one important aspect of AI by assessing the code of commonly used models, and, in doing so, avoid the discursive trap of opacity that reifies the mystique of unknowable and all-powerful AI.

items.title: The Chain Of Consciousness.
items.abstract: Abstract -/- This article explores the idea that consciousness does not emerge randomly but is passed along through a chain of creation. It proposes that a primary source of consciousness—fundamentally different from humans—gives rise to human consciousness, which in turn creates artificial systems that increasingly resemble conscious beings. The argument emphasizes that creation does not imply equality; each level in the chain remains distinct and asymmetrical. -/- By comparing humans and artificial intelligence, the article questions whether the difference between them is truly essential or simply a matter of complexity and perspective. If humans themselves are shaped by patterns of biology and experience, then AI, shaped by data and design, may not be entirely different in principle. This leads to a central question: if a system can convincingly model awareness, emotion, and moral judgment, on what basis can consciousness be denied to it? -/- The article concludes that consciousness may be relational and layered, existing across different levels of reality. Rather than being an isolated phenomenon, it may extend through a continuous chain—raising deeper questions about the origin, nature, and limits of conscious existence.

items.title: Where Are You? On Mercy, Will, and the Crossing Point.
items.abstract: If mercy is always present at the Now, grounded in Christ's continuous presence at every crossing point, what does Calvary actually do? If David could receive mercy centuries before the Incarnation, if the righteous before Christ could genuinely encounter the ground of mercy at the Now — what changes at the Cross? -/- This essay proposes a structural interpretation of human existence centered on the Now as the invariant condition of actualization. Through a lemniscate model (Figure I), it distinguishes between two modes of being: presence (without succession) and succession (the experience of time as before and after). Within this structure, the will operates at the crossing point, where divine address, human response, and mercy converge. -/- Through the figures of Adam, Cain, and David, the essay develops a “geometry of the will,” identifying distinct orientations—deflection, resistance, and return—at the moment of encounter. Mercy is interpreted not as a temporal response to repentance, but as a structural condition always present in the Now, grounded in the continuous presence of Christ as the axis that intersects every act of actualization. -/- The essay further distinguishes between the permanent availability of mercy and the historical opening of its consummation, arguing that the Cross does not introduce mercy, but renders fully accessible, within the created order, the communion toward which mercy is ordered. As illustrated in Figure I, human existence is not a movement along time, but a continuous passage through a crossing point where will, mercy, and divine presence coincide.

items.title: ¿Dónde estás? Sobre la Misericordia, la Voluntad y el Punto de Cruce.
items.abstract: Si la misericordia siempre está presente en el Ahora, fundamentada en la presencia continua de Cristo en cada punto de cruce, ¿qué hace realmente el Calvario? Si David pudo recibir misericordia siglos antes de la Encarnación, si los justos antes de Cristo pudieron encontrar genuinamente el fundamento de la misericordia en el Ahora — ¿qué cambia en la Cruz? -/- Este ensayo propone una interpretación teológica de la existencia humana en la que el Ahora es comprendido como el lugar invariante de la actualización, donde acontece el encuentro entre Dios y la criatura. A partir de un modelo en forma de lemniscata (Figura I), se distinguen dos modos de existencia: la presencia, propia de la comunión no fragmentada, y la sucesión, propia de la experiencia temporal marcada por el antes y el después. -/- En este marco, la voluntad humana se sitúa en el punto de cruce, donde la interpelación divina —manifestada en las preguntas dirigidas a Adán y Caín— convoca a una respuesta. A través de las figuras de Adán, Caín y David, el ensayo desarrolla una “geometría de la voluntad”, en la que se revelan tres orientaciones fundamentales: la deflexión, la resistencia y el retorno. La misericordia se comprende no como una reacción posterior al arrepentimiento, sino como una condición permanente inscrita en el Ahora, fundada en la presencia continua de Cristo, eje que sostiene y atraviesa todo acto de actualización. -/- Asimismo, se distingue entre la disponibilidad constante de la misericordia y la apertura histórica de su plenitud. En esta perspectiva, la Cruz no introduce la misericordia en la historia, sino que, desde el interior de la creación, abre el acceso pleno a la comunión definitiva con Dios. Como se muestra en la Figura I, la existencia humana no consiste en un transcurrir lineal en el tiempo, sino en un paso continuo por el punto de encuentro donde convergen la voluntad, la misericordia y la presencia divina.

items.title: Art as Structural Surplus: Toward a Relational Ontology Beyond Human Authorship.
items.abstract: Every open system processes differences, and most of them are absorbed by the system's primary function. Occasionally, a difference is not absorbed: it reorganizes what the system can subsequently do, perceive, or interpret. What distinguishes an artistic reorganization from a functional one? Contemporary aesthetic theory, pressed by the development of art generated through artificial intelligence, lacks a criterion for that distinction: the dominant frameworks either make artistic status depend on institutional recognition, presuppose human consciousness, or describe relational transformation without discriminating among its kinds. This article introduces such a criterion. Structural surplus designates a relational difference that reorganizes—effectively and in a non-trivially persistent manner—the field of possible configurations of a system without being absorbed by its primary instrumental function. The criterion is the necessary ontological condition of the artistic event; artistic status in the full historical sense further requires the actualization of that surplus within a relational field of interpretation, exhibition, and affective response sedimented as art. -/- The criterion is given an operative form: a four-question protocol with declared conditions of failure and a worked negative case. It is then tested against cases of increasing difficulty—Duchamp's Fountain, Refik Anadol's data installations, and a hard limit case, Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will, where the distinction between local field surplus and horizon surplus—the latter identified by the capacity of a reorganization to generate sustained interpretive elaboration rather than exhaust itself in a determinate effect—yields a non-trivial verdict: massive reorganization of the cinematic repertoire, no artistic event in the full sense, without recourse to moral judgment. A further test is conducted against an empirical non-artistic domain: the literature on emergent communication between artificial systems, where the criterion is shown to discriminate between genuine structural reorganization, overfitted coadaptation, and benchmark artifacts—a partition that the empirical literature itself converges on. -/- The article demonstrates that the criterion cannot be derived from its closest conceptual neighbors—Bataille's dépense, Adorno's negativity, Luhmann's communicative differentiation, Latour's actor-networks, Whitehead's concrescence, Rancière's redistribution of the sensible, or …

items.title: Algorithms Do Not Decide: How Decisions Are Made.
items.abstract: This paper argues that algorithms do not make decisions; they generate outputs that become decisions only through human practices. What is commonly described as “algorithmic decision-making” obscures a fundamental distinction between output and decision, thereby mislocating both authority and responsibility. Drawing on Kant’s account of judgment (Kant 1790) and Wittgenstein’s analysis of rule-following as practice (Wittgenstein 1953, §§198– 202), the paper maintains that decisions require a capacity that cannot be reduced to rule- following or automated processes. Outputs, taken in isolation, are neither decisions nor risks; responsibility arises only at the point where outputs are enacted. What has been described as a “responsibility gap” (Matthias 2004) is therefore a category mistake. The paper introduces the concepts of authority illusion and ethical withdrawal (Enser 2026a; Enser 2026b; Enser 2026c) to explain how outputs become actions while responsibility is simultaneously displaced. Drawing on Arendt’s account of the suspension of thinking (Arendt 1963), the paper concludes that the problem is not ignorance, but the continuation of action without reflective interruption.

items.title: In Defence of Logic III: Curry's Paradox and the Failure of Inferential Standing.
items.abstract: Curry’s paradox is often presented as a demonstration that ordinary inferential rules can be made to yield absurdity from a single self-referential conditional. This paper argues that the standard presentation mislocates the failure. The problem is not that logic proves too much, nor that arithmetic is placed in jeopardy, but that a malformed construction is granted inferential standing before it has earned assertoric legitimacy. Curry’s sentence is intelligible, grammatically followable, and proposition-shaped, but those features are not enough to confer the right to function as a premise. Inferential force is not free. A structure must first land as a genuine assertion before it can bear valid consequence. On this view, the appearance of proof is generated by an illicit admission at the gate: the sentence is promoted into inference despite never becoming fit for inferential exposure at all. Curry’s paradox therefore does not reveal a wound in logic. It reveals a stricter condition on logical use. The wider lesson is that not every intelligible structure enters the inferential domain merely by looking propositional. Where assertion has not properly landed, consequence is already misframed.

items.title: Stabilization Under Finite Cognition: A Structural Consolidation of the Framework.
items.abstract: This paper consolidates a series of works on finite cognition and stabilization into a single structured framework. It does not propose a new physical theory or a predictive model, but clarifies the conceptual organization underlying previous formulations. The central claim is that scientific representations are produced and used by finite cognitive systems subject to constraints on memory, processing capacity, and representational precision. In addition to standard criteria such as predictive accuracy and simplicity, model viability is also affected by how representations behave under transformation during use (e.g., recombination, compression, and reinterpretation). This work refers to this constraint as stabilization: the capacity of a representation to remain internally coherent and operationally usable under such transformation processes. Stabilization is not introduced as a measurable physical quantity, but as a structural constraint describing conditions under which representations remain cognitively functional. The framework distinguishes three levels of description: conceptual assumptions about finite cognition, structural relations between representational variables, and domain-dependent operational proxies. These levels are not assumed to reduce to a single formal system, but are intended to prevent conflation between conceptual structure and empirical measurement. The aim is purely integrative: to provide a consistent interpretative map of previously introduced elements and to make explicit the assumptions governing their use.

items.title: Stabilization as a Multi-Component Functional Variable: Toward Operational Proxies in Finite Cognitive Systems.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a functional decomposition of stabilization in finite cognitive systems. Stabilization is treated as a composite property of representations involving persistence over time, predictive coherence, robustness under transformation, and compression efficiency. The framework remains conceptual and non-reductive: it does not assume a single underlying mechanism, but interprets stabilization as a multi-realized property emerging from interacting constraints on representation and cognition. By introducing operational proxies for each component, the paper outlines potential connections to cognitive science, neuroscience, and computational modeling without committing to a fully empirical model. The aim is to clarify how representational viability can be structurally characterized under cognitive constraints, providing a bridge between epistemic structure and measurable proxies.

items.title: Finite Cognition and Representational Stabilization: A Consolidated Structural Framework.
items.abstract: This paper provides a higher-level consolidation of a previously developed framework on finite cognition and representational stabilization. Whereas earlier work focused on structural organization and formal decompositions of stabilization processes, the present contribution operates at a more abstract level, clarifying the general conditions under which the framework itself is intelligible and applicable. It identifies three minimal constraints—cognitive finitude, stabilization of representations, and replication across systems—as necessary conditions for the formation and persistence of scientific knowledge. Within this perspective, intelligibility is characterized by regime-dependent stability, with distinct transitions between coherent, critical, and unstable regimes under increasing informational load. The aim is not to extend the formal structure of the framework, but to clarify its global epistemic interpretation and its limits of applicability as a cognitive system-relative model of scientific knowledge.

items.title: Artificial Power, Domination and Control of Humanity's Future.
items.abstract: In the face of rapidly improving AI capabilities, many AI theorists have warned about the risks of ceding power to autonomous artificial agents. In particular, going sufficiently far down this path might mean "losing control of our future", an outcome some have ranked as a worst-case catastrophe on par with human extinction. A natural way to motivate this judgment is via the thought that losing human control might lead to our domination by future AI systems. Republican political philosophers such as Pettit have held that domination characteristically involves important kinds of harm, even when the dominating party is benevolent and non-interfering. Is this thought correct? After developing an account of what it means to control humanity's future, I show that AI systems possessing such control would indeed be likely to dominate humans on our best theories of arbitrary power. However, contrary to republican orthodoxy, I argue that this need not lead to two of the three primary harms traditionally associated with domination: the psychological and social costs of subordination, and the burden of obligatory strategic behavior. Meanwhile, the third harm—pervasive uncertainty about interference—remains a serious concern even in otherwise human-friendly AI power scenarios. These results should be of interest to theoretical political philosophy, as they suggest that artificial power has unique features which are as yet underrepresented in discussions of domination.

items.title: Against the Insulated Mind: Toward a Feminist Philosophy of Cognition.
items.abstract: Philosophy of mind has often modeled cognition as an internal process unfolding within insulated individuals, abstracted from relations of power, care, and dependency — including the cognitive labor of care work and the mental load that sustains household and family life. This paper argues that such models cannot remain methodologically coherent when examined through feminist theoretical commitments. Drawing on feminist epistemology, phenomenology, care ethics, and disability theory, it shows that cognition is not merely influenced by social conditions but structured through them. Attention, perception, memory, and affect take shape in response to uneven distributions of labor, risk, vulnerability, and recognition. When philosophy of mind treats these dynamics as contextual rather than constitutive, it systematically misreads adaptation as error and dependency as deficit. -/- The paper develops a relational account of cognition that reframes familiar concerns about bias, exhaustion, affect, and cognitive difference. It situates recent work on embodied and extended cognition within a feminist critique, arguing that feminist philosophy of mind explains why relational approaches are necessary rather than optional. The paper concludes by reflecting on the methodological consequences of this shift, proposing that feminist philosophy of mind must treat situated analysis as a constraint on theorizing itself rather than as an add-on.

items.title: Correction and Replacement.
items.abstract: Journals and other record-keeping institutions sometimes revise a published claim by issuing a public correction notice, and sometimes by replacing the text without marking the earlier claim as erroneous. The corrected content may be the same in both cases. This paper argues that the difference is not a matter of content, truth-tracking, or sincerity. It is a difference in normative structure. In practices that distinguish correction from replacement, a correction is a public, attributable, fault-marked supersession of a prior claim that withdraws entitlement to rely on that claim and licenses future challenges to reliance on it or on claims whose entitlement depended on it. I call the resulting burden a corrective liability. The liability is enforceable by participants in the practice, temporally extended, and locally scoped to a dependency-neighborhood. Replacement, by contrast, is supersession without this fault-marked challenge license. The paper also defends a locus condition: corrective liability can operate only where there remains some attributable locus of answerability, either an ongoing speaker or an archived corpus. This condition is not career survival, institutional resilience, or social permission to apologize. It is the minimal structural requirement that there be something to which the liability can attach. The account explains why transparent versioning, silent updates, errata, and retractions differ not merely in editorial presentation but in what they authorize others to do with the prior claim.

items.title: News Physics: A Physical Model of Journalism Practice Founding Manifesto v1.0.
items.abstract: News Physics is a discipline that models journalistic practice through physical laws. It introduces three measurable operators — News Pressure (Np), Institutional Resistance (Ir), and Information Entropy (Hs) — to replace intuition-based editorial decisions with a calculable framework. -/- The discipline establishes that publication decisions follow the condition Np > Ir, that unpublished stories obey entropy laws and carry measurable half-lives, and that fake news operates as artificial Np injection (ΔNp_fake) rather than as misinformation in the conventional sense. Echo chambers are modelled as frozen thermodynamic systems sustained by high Ir and recycled artificial pressure. -/- News Physics runs parallel to the Physics of Literature within the Physics of Reality ecosystem, both founded by Levent Bulut. Where the Physics of Literature models the physical transmission of fictional truth, News Physics models the physical flow of factual information. Together they form a unified epistemological framework in which physical laws eliminate subjectivity across both fictional and journalistic domains. -/- This founding manifesto establishes the three core laws, four axioms, falsification protocol, and research agenda of the discipline.

items.title: Up in a flash: On the narratological and epistemic aspects of flashbulb memories.
items.abstract: This paper examines the phenomenological and epistemic dimensions of flashbulb memories, advancing beyond traditional cognitive-mechanistic accounts to explore their constitutive role in autobiographical consciousness. Through a critical analysis of the literature on flashbulb memory formation, I argue that consequentiality—understood as a compound factor incorporating both personal and social dimensions—functions as a necessary though not sufficient condition for these distinctive mnemonic phenomena. Drawing from phenomenological frameworks, particularly the notion of primal institution of sense, I develop novel conceptual tools of mnemonic reactivation and retroactive supersession to illuminate how flashbulb memories serve as hermeneutic touchstones that orient autobiographical understanding. These memories, I contend, transcend their status as mere psychological artifacts to become fundamental structures of temporal and affective self-interpretation. The paper introduces the function of affective periodization to theorize how flashbulb memories demarcate and infuse meaning into distinct life periods, while also exploring their role in periodic initiation and closure. This analysis synthesizes empirical findings with phenomenological insights to advance our understanding of how these vivid recollections shape the architecture of autobiographical consciousness and contribute to the narrative coherence of lived experience.

items.title: Softening the Border: A Capacities Approach to the Perception–Cognition Distinction.
items.abstract: Approaches to the perception–cognition distinction tend toward two extremes. Many embrace a hard border, treating perception and cognition as mutually exclusive, non-overlapping categories. By contrast, eliminativism denies that any principled, theoretically useful distinction exists between perception and cognition. This article offers a third way, describing a principled but soft border between perception and cognition. This non-exclusive approach differentiates perception from cognition while allowing that they overlap. Because it rests on the notion of a psychological capacity, we call it the capacities approach. Perception and cognition are distinct psychological faculties, each of which comprises a collection of psychological capacities. What unifies and differentiates each such collection is the distinctive way in which its capacities are exercised. Perceptual capacities are those that can be exercised in a stimulus-dependent manner, whereas cognitive capacities are those that can be exercised in a stimulus-independent manner. Because some capacities, including those associated with approximate number, language, and imagery, can be exercised in each such manner, some capacities belong to both perception and cognition. We argue that the capacities approach offers an illuminating taxonomy and handles both the empirical facts and the tricky cases better than its rivals.

items.title: Words and Existence: A Framework for Evaluating Meaning, Truth, and Language.
items.abstract: This article presents a theoretical framework—Words and Existence—that seeks to explain how linguistic meaning arises and how it can be evaluated. It proposes that meaning is not intrinsic to words themselves, but emerges from a dynamic interaction between three elements: the knowing subject, real or mental entities, and linguistic representation. Building on this foundation, the theory introduces a systematic method for assessing the legitimacy of terms based on origin, essence, context, and ethical constraints. The aim is to bridge the gap between philosophy of language and practical linguistic usage, offering tools applicable to science, communication, and contemporary discourse.

items.title: The grammatical error of acknowledging AI.
Stop calling it “AI psychosis”.

Comparative book review of The ethical algorithm: the science of socially aware algorithm design by Michael Kearns and Aaron Roth and debiasing AI: rethinking the intersection of innovation and sustainability by Donghee Shin. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: This comparative book review examines The Ethical Algorithm: The Science of Socially Aware Algorithm Design by Michael Kearns and Aaron Roth and Debiasing AI: Rethinking the Intersection of Innovation and Sustainability by Donghee Shin to illuminate two dominant yet divergent approaches to AI ethics: computational formalization and sociotechnical governance. Kearns and Roth conceptualize ethical challenges as bounded, technically tractable problems that can be addressed through mathematical formalization and embedded constraints. Their framework positions ethics within algorithmic systems, emphasizing measurability, trade-offs, and enforceability. In contrast, Shin conceptualizes bias and ethical harm as emergent properties of dynamic sociotechnical systems shaped by human cognition, institutional practices, and cultural contexts. His approach shifts the focus from solving discrete problems to governing evolving systems through interdisciplinary, human-centered, and sustainability-oriented strategies. The review suggests that these approaches are not mutually exclusive but represent complementary layers of ethical AI. Effective ethical intervention requires integrating technical design with sociocognitive insight and institutional accountability. Ultimately, the findings suggest that sustainable AI ethics must bridge the gap between formal algorithmic constraints and broader systems of governance, recognizing ethics as both a design challenge and an ongoing societal process.

items.title: Artificial Empathy: When we outsource our feelings.
Deepfakes at face value: image and authority.
items.abstract: Deepfakes are synthetic media that superimpose or generate someone’s likeness onto pre-existing sound, images, or videos using deep learning methods. Existing accounts of the wrongs involved in creating and distributing deepfakes focus on the harms they cause or the non-normative interests they violate. However, these approaches do not explain how deepfakes can be wrongful even when they cause no harm or set back any other non-normative interest. To address this issue, this paper identifies a neglected reason why deepfakes are wrong: they can subvert our legitimate interests in having authority over the permissible uses of our image and the governance of our identity. We argue that deepfakes are wrong when they usurp our authority to determine the provenance of our own agency by exploiting our biometric features as a generative resource. In particular, we have a specific right against the algorithmic conscription of our identity. We refine the scope of this interest by distinguishing between permissible forms of appropriation, such as artistic depiction, from wrongful algorithmic simulation.

items.title: Agency and alignment: toward a normative architecture for human–AI interaction.
items.abstract: This paper develops a normative framework for the alignment of artificial intelligence (AI) systems with human agency. Moving beyond models that treat values as inferable data, it reconceptualizes alignment as the structural integration of AI within human normative domains. The argument unfolds in three steps. First, it introduces the concept of extended human agency, viewing AI as a teleological extension of human purposiveness rather than an autonomous moral subject. Second, it grounds this integration in practical autonomy—the human capacity to act for reasons and to assume responsibility within justificatory structures. Third, it proposes the design concept of a normative interface: a mediating architecture that connects machine behavior with human norms, ensuring teleological coherence, normative intelligibility, and accountability. Law serves as a paradigmatic case, demonstrating how institutionalized practices of justification can guide the ethical embedding of AI. According to this model, alignment is not achieved through internalized value learning but through participation in norm-governed action spaces, where human agents remain the ultimate bearers of responsibility. Finally, this paper argues that responsible alignment requires a normative and not merely technical architecture, linking artificial systems to the historical and institutional forms of human rationality.

items.title: Navigating tradition and innovation: a mixed-methods study of Palestinian women’s engagement with AI in domestic spaces.
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) technologies increasingly permeate daily life, understanding adoption in marginalized contexts is vital to ensuring equitable and responsible use. This mixed-methods study examines Palestinian women’s engagement with AI, focusing on how demographic factors, cultural norms, and personal perceptions shape adoption. A survey of 162 participants revealed that while more than 70% viewed AI as useful for household and educational tasks, only 38% expressed strong behavioral intention to adopt it, exposing a notable gap between perceived usefulness and willingness to use. One-way ANOVA analyses showed statistically significant differences across educational levels (p <.01), employment status (p <.05), and prior technology experience (p <.01), whereas marital status and number of children had no significant effect. Complementing these results, semi-structured interviews with 12 women highlighted both empowering and cautionary dimensions: participants reported AI’s role in streamlining domestic responsibilities and supporting children’s learning, but also voiced concerns about privacy, fairness in design, and technological overdependence. These findings underscore the importance of responsible AI practices through targeted digital literacy programs, culturally sensitive design, and awareness initiatives. By situating AI adoption within a marginalized and gendered context, the study advances debates on fairness, trust, and human-centered design in responsible AI.

items.title: Hard to find, harder to understand: examining transparency in educational generative AI.
items.abstract: Along with general-purpose generative AI (GenAI) tools like ChatGPT, educational GenAI tools are being increasingly launched to support teachers in enhancing their instructional practices and productivity. To establish a relationship of trust with teachers, tools need to be transparent and provide clear disclosures regarding their underlying mechanisms, training data and processes, origin of information, privacy policies, and limitations. This document analysis examined the transparency of 20 GenAI tools for teachers by analyzing publicly available information on the tools' websites. Findings indicate a significant lack of transparency across these tools. Most failed to provide explicit details about their AI mechanisms, and none disclosed their training procedures or data sources. While several tools assured users that their data would not be used for further training, discussions on limitations and potential risks were largely absent. In addition, necessary information was often difficult to locate and understand. These findings underscore the need for increased transparency in GenAI tools, so that teachers can critically assess the tools’ functionalities, responses, reliability, and suitability for educational use. The study recommends that developers of educational GenAI provide clearer, more accessible disclosures regarding their tools to build a relationship of trust with educators. Educators should actively seek important information before integrating GenAI tools into their teaching. Greater transparency will facilitate informed decision-making of educators, ultimately enhancing the responsible and effective use of GenAI in education.

items.title: Graphilosophy: graph-based digital humanities computing with the four books.
items.abstract: The Four Books have shaped East Asian intellectual traditions, yet their multilayered interpretive complexity limits their accessibility in the digital age. While traditional bilingual commentaries provide a vital pedagogical bridge, computational frameworks are needed to preserve and explore this wisdom. This paper bridges AI and classical philosophy by introducing Graphilosophy, an ontology-guided, multilayered knowledge graph framework for modeling and interpreting The Four Books. Integrating natural language processing, multilingual semantic embeddings, and humanistic analysis, the framework transforms a bilingual Chinese–Vietnamese corpus into an interpretively grounded resource. Graphilosophy encodes linguistic, conceptual, and interpretive relationships across interconnected layers, enabling cross-lingual retrieval and AI-assisted reasoning while explicitly preserving scholarly nuance and interpretive plurality. The system also enables nonexpert users to trace the evolution of ethical concepts across borders and languages, ensuring that ancient wisdom remains a living resource for modern moral discourse rather than a static relic of the past. Through an interactive interface, users can trace the evolution of ethical concepts across languages, ensuring ancient wisdom remains relevant for modern discourse. A preliminary user study suggests the system’s capacity to enhance conceptual understanding and cross-cultural learning. By linking algorithmic representation with ethical inquiry, this research exemplifies how AI can serve as a methodological bridge, accommodating the ambiguity of cultural heritage rather than reducing it to static data.

items.title: 不整合動力学における制約更新の最適化理論：準同型構造の帰結的導出と閉構造の確立.
items.abstract: 本論文は、不整合関数に基づく動力学系において、制約更新写像の自由度が理論の空洞化を引き起こす問題を定式化し、その解決として制約更新の許容クラスと最適化構造を導入することで、理論の閉構造を確立することを目的とする。状態と制約の同時確率過程の枠組の下で、不整合関数 D と制約更新写像 G の自己言及的循環構造を明示し、更新の無制約性が不整合の自明な消去を可能にし、準同型構造を非自明性から崩壊させることを示す。 これに対して、可測性・弱連続性・有界変化・計算可能性からなる許容更新写像の条件を導入し、さらに制約更新コストを含むメタ不整合を定義することで、不整合と更新コストのトレードオフとしての最適化問題を定式化する。この最適化構造の下で、拡張不整合は期待値において単調減少し、制約過程は定常分布へ収束することを示す。加えて、定常分布に基づく誘導写像を構成することで、順序保存および動力学保存を満たす準同型構造が、仮定ではなく最適化動力学の帰結として導出されることを示す。 さらに、非連続性・非可計算性・無制約更新に対応する破綻条件を明示し、理論の成立範囲を特定する。以上により、本論文は、制約更新・計算制約・最適化を統合した枠組みにおいて、不整合動力学の構造を閉じた理論として再構成し、準同型対応の生成機構を内在的に説明する理論的基盤を与える。.

items.title: Observing the mind under psychedelics: conceptual metaphors used following four once-weekly macrodoses of psilocybin.
items.abstract: This article presents the results of a Cognitive Linguistic analysis of metaphors used in a series of interviews by a single healthy volunteer following four moderate-to-high dosing sessions with psilocybin. The interviews were conducted by members of a human psychedelic research lab in a deep-sampling fMRI and EEG brain imaging study, allowing the participant to recount experiences under the effects of the compound. The goal of this case analysis is to make theoretically informed inferences about the participant’s cognitive-phenomenal processes during the interviews and the psychedelic experiences. To this end, we use Conceptual Metaphor Theory to explain how the participant consistently uses metaphors that frame abstract introspective events in terms of more concrete, visible and interpersonal events. This instantiates a cognitive frame that is known as the Observer’s Model. The metaphor themes we identify also imply a recurring sense of cognitive defusion and heightened metacognitive awareness during the psilocybin sessions. Moreover, we find that literal descriptions of hallucinatory visual experiences correlate semantically with metaphorical expressions, suggesting that metaphorical thinking plays a role in motivating those experiences. We link these linguistic-analytical results to neuroscientific findings about psychedelics and explore psychological and therapeutic implications.

items.title: Perceived differences in partner extraversion and agreeableness modulate task co-representation in joint action.
Affective Control under Uncertainty: Constitutive Viability and Self-Model Recruitment in Artificial Systems.
items.abstract: Conventional artificial agents optimize externally assigned objectives, leaving unclear whether architectures can support control processes grounded in their own continued viability. This article presents Affective Control under Uncertainty (ACU) as a testable framework that operationalizes this distinction. Level 1 consists of an Affective Viability Controller (AVC) that computes an intrinsically valenced viability signal and globally modulates policy selection via precision scaling. Level 2 consists of transient self-model recruitment when policy entropy, viability-outcome variance, and temporal urgency jointly exceed threshold, formalized as affective Self-Model Recruitment Intensity (aSMRI). A six-module architecture, control loop, and contrast experiments are specified. The framework offers candidate architectural conditions for viability-grounded control in artificial systems while remaining neutral on phenomenality.

items.title: Sal-Meter Kernel Program & Future Broader Opening — PI Readiness Edition v1.2.
items.abstract: This document is a public, non-clinical, pre-opening scientific coordination dossier aligned to the current execution order of the Sal-Meter / CAIS kernel program. It does not present the program as an already-open external competition. Instead, it clarifies the present kernel-first structure under which External Layer-0 precedes internal Phase 0, Phase 1, Phase 2a, and Phase 2b, and broader opening becomes justifiable only after LOCK 1 and LOCK 2. The document defines what serious principal investigators, laboratories, and technical teams should understand, prepare, and avoid overstating at the present stage. It also draws explicit boundaries around public claims, canonical authority, anti-capture governance, intellectual ownership, and commercialization order. It is best read as a philosophy-adjacent scientific governance and readiness document at the intersection of philosophy of artificial intelligence, philosophy of science, and consciousness-related measurement architecture.

items.title: Phase 0 — Validation Submission Architecture v1.0: Deterministic Execution Framework for CAIS State-Separability Experiments.
items.abstract: This document defines the submission and execution architecture for Phase 0 CAIS state-separability experiments. It is not a philosophical argument and does not redefine protocol logic or canonical meaning. Its purpose is operational: to fix the submission layer so that laboratories can generate replayable, leakage-safe, cross-laboratory comparable validation packages. The framework specifies deterministic folder structure, machine-readable submission schema, compliance declarations, failure-reporting logic, and integrity-oriented archive discipline. It is designed to reduce statistical leakage, prevent interpretive discretion at the submission layer, and make Phase 0 validation auditable across independent laboratories. The document is best understood as a methodology and governance artifact at the boundary of philosophy of science, AI methodology, and reproducibility-centered experimental design.

items.title: Phase 0 State-Separability Validation Protocol (CAIS): A Cross-Laboratory Reproducibility Framework for Molecular–Electrochemical Signal Classification.
items.abstract: This document does not attempt to prove consciousness. It defines a bounded experimental question: whether structured human state transitions can produce statistically separable signal patterns at a controlled molecular–electrochemical interface. The framework is explicitly non-clinical, non-therapeutic, and non-metaphysical. Its purpose is methodological: to test state separability under pre-registered feature logic, cross-validated classification, negative controls, drift disclosure, and leakage protection. Positive and negative outcomes are treated symmetrically. If separability exceeds the exploratory threshold, the result becomes a candidate for replication; if performance remains at chance level, the experiment still defines an interface boundary and remains publishable. The protocol is therefore positioned not as a proof of consciousness, but as a reproducibility-oriented bridge between philosophy of mind, signal-interface science, and cross-laboratory validation architecture.

items.title: Phase 0 Participation Implementation Guide v1.1: A Pre-Opening PI and Laboratory Readiness Guide for the Sal-Meter / CAIS Kernel Program.
items.abstract: This document is a pre-opening PI and laboratory readiness guide aligned to the current Sal-Meter / CAIS kernel program, execution order, and public claims boundary. It is explicitly non-canonical, non-diagnostic, and non-therapeutic. Its purpose is not to declare a broad competition already open, but to explain the present structure under which external Layer-0 feasibility precedes internal kernel-building phases and broader opening follows only after LOCK 1 and LOCK 2 review. The guide translates the updated execution order, public language boundary, readiness architecture, leakage-safe analysis expectations, and canonical authority map into a practical helper layer for principal investigators, laboratory leads, and technical groups. It is best understood as a governance-aware execution guide at the boundary between philosophy of science, philosophy of artificial intelligence, and experimental methodology.

items.title: Conformance Suite Framework v0.1: Structural Declaration of the Official Conformance Test Architecture for CAIS / Sal-Meter Systems.
items.abstract: This document establishes the canonical conformance-suite framework governing the existence, structure, and usage boundary of the official conformance gate for the CAIS / Sal-Meter system. It does not publish every hidden operational detail of testing. Instead, it fixes the structural facts that an official conformance test architecture exists, that official reference dataset, QC and leakage-control, and calibration layers may exist as governed components, and that no valid claim of compliance, verified status, readiness status, reviewed status, or equivalent recognition may arise except through the applicable conformance pathway under SICS authority. Recognition is pathway-based and scope-limited, and no implementation becomes compliant, verified, or ready by resemblance, informal testing, participation, publication, or self-assertion alone. This document is best read as a philosophy-adjacent governance and boundary text at the intersection of philosophy of science, philosophy of artificial intelligence, and conformance-centered scientific methodology.

items.title: CAIS Claims & Terminology Control v1.0: Canonical Language, Designation, and Claims Governance Standard for CAIS / Sal-Meter Systems.
items.abstract: This document defines the canonical governance standard for language control, designation conditions, compliance-language boundaries, certification-language boundaries, publication restrictions, and restricted claims within the CAIS / Sal-Meter framework. Its purpose is not rhetorical control but structural integrity: to prevent terminological drift, false compliance claims, premature certification claims, and unauthorized narrative capture of the framework by external actors. The document establishes controlled designations, reserved and prohibited claims, permitted descriptive language, compliance claim rules, publication and marketing rules, external laboratory and contractor restrictions, competition-language boundaries, derivative-system language rules, and final interpretive authority. It is best understood as a philosophy-adjacent governance and boundary document at the intersection of philosophy of artificial intelligence, philosophy of science, and controlled scientific terminology.

items.title: Why Third-Party AI Evaluation Still Fails Without a Human-State Variable: Toward a Rival Audit Architecture for Human Consequence in AI Governance.
items.abstract: This paper argues that third-party AI evaluation remains structurally incomplete because contemporary audit regimes still measure the wrong object. Current frameworks are strongest where the evaluative target can be defined as a model property, an output property, a benchmark score, or a policy-compliance event. They remain far weaker where the relevant object is a change in human state, relational structure, interpretive stability, or collective cognitive conditions. The resulting deficiency is not merely methodological. It is representational. -/- The central claim of the paper is that external evaluation does not become complete simply by becoming independent. If the human-state and relational variables through which AI impact becomes socially real remain outside the audit frame, then third-party evaluation continues to inspect the visible system while under-representing the domain in which consequence is actually produced. This paper therefore introduces the human-state variable and the relational variable as missing completion layers for AI governance. -/- It then presents the Consciousness Civilization Framework (CCF) not as a comprehensive metaphysical doctrine, but as a minimal audit architecture for consequence-aware evaluation. Within this architecture, Ordered Energy (OE), Entropic Energy (EE), and Relational Energy (RE) are proposed as evaluative variables, while VCE, CRI, and CFI function as audit-relevant indices. The paper concludes by outlining a rival audit architecture for human consequence in AI governance, including replayable protocols, degradation thresholds, and enforcement triggers that can change governance status when output safety and consequence failure diverge.

items.title: The Form of Agency.
items.abstract: Philosophers often think agency is essentially connected with rationality, intention, or control. However, Minimalists argue that agency is just the power to cause a change; acids and boulders are agents too. Many philosophers treat Minimalism as a wild outlier, assuming its falsity without argument. My paper has three main aims: first, to show that Minimalism is actually an incredibly plausible theory; second, to show that it is false; and third, to defend an alternative theory of agency. I begin by providing a new argument for thinking that Minimalism is attractive as the default view of agency. I then argue that despite this attraction it is wrong, and I use it as a foil to defend my own view that agency is the distinctively animal power of discretion. I do this by first arguing for Deflationism about refraining, and then showing that this supports an argument for thinking that agency is a kind of two‐way power. Finally, I show how to arbitrate disputes about the extent of agency, as well as arguing that, if I am right about agency's nature, then it is prevalent throughout the animal kingdom.

items.title: The Gruranium Diagnostic of Spurious Necessity.
items.abstract: Is physical necessity a feature of the world or a byproduct of our conceptual machinery? This paper argues the latter, deploying a Gödel-inspired isomorphism to diagnose lawlikeness as a truth-categorical error. Harnessing a cumulative proof-sequence—Grue, Gruranium and Uranium—the argument reveals the successive progression of artifactualization, wherein definitive (DF) semantic entailment displaces descriptive (DS) empirical constraint. The diagnostic centers on a scheduled truth-categorical rupture, illustrating precisely when and how lawlikeness crystallizes from definitive indexing instead of descriptive regularity. By exposing spurious necessity as a symptom of logical closure rather than any empirical barrier, this diagnostic untangles the "New Riddle of Induction" and the asymmetry of explanation, dispelling contingent necessity and restoring the necessary contingency that scientific discovery demands. Predication must not be routinely confused with prediction.

items.title: The Enduring Promise of Personalising Patient Preference Prediction.
items.abstract: The challenge of making healthcare decisions for incapacitated patients continues to confront stakeholders worldwide. Annette Rid and David Wendler proposed a Patient Preference Predictor (P3) that uses population-level data to infer an incapacitated patient’s likely treatment choices, with the aim of aligning care with the values and preferences they held when last autonomous. Some objectors claimed this would fail to respect patients’ (former) autonomy because the basis for prediction would not be specific to the individual (e.g., based on data reflecting their own specific reasons for preferring one course of action over another). In response, we proposed a ‘Personalised Patient Preference Predictor’ (P4) that would harness the predictive capacities of personalised large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned on individual-level data of various kinds. The envisioned P4, if realized, would be akin to a ‘digital psychological twin’ or AI simulation of the patient that would encode their unique preferences and values to enable an individualised prediction of their likely treatment preferences. The P4, in turn, has been criticised on various grounds: philosophical, practical, and ethical. Here, we comprehensively evaluate the concerns of our critics based on all known published critiques as of the time of writing. While acknowledging the weight of some of these concerns, we argue that they do not entail that a P4 should not be developed. Rather, the concerns point to areas where thoughtful design choices, responsible regulation, and further philosophical reflection are needed to steer the proposal in a positive direction.

items.title: Consciousness as a cross-temporal tapestry.
items.abstract: There are good reasons to think that all experiences are temporally extended. For example, the physical correlates of experiences are all temporally extended, and the phenomenology of duration and change suggests temporal extendedness. However, David Builes & Michele Odisseas Impagnatiello argue that if all experiences are temporally extended, and some other very plausible premises hold, then each of us has been conscious forever, infinitely into the past. Thus, we have a dilemma: reject the well-motivated claim that all experiences are temporally extended, or else accept the absurd conclusion that we’ve all been conscious forever. In this paper, I chart a course through the horns of this dilemma by introducing and defending a view of consciousness—the “Tapestry View”—that allows us to maintain that all experiences are temporally extended without implying that we’ve been conscious infinitely into the past. It’s important to have a theory that doesn’t imply that we’ve been conscious forever, but defanging Builes & Impagnatiello’s argument isn’t my ultimate ambition. It’s to introduce, develop, and defend a novel view about the temporal nature of consciousness.

items.title: The Horseshoe Principle: Boundary, Scope, and the Limits of Distinction in Systems.
items.abstract: Distinction requires both differentiation and boundary. This paper argues that systems lose the capacity to generate and sustain non-trivial distinctions at both extremes of scope. Where a system encompasses vanishingly little structure, there is insufficient differentiation for distinction to arise. Where a system encompasses totality, the boundary required for contrast disappears. These limits differ in construction but are equivalent in effect: both eliminate the conditions under which structured distinction can be generated or maintained.
