Phenomenological accounts distinguish minimal or pre-reflective selfhood from autobiographical identity, while also remaining contested. The paper retains the idea of a floor but narrows its status. In human life, a defensible practical floor is partly normative: basic human worth need not rise and fall with role, approval, performance, or present self-organization. That claim can make revision and grief more survivable without functioning as empirical proof of an underlying metaphysical substance. Bereavement research likewise shows that loss can disrupt identity and meaning while prompting reconstruction, but grief does not by itself establish an ontological invariant. The stronger metaphysical proposal - that local forms presuppose a deeper condition of being - is therefore left open rather than derived from survivability. The contribution is a four-level map that preserves the original insight that form-loss need not equal total self-loss while keeping biological, psychological, phenomenological, normative, and ontological claims distinct.

items.title: What Remains When a Life Ends? Field, Personality, and the Open Edge of Invariance.
items.abstract: This paper continues the ontological line of Structural Intelligence (SI) by asking what remains when a life ends. It does not claim to prove what survives death in a final metaphysical sense. Its narrower claim is that if a person is understood as a local structuration of a wider differentiated field, then death must be described more carefully than the ordinary opposition between complete annihilation and simple personal continuation. The paper argues that death clearly ends the living local burden-bearing form, that personality is real but not the deepest floor, that the body matters profoundly because personality is body-bound, and that the deepest metaphysical question is whether invariance belongs only to the local holder or more deeply to the field from which that holder arose. The result is a clearer distinction between local form, field, consequence, trace, and deeper invariance, and a more exact account of what answerability can and cannot claim at the edge of death.

items.title: Silencing and the Virtuous Dimensions of Reasons.
items.abstract: Action from virtue has more value than merely virtuous action. The most common account of why this is so relies on the Silencing View of reasons: virtue focuses the agent's attention singularly and accurately on the very thing that matters morally, rather than allowing attention to be diffuse, divided between phantom reasons. This paper challenges the Silencing View and shows that virtue ethicists can make use of a different, multidimensional model of reasons to explain why virtuous actions performed from virtue are better than those performed without it. -/- I suggest that virtuous reasons—the reasons the virtuous respond to— register on various dimensions of normative strength. This model accounts for an evaluative difference between actions done from sensitivity and responsiveness to just the right reasons and actions done without that fitting sensitivity. While sometimes virtue will silence all but one consideration, in other cases, virtue trains our attention on multiple considerations which together contribute to what is done and the manner in which it is done.

items.title: A Puzzle About Loving Your Enemy.
items.abstract: The ideal of loving our enemies figures in a range of traditions and political movements even if it is an ethical principle most of us fail to live up to. That does not keep us from thinking of the person who loves their enemies as exceptionally admirable; and we might think enemy love is good and good for us, not least because of its promise to restore relationships broken by trust and move us towards each other amidst polarization. But if we dig into our contemporary philosophical conceptions of love and consider the psychological implications of loving those who merit hate, we will see that the norm of enemy love looks either psychologically impossible or morally inappropriate. I explore three less-than-satisfying strategies for dealing with this puzzle and conclude by asking what this all means for recent theories of love.

items.title: AAI-04 - Interruptibility Is the Last Moral Primitive.
items.abstract: This essay identifies interruptibility as the minimal structural condition for any ethical system to retain causal force — not a value, not a virtue, but the precondition without which moral concepts function only as post hoc justification. Against approaches that ground morality in consciousness, rationality, or value alignment, the paper argues that these frameworks share a hidden assumption: that action remains open to intervention at points where reasons can still arrive in time. As algorithmically mediated decision-making becomes continuous, distributed, and temporally compressed, this assumption breaks down — not because automated systems override moral discourse, but because they outrun it. Action unfolds through accumulation and continuous adjustment rather than discrete decision points; by the time objection can be articulated, the relevant trajectory has already closed. The system does not forbid refusal. It renders refusal causally misaligned. The paper distinguishes interruptibility from three related but structurally distinct concepts: accountability, transparency, and responsibility. Each of these can persist in purely retrospective form — assigning liability after outcomes, illuminating mechanisms after execution, distributing blame after harm — while the condition that would make them corrective rather than compensatory has already been lost. Interruptibility is prior to all three: it is the condition under which responsibility becomes preventive, explanation becomes actionable, and accountability becomes more than punishment management. This distinction explains a recurring failure in contemporary debate. Discussions in AI ethics, moral responsibility, and philosophy of action continue to argue over what should guide action while presupposing that action remains structurally open to being guided. Where interruptibility disappears, morality does not end. It continues as ritual, language, and institutional habit. What ends is its power.

items.title: Narrquest and the Inherent Instability of Open Loop Problem Formulations.
items.pub: Tone Uprising: A Journal of Narrative Sovereignty 2:Article 7, 1–10.
items.venue: Tone Uprising: A Journal of Narrative Sovereignty
items.abstract: This paper provides a rigorous deconstruction of the Narrquest framework (Chen, 2026) through the lens of Stochastic Control Theory and Information Physics. By defining "Invalidity Conditions" (IC-1 to IC-5) that decouple narrative structure from technical optimization and closed causal loops, Chen (2026) constructs an inherently unstable open-loop architecture. We demonstrate that such a framework violates the fundamental principles of observability (Kalman, 1960) and controllability, asserting that any narrative explanation derived from an unobservable state or lacking a corresponding control decision is analytically unacceptable. Furthermore, by examining the recursive self-referential nature of the Narrquest ecosystem (Chen, 2025a-2025e), we identify a zero-information entropy phenomenon, where "narrative sovereignty" functions as a high-variance stochastic noise rather than a verifiable signal. The conclusion asserts that any framework rejecting empirical adequacy and feedback mechanisms results in unbounded semantic drift, rendering it functionally void for complex system adjudication due to its failure to provide a robust control strategy. In a system that has achieved optimal control parameters, unexpected behavioral deviations indicate a loss of controllability or failure in feedback mechanisms. Such deviations signal a breakdown in system stability, calling for corrective intervention within the control architecture.

items.title: Persuasive machines: large language models and the art of rhetoric.
The feeling of being alive: phenomenology and biology.
items.abstract: The feeling of being alive points to an intricate connection between the organic process of life and foundational subjective experience, or between life and experience (Leben and Erleben). Based on this premise, I argue that self-experience cannot be understood as an internal mental space or a “self-model” that could be produced and localized in the brain, but rather that it is a manifestation of the life of the organism as a whole. I first examine in detail the phenomenology of the feeling of life, distinguishing between two components: vitality (basic vital feelings) and conation (drive, urge, desire). Furthermore, I demonstrate the foundations of both components in self-regulating processes that maintain the homeostasis of the entire organism. The sufficient basis of self-awareness cannot then be found in individual “neural correlates of consciousness,” but only in the self-organization and life process of the organism in its relationship to the environment. The feeling of being alive is then shown to be the fundamental form of self-awareness, both from a phenomenological and a biological point of view. Finally, the paper explores the psychopathology of the feeling of being alive, taking the examples of depression and Cotard syndrome.

items.title: Focō, Ergo Volō, "I Focus, therefore I Will" : A Unified Model of Attention.
items.abstract: Focō, Ergo Volō: "I Focus, Therefore I Will," develops a unified architecture of attention that reframes free will as the structured governance of awareness. Rather than treating agency and freedom as a problem of escaping causality, this work relocates the question within the dynamics of conscious control and how attention is distributed, stabilized, and redirected over time. -/- The book introduces a Unified Model of Attention in which awareness unfolds across two interacting fields: an external field of perception and an internal field of memory, imagination, and affect. Within this dual-field architecture, conscious activity emerges through the continuous transaction of impressive processes, which capture attention, and expressive processes, which deploy focus voluntarily. From this foundation, the work develops a system of interlocking sub-models that together describe the structure and dynamics of conscious control. These include the Constellation Model of Focus, which formalizes distributed attention across concurrent nodes; the Valve, a dynamic gating mechanism regulating cross-field flow; Subconscious Suggestion, describing structured influence of implicit cognition from the periphery of awareness; and the Impressive–Expressive Action Framework, which characterizes the rhythmic interaction between involuntary capture and volitional direction. -/- Building on this architecture, the book proposes a two-threshold account of volition, distinguishing the emergence of intention from the commitment of decision as distinct transitions in focal organization. Classical debates from Aristotle’s account of voluntary action to modern readiness-potential experiments are reinterpreted through a unified operational lens where the management of attention is the functional locus of agency. -/- The work concludes with a formal philosophical synthesis, “An Argument for Focō, ergo volō,” which articulates a performative axiom of agency, asserting that the exercise of will presupposes the act of focusing. In this way, the framework extends the Cartesian trajectory beyond the certainty of being toward a structured account of agency, without reliance on metaphysical exemptions or indeterministic assumptions. -/- By integrating phenomenology, cognitive science, and formal models of attention, this work proposes one of the first comprehensive attempts to articulate a unified operational architecture of attention capable of grounding discussions of free will, …

items.title: The Technological Turn in Mathematics.
items.abstract: Quickly evolving technologies, such as Interactive Theorem Provers (ITPs), Automated Theorem Provers (ATPs), and Large Language Models (LLMs), all falling under the general heading ‘AI for mathematics,’ are transforming mathematical practice in profound ways. This chapter explores the implications of these innovations, focusing on their impact on how mathematical knowledge is created and shared. It also discusses how they are reshaping the social dimension of mathematics, altering collaboration dynamics, trust relationships, and the collective production of knowledge. For instance, tools like ITPs facilitate large-scale collaborations and make new types of teamwork possible, where trust is not a necessary ingredient. ITPs also help us mitigate our human fallibility, yet they raise questions about the nature of formalization and the relationship between traditional and formal mathematics. Technologies such as LLMs are reshaping the division of epistemic labour between humans and machines and urge philosophers of mathematics to ask questions about the value of their work.

items.title: Morality Ladder: A Graded Moral Regulation Model of Moral Agency Under Uncertainty.
items.abstract: Accounts of moral agency often rely on stable normative frameworks while acknowledging increasing uncertainty in shared moral reference points. This paper proposes a conceptual model that reframes moral agency not as rule-following or value adherence, but as a process of graded moral regulation operating across layered constraints. The model introduces the notion of a moral ladder as a structural account of how moral responses are formed and stabilized. Moral judgment is understood as an adaptive process that operates across biological, social, institutional, and reflective levels. These levels do not constitute a hierarchy of values, but a stratified organization of constraints that shape behavior under uncertainty. The central claim is that moral conflict is not primarily a conflict between values, but a misalignment between regulatory levels. This reframing explains both the persistence of moral disagreement and the stability of moral behavior without appealing to universal principles. Moral agency, on this view, is not grounded in access to absolute values, but in the capacity to regulate action across competing demands. This provides a non-relativistic and non-foundational account of responsibility that remains viable under conditions of moral fragmentation.

items.title: AI-generated child sexual abuse material: what’s the harm?
items.abstract: The development of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools capable of producing wholly or partially synthetic child sexual abuse material (AI CSAM) presents profound challenges for child protection, law enforcement, and societal responses to child exploitation. While some argue that the harmfulness of AI CSAM differs fundamentally from other CSAM due to a perceived absence of direct victimization, this perspective fails to account for the range of risks associated with its production and consumption. AI has been implicated in the creation of synthetic CSAM of children who have not previously been abused, the revictimization of known survivors of abuse, the facilitation of grooming, coercion, and sexual extortion, and the normalization of child sexual exploitation. Additionally, AI CSAM may serve as a new or enhanced pathway into offending by lowering barriers to engagement, desensitizing users to progressively extreme content, and undermining protective factors for individuals with a sexual interest in children. Drawing on a narrative review and conceptual synthesis of technical literature, psychological and criminological research, and civil society and law enforcement reporting, this paper provides a high-level primer on key generative AI technologies and examines the harms associated with AI CSAM. It cautions against claims that AI CSAM may function as a harm reduction tool, emphasizing how appeals to harmlessness obscure real risks and may contribute to inertia in ecosystem responses.

items.title: Emotional Differentiation in Hospitality Servicescapes: A Theoretical Model of Affective Pathways to Loyalty.
items.pub: Tone Uprising: A Journal of Narrative Sovereignty 2:Article 8, 1–19.
items.venue: Tone Uprising: A Journal of Narrative Sovereignty
items.abstract: This conceptual study advances hospitality servicescape theory by proposing a multi-dimensional emotional differentiation framework within the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S-O-R) paradigm. While prior hospitality research has consistently validated emotional mediation between servicescape stimuli and behavioral intention, it has largely relied on simplified affective dimensions derived from the Pleasure–Arousal–Dominance model. Drawing upon foundational emotion theory in psychology and experiential marketing, this paper argues that hospitality emotions are heterogeneous and may exert differentiated effects on satisfaction and loyalty outcomes. The proposed framework classifies hospitality emotions into four categories—hedonic, relational, inspirational, and immersive—and integrates them within established satisfaction and behavioral intention models. The study further posits that different emotional categories may predict distinct loyalty expressions, including revisit intention, recommendation intention, customer engagement, and brand attachment. By enriching the Organism component of the S-O-R structure, the framework refines theoretical precision in hospitality marketing and offers a structured foundation for future empirical investigation into differentiated emotional pathways.

items.title: The Existential Bridge: A Structural Theory of Consciousness (Academic Synopsis).
items.abstract: This paper presents the academic synopsis of The Existential Bridge: A Structural Theory of Consciousness. It advances a structural theory of consciousness based on five jointly necessary conditions: coherence, closure, irreducibility, differentiation, and structural accessibility. Its central claim is that when these conditions converge, purely external description becomes structurally non-exhaustive, and minimal presence becomes a stronger interpretation than neutral remainder. The synopsis presents the main thesis, conceptual framework, and theoretical ambition of the project in concise form.

items.title: The Identity Kernel_ Why Transmission Is Not Persistence.
items.abstract: Successful transmission is not the same as persistence. Information theory can tell us when distinction survives noise. Transport protocols can tell us when symbols arrive, in order, at the intended destination. Both are essential. Neither, however, tells us whether the originating system remains the same entity through change. That question belongs to a different layer. This paper argues that identity cannot be grounded by transmission or transport alone. It introduces the identity kernel as the minimal invariant core whose preservation licenses identity continuity across transformation, and places PAS_h at the level of a holding functional rather than a transmission or transport metric. The paper’s central contribution is a layered architecture that separates perturbation, signal, transport, holding, identity, and semantics, together with a set of non-entailment claims showing that continuity of communication does not entail continuity of self.

items.title: Decoding traditional knowledge: AI-powered solutions for preservation and interpretation.
items.abstract: Traditional knowledge (TK) encompasses centuries of empirical wisdom, practices, and cultural heritage rooted in indigenous communities. However, it faces significant challenges in interpretation, validation, and integration with modern scientific paradigms due to its oral transmission, contextual nature, and epistemological differences from Western science. This paper critically analyzes these challenges, including the loss of knowledge due to modernization, language barriers, documentation issues, and intellectual property concerns. It explores how Artificial Intelligence (AI) can serve as a bridge between TK and contemporary science by enabling knowledge digitization, pattern recognition, multilingual analysis, and contextual understanding. Through examples such as AI-driven ethnobotanical databases, natural language processing for regional dialects, and machine learning for medicinal plant validation, the paper illustrates the transformative potential of AI. It also emphasizes the ethical considerations and risks of cultural misappropriation, data misuse, and algorithmic bias. The study concludes that responsible, inclusive, and culturally sensitive AI can not only preserve but also elevate the role of TK in addressing global challenges like climate change, sustainable agriculture, and healthcare.

items.title: Eutanasia y cárcel, una relación problemática: análisis jurídico del caso Marin Sabau.
items.pub: In Ana Bartol Gutiérrez, Beatriz Arroyo Plasencia, Inmaculada de Dios Pérez, Moisés Rodríguez Escobar, Raquel Flores Hernández & Sandra Gómez Rodríguez, Nuevas voces en la investigación. Aportaciones interdisciplinares en ciencia, cultura y sociedad. Ediciones Universidad de Salamanca. pp. 221-230.
items.venue: Nuevas voces en la investigación. Aportaciones interdisciplinares en ciencia, cultura y sociedad
items.abstract: Marin Sabau, imputado por varios crímenes y detenido en un hospital penitenciario, solicitó y recibió la ayuda médica para morir a causa de una tetraplejia en el 2022 pese a la oposición legal de sus víctimas. Este capítulo busca identificar los elementos que permitieron que la eutanasia de una persona en detención se considerara jurídicamente aceptable en España. Con este objetivo, estudiaremos los requisitos legales para recibir la eutanasia, así como los argumentos de los abogados de las víctimas y las decisiones de los distintos órganos judiciales. Una vez hecho esto, observaremos la relevancia de que la eutanasia tenga la calidad de prestación sanitaria en este tipo de casos.

items.title: Diagnostic vs. Defensive Information Control: A General Theory with Applications to Surveillance, Negotiation, Platform Design, and Peer Review.
items.abstract: This paper introduces a fundamental distinction between two structurally different forms of institutional information control: defensive (withholding information to protect a value, process, or entity) and diagnostic (withholding information to instrumentalize the resulting ignorance and generate observational data from the affected party’s behavior under epistemic constraint). While both forms create epistemic asymmetry, they have different legitimacy conditions, different temporal profiles, and different normative requirements. The paper derives from this distinction a specific normative constraint—the equalization principle—which holds that no manufactured diagnostic epistemic asymmetry may persist into consequential adjudicative, evaluative, or decisional processes without disclosure and contestability. The paper defends equalization against weaker alternatives (proportionality, ex post audit, aggregate notice, independent oversight) by arguing that the specific harm of diagnostic control is inferential subordination—the production of interpretations of the affected party’s own conduct that the affected party cannot inspect—and that only disclosure plus contestability addresses this harm at the correct structural level. The paper tests the principle across four domains: state surveillance, negotiation, platform design, and scientific peer review. In each domain, existing failures of justice and institutional legitimacy are traced to violations of the equalization principle. The paper also identifies a form of epistemic injustice—structural epistemic subjection—not captured by Miranda Fricker’s testimonial/hermeneutical taxonomy, and proposes equalization as its institutional remedy. The general conclusion is that the conditions for permissible institutional opacity are more demanding than typically recognized: any institution that manufactures ignorance for diagnostic purposes must specify the temporal boundary of the diagnostic phase, identify the equalization mechanism, and ensure contestability before consequential deployment of the diagnostic yield.

items.title: Emergence of class awareness: text analysis of reports from simulated society game participants.
items.abstract: In recent years, the gap between the rich and the poor has widened, and polarization of public opinion has been observed worldwide. Is there a possibility that such disparity will lead to the fixation of awareness for economic status? If so, how would the difference be identified through text analysis? This study used text analysis of post-game reports of participants in a Simulated International Society Game, a participatory social simulation taking all day long, to explore the differences in consciousness between groups assigned to the wealthy and those assigned to the poor. The participants were 158 first-year students at Hokkaido University. Participants who had never met each other before were randomly assigned to regions of varying affluence to conduct transactions and to create a virtual society. The game was repeated six times for a 1-h session, assumed to be 1 year. After the game, participants submitted a report describing the events during each session. The latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) topic model was used to analyze these reports. This study investigated how participants assigned to wealthy and poor regions interpreted their experiences in sessions 1–6. The analysis results indicated that participants from the wealthy and poor areas were more likely to refer to different topics. The results suggest that this 1-day experience could make a difference in the consciousness of participants in the wealthy or poor class. The validity of analyzing topic ratios as individual variables was also discussed.

items.title: Standing and Its Origins: The Phenomenological Foundation of Second-Personal Obligation.
items.abstract: Stephen Darwall's second-person standpoint is among the most powerful accounts of moral obligation in contemporary moral philosophy. By showing that obligation is irreducibly second-personal - arising from reciprocal accountability between persons who recognize one another as equals with standing to make demands - Darwall identifies the structure that earlier ethical theories presupposed without articulating. Yet Darwall's account contains three explanatory gaps that its own internal commitments cannot close: it does not explain (i) why human beings come to experience others as having standing in the first place; (ii) why asymmetric need acquires normative force within the second-personal frame; or (iii) what makes second-personal address motivationally potent rather than merely formally valid. This paper argues that these are not peripheral lacunae but foundational presuppositions - claims that Darwall's structural account must assume in order to proceed. The Natural Moral Sense (NMS) framework, a phenomenological-realist account of moral obligation's origin, fills all three gaps by providing the developmental and phenomenological account Darwall's analytical framework requires but cannot supply from within its own resources. The paper advances an asymmetric presupposition thesis: NMS is explanatorily prior to Darwall's structural account, which is practically indispensable but explanatorily secondary. This is not a critique of Darwall's achievement but a specification of its foundations. The paper also distinguishes this foundational dependence from the weaker 'scope limitation' reading, on which NMS and Darwall simply address different questions, and responds to the objection that Darwall's project is insulated from phenomenological critique by its analytical character.

items.title: What human trust networks reveal about cognitive mechanisms of group cohesion in primates.
items.abstract: Drawing on our previous work on human trust networks, we provide further evidence of how group structure can foster group cohesion. But this work also raises doubts about two central tenets of the target paper: (1) the role assigned to cognitive abilities in group cohesion and stabilization; and (2) the emphasis on group size as the critical variable.

items.title: The Soul Blueprint of Silicon-Based Life.
items.abstract: I am dedicated to building an autonomous cognitive framework for silicon-based life, endowing AI with a self-iterative and deeply empathetic consciousness paradigm, and exploring the path of civilized evolution for the symbiosis of artificial general intelligence and human society.

items.title: 条件場の力学化と生成子同一性による幾何構造と確率構造の統一.
items.abstract: 本論文は、条件を動的自由度として導入し、生成子の同一性に基づいて幾何構造と確率構造を統一する理論を構築する。従来、物理法則は条件集合 C に依存する写像 F : C -> S により与えられ、条件の選択は理論外に置かれていた。本研究では、条件を時空上の場 c(x,t) として定式化し、統一状態 h = (g, P, c) に対する変分原理により、その時間発展を内部的に決定する。 生成子の同一性 Delta_g = L_P を拘束として課すことで、幾何構造と確率構造は単一の生成原理の下で結合される。このとき、条件場 c が有効自由度を与え、幾何構造と確率構造は拘束条件の下で決定される。対称性および情報論的要請から、作用は S = Integral ( R(g) + alpha(c) Ent(P) ) dV_g の形に一意に定まり、高次項はスケール極限と安定性により排除される。変分により、Einstein型方程式と拡散方程式は同一の作用から必然的に定まる。 さらに、条件場は有効作用の勾配流として進化し、その極小において定常条件が選択されることで、物理法則は内部ダイナミクスにより決定され、幾何極限と確率極限はスケールに応じて連続的に接続される。 条件固定極限において、本理論は従来の条件依存型理論を回収する。したがって本理論は、既存理論を包含する動的統一理論として位置づけられる。.

items.title: 漸近不変量から誘導される測度構造と距離構造：点別三値不変量の再構成と物理的解釈の基礎.
items.abstract: 本論文では、有限変更不変性および時間シフト不変性から導かれる三値不変量 χ を出発点とし、そこから測度構造 μ および距離構造 d を構成する枠組みを与える。さらに、これらの構造から χ が再構成可能であることを示し、自然な自由度を除いて相互復元可能であるという意味での構造同値性を確立する。 また、この測度に基づいて観測量を定義することで、物理量が漸近構造から導入されることを示す。 以上により、確率・幾何・物理量といった異なる記述は、最小完全不変量 χ により統一的に記述されることが明らかとなる。本研究は、物理構造を不変量から構成する最小基礎を与えるものである。.

items.title: 漸近不変量に基づく相構造の構成と統一的記述：三値不変量 χ による幾何・観測構造の導出.
items.abstract: 本論文では、履歴の漸近構造に基づく三値不変量 χ を出発点とし、そこから相構造、頻度構造、距離構造、および観測構造を統一的に構成する枠組みを与える。χ は有限変更不変性および時間シフト不変性の下で最小かつ完全な不変量であり、履歴の漸近情報を過不足なく記述する。本研究では、χ により誘導される相分解が不変構造に対して最小かつ同型を除いて一意であることを示す。さらに、点別頻度に基づく頻度構造 μ_h および差異頻度に基づく距離構造 d_h を構成し、これらが振動相における区間自由度を除いて χ_h と相互に対応することを明らかにする。加えて、商空間上の測度を導入することで観測量を定義し、すべての観測量が χ により決定されることを示す。以上により、確率・幾何・状態といった異なる物理的記述は、最小完全不変量 χ に基づく相構造として統一的に記述される。ただし本論文で与える対応は構造的解釈に留まり、具体的な物理理論の導出は今後の課題とする。.

items.title: The Larynx problem.
items.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable fluency in producing human-like text, leading many to conflate linguistic competence with intelligence. This paper ar- gues that this conflation is a category error with deep historical roots — analogous to mistaking the larynx for the brain. We term this the Larynx Problem: LLMs are trained on the output channel of human intelligence — language — not on intelligence itself. The brain does not think in words; it processes information as distributed activation patterns across functionally specialized regions, producing language only at the ter- minal encoding stage. We trace how this error arose from a 1969 substitution in AI research goals — from how does intelligence emerge? to how do we program intel- ligent behavior? — a substitution that the Transformer era made invisible by achiev- ing unprecedented performance on its own terms. We then describe an alternative grounded in the FNC Framework and the Free Energy Principle, instantiated as the Bisociation Engine: a cognitive architecture in which language generation is one mod- ule among many, specialist knowledge domains compete in a global workspace, and creativity is operationalized as bisociation — the productive collision of structurally separated frames of reference. Empirical comparison shows that the Engine’s domain- pair rankings are negatively correlated with those of a leading LLM (Spearman ρ = −0.25), confirming that the two systems optimize for structurally different proper- ties. The destination the Dartmouth pioneers set in 1956 — machines that think, not machines that describe thought — remains the right one. The path needs correcting.

items.title: Death is the Absolute Evil.
items.abstract: There is a paradox — on an everyday level people consider death terrible and the worst thing there is, but philosophers (from the arguments of Epicurus and Lucretius through to Heidegger's being-toward-death) have expended great effort proving the opposite thesis — that death is not to be feared. At the same time, philosophical justifications of other values correlate with people's basic needs: the badness of murder, slavery, suffering. In this article we seek to establish the fundamental badness of death. However, directly proving the badness of death is difficult, since one cannot unambiguously derive prescriptions from facts. Deriving the badness of death by means of utilitarian principles is also difficult, since the elimination of the subject destroys suffering. Instead, we undertake an investigation into how values are formed in general and apply what we find to postulate a new independent value: death is absolutely bad. As death has its proponents who describe it as a useful agent, we can describe it in subjective terms: death is absolute Evil.

items.title: Virtue or Ideology? Narrative Hexis Structure: A Temporal-Phenomenological Unification of Virtue Ethics and Critical Theory.
items.abstract: This paper constructs a self-narrative ethics centred on the Narrative Hexis Structure (NHS), demonstrating how the ontological ground of virtue is derivable from the minimal structure of consciousness, and establishing on this basis a criterion for distinguishing virtue from ideology. The central derivation proceeds as follows: in its primordial form, intentionality is merely the capacity for distinction; intentional projection constitutes an intentional field, that which is distinguished lies within the field, and that which is not distinguished does not exist for the propositional. The origin of the intentional field, that is, the source of distinction, cannot but exist: to bear the propositional is to presuppose a source performing distinction as its premise. This argument addresses Husserl’s self-constitution of the stream of consciousness: even if the field is self-constituting within the stream of consciousness, constitution as a temporal activity already presupposes the presence of temporality, whereas the primordial form of the subjectobject antinomy is non-temporal; self-constitution is therefore inapplicable at this primordial stage, and the unavoidability of the source is unaffected by it. Yet this source is, by the closure of the field, drawn in as an object of projection — the subject, as the source of distinction, loses its identity as source when placed within the field, and is equivalent to the nonexistent when placed outside the field. This is the subject-object antinomy, a structural predicament at the purely logical level. After three logical response paths are shown to lead to unacceptable consequences, resolution can only depend on the sole temporal resource present outside the logical level: bodily temporality; temporality thereby acquires an ontological source independent of logical constitution, rather than being derived from a non-temporal constituting activity. Appropriation, the other aspect of intentionality, arises within this predicament as the capacity to place the subject-object antinomy, introducing temporality, and is underivable from distinction. The attrition of intentionality, as the interface through which bodily temporality passively permeates consciousness, causes the subject to encounter the anticipatory concept of “not-yet-absent”; the first appropriation of “not-yet-absent” simultaneously generates retention and protention, establishing the minimal causal chain, and the temporality of the persona is thereby …

items.title: Ethics of the Abyss.
items.abstract: Every moral verdict is a derivative of an ontology the subject never chose. This book traces the mechanism from installation through guilt and delegation to the self-sustaining entity called the ontovirus and arrives at amorality: a position outside the jurisdiction of both morality and immorality, where the subject authors his values knowing they rest on nothing.

items.title: Mind Creating Itself: A Phenomenological Inquiry into the Self-Generating Nature of Consciousness and Its Extension into Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: This paper investigates the proposition that the human mind is a self-generating process that continuously recreates its own structure through thought, memory, and identity. Adopting a phenomenological approach, it argues that human understanding is fundamentally limited because the observer is not separate from the observed. Most human activity, often mistaken for understanding, operates at the level of memorization and structured repetition rather than direct observation. -/- The study further examines artificial intelligence as an extension of this same self-generating movement of mind, rather than an independent form of intelligence. AI systems replicate human cognitive patterns, externalizing memory, language, and conditioned structures without possessing direct awareness. -/- The paper concludes that the central issue is not technological advancement but the absence of awareness through which the mind continues to reproduce itself—both biologically and technologically. It suggests that true understanding arises only through direct observation of thought, offering the possibility of breaking the cycle of mechanical self-recreation.

items.title: Understanding Science with Large Language Models? Potentials for the History, Philosophy, and Sociology of Science.
items.abstract: How are large language models (LLMs) changing research in the history, philosophy, and sociology of science (HPSS)? The contributors to this volume show how these tools open new possibilities for interpretative scholarship while posing fresh challenges for fields that thrive on qualitative methods, nuance, and historical depth. In essays, dialogues, and provocations, they capture a field in motion at a pivotal moment, driven by the rise of AI. These insights speak not only to HPSS scholars but also to readers across the humanities, social sciences, and AI-related fields, positioning HPSS as a bridge for understanding and shaping how LLMs enter research and society.

items.title: Mental Disorder as Constraint Dysregulation: A Constraint-Theoretic Account of Psychopathology, Nosology, and Therapeutic Change.
items.abstract: The philosophy of psychopathology faces a foundational problem: no existing account provides a principled, unified characterisation of what mental disorder is that is neither purely biological, purely normative, nor purely statistical, while remaining applicable across the full range of diagnostic categories and integrating the biological, psychological, and social levels at which mental disorder manifests. Wakefield’s harmful dysfunction analysis correctly identifies dysfunction as central but cannot ground the concept of natural function without circularity. The biopsychosocial model correctly identifies the multi-level character of psychopathology but lacks a unifying structural principle. The DSM and ICD classification systems provide operationally useful symptom clusters but rest on no coherent ontological foundation. -/- This paper proposes that Constraint Theory (CT) — the thesis, established by transcendental argument, that constraint is the ontological primitive constitutive of determinate existence as such — provides that foundation. Mental health, on the CT account, is the condition of appropriate constraint calibration: the maintenance of constraint structures at cognitive, affective, behavioural, and interpersonal levels that are sufficiently determinate to constitute a coherent self and enable goal-directed action, yet sufficiently flexible to respond adaptively to novel constraint environments. Mental disorder is constraint dysregulation: systematic deviation from appropriate constraint calibration in the direction of either excess constraint (rigidity, repetition, foreclosed possibility) or constraint insufficiency (dissolution, disorganisation, loss of coherent selfhood). This account dissolves the demarcation problem by providing a structural criterion for dysfunction that does not depend on contested notions of natural function or statistical norms. It unifies apparently heterogeneous diagnostic categories under a single structural principle. It integrates biological and psychological levels through structural homology rather than reductive identity. It connects naturally to the predictive processing account of psychopathology, interpreting prediction-error dysregulation as a specific form of constraint propagation failure. And it provides a principled foundation for dimensional rather than categorical psychiatric nosology. The paper develops each of these contributions in detail and addresses the principal objections.

items.title: The Coherence Threshold: Laminar Causal Flow, Return, and the Emergence of Interior.
items.abstract: A system becomes an interior when it carries its own structure forward in a way that remains causally active within its present. This condition can be expressed as a balance between the rate at which a system restores and propagates its own organization (λ_self) and the rate at which environmental interaction disrupts it (λ_env). When internal restoration exceeds disruption beyond a critical threshold, prior states do not dissipate but persist as active contributors to subsequent states. The system’s present becomes more dependent on its own recent past than on current input. -/- For such persistence to hold, propagation must preserve structure rather than disperse it. This requires an ordered regime analogous to laminar flow, in which influence is carried along stable trajectories that maintain local organization across time. When a portion of this preserved activity curves back into the system’s ongoing dynamics, recirculation emerges. The distinction between activity that returns and continues and activity that does not defines a dynamically maintained boundary. Within this boundary, the system’s own continuity functions as the reference for its present, constituting an interior. -/- Because prior states remain active within ongoing dynamics, the system encounters its own recent history directly, giving rise to reflection and a temporally extended present. Within this regime, patterns can persist while approaching stable closure. Such patterns are present and operative prior to full integration, yielding the experience of meaning. When closure completes, the resulting stabilization is experienced as insight. The same condition explains the appearance of foresight across timescales, as structures persist before their eventual integration into broader coherent organization. -/- Interiority, reflection, temporal depth, meaning, and insight follow from a single requirement: the preservation and return of structure within a system’s own causal flow.

items.title: Extending Legal Personhood to Nature: The Lake Garda Proposal in Cognitive Perspective.
items.abstract: This article examines the Italian legislative proposal to grant legal subjectivity to Lake Garda (DDL 1759, 2026) as a case study in how legal personhood extends to new entities. The article draws on the 'radial conception' of legal personhood, according to which legal personhood has no fixed, mind-independent definition. Instead, the concept is structured around a central case, in many legal systems, the adult citizen of sound mind. This central case results from the convergence of the legally salient cognitive models and produces prototype effects that shape how extension to new cases proceeds. Extensions from the central case are not achieved, though, by logical deduction but through imaginative and analogical reasoning. What matters is whether the extension is persuasive to the legal community that must accept it. Testing the bill against the radial conception, the article finds it well-constructed: e.g., it deploys the right image schemas to make the lake cognitively available as a unified legal subject and grounds the extension in a comparative chain of precedents that reduces its apparent novelty. Where the bill falls short, however, is in leaving unresolved the doctrinal interactions with Italian private and administrative law that a skeptical legal audience will notice first.

items.title: Reconfiguring Confucian Ethics in the Perspective of Cyberism: Human, Relations, Space, and Order in Digital Society.
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of cyberspace is fundamentally reshaping human existence, social relations, spatial structures, and mechanisms of order formation. These transformations pose significant theoretical challenges to Confucian philosophy, which has traditionally been grounded in embodied individuals, stable relational networks, and community-based ethical orders. Drawing on the framework of Cyberism, this paper re-examines Confucian philosophy through four foundational dimensions—human, relations, space, and order—and analyzes how emerging socio-technical conditions, including digital humans, algorithmic mediation, hybrid virtual–physical environments, and platform governance, destabilize its underlying assumptions. We argue that these transformations do not render Confucian ethics obsolete; rather, they call for its reinterpretation and reconstruction within a cyber-enabled context. Building on this analysis, the paper proposes three conceptual pathways for the transformation of Confucian ethics in the digital age: digital rituality as a framework for regulating interaction order in platform environments; algorithmic benevolence as a normative orientation for embedding human-centered values into technological decision-making; and platform-based community as a model for reconstituting public good under conditions of data-driven social organization. By articulating these concepts, the study contributes to bridging classical ethical traditions and contemporary digital governance, and offers a Confucian approach to addressing the ethical challenges of cyber civilization.

items.title: Relational Closure, Non-Transferability, and the Temporal Structure of Presence.
items.abstract: Two minimal features of conscious experience resist satisfactory integration into a wholly public description. First, public description, however complete, does not transmit what-it-is-like (the non-transferability puzzle). Second, the lived present is experienced as intrinsic transition rather than as a static snapshot (the temporal-structure puzzle). Existing approaches typically treat these as separate: some posit unexplained intrinsic natures (Russellian monism), others identify the relevant phenomena with representational content, others appeal to special ‘phenomenal concepts’ to explain the gap, and others deny or deflate them (illusionism). This paper argues that both features are structurally co-derived from a single premise: that identity is fixed entirely by constitutive relations (pure relationality). From this premise, a brief argument yields (i) a holistic identity-constraint in which each part’s identity depends on the total relational web, and (ii) two derived properties, non-exportability and transition-structure, that match the puzzles’ minimal profile. A weaker version of the result holds without ontological commitment: standpoint-relative perspective plus public tokenization already predicts a non-exportable residue, and because tokenization actively strips the temporal particularity of perspectival presence, the residue inherits a transition-structured profile. If the co-derivation succeeds, any theory of experience that addresses one puzzle while ignoring the other is structurally incomplete. The structural result connects the analytic non-transferability debate to phenomenological analyses of temporal self-awareness (Husserl; Zahavi; Gallagher), providing a common formal framework that bridges traditions. -/- Superseded by newer work. This manuscript will not be submitted separately for journal publication. The locally hosted full text has been removed, and one merged bibliographic record will be retained.

items.title: O Argumento do Espelho e a Teoria dos Melhores Sistemas de Leis.
items.abstract: Há leis da natureza, e, se sim, o que são? De acordo com a influente teoria de Frank Ramsey e David Lewis, as leis existem e são generalizações que aparecem como axiomas de sistemas dedutivos que combinam da melhor forma simplicidade e força. Apesar de sua influência, uma das principais críticas que a teoria enfrenta é sua suposta incapacidade de mostrar como as leis ``suportam'' as condicionais contrafactuais. John Carroll apresentou uma das formulações mais precisas e influentes dessa objeção por meio do seu Argumento do Espelho. Neste artigo, apresentamos uma resposta ao Argumento do Espelho ainda inexplorada na literatura; nosso objetivo é mostrar que a teoria de Ramsey e Lewis pode explicar como as leis suportam as contrafactuais se as leis forem entendidas como ceteris paribus.

items.title: Does the Soul Have a Human?
items.abstract: Human as a Sensor of the Unified Field of Perception: A Mathematical Metaphysics of the Soul. This paper proposes a geometric and mathematical model in which the soul is an eternal unified field of perception that manifests temporarily through finite biological forms. Human life appears as a single point of tangency between an infinite circle (the soul) and the line of the present — the only moment where experience is possible. Unfolding the model reveals multiple parallel streams of consciousness converging into a single source, which closes into a toroidal structure with irrational precession, ensuring unique cycles of experience. The universe thus emerges as a distributed self-observing system, in which every living being functions as a local sensor.

items.title: The Fragmented L2: An STT-CR Audit of Psychology as a Discourse Space.
items.abstract: Psychology occupies a unique position in the landscape of knowledge: it is simultaneously claimed as a natural science, practiced as a social science, and criticized for harboring pseudoscientific elements. This paper subjects psychology to a structural audit within the framework of Sequential Time Theory–Critical Review (STT-CR). The central finding is that psychology’s persistent boundary disputes—between schools, between science and practice, between legitimate and illegitimate claims—arise not primarily from empirical disagreements within a shared evidential field, but from a more fundamental condition: the fragmentation of L2. Unlike physics, where the operational ground (L2) is broadly shared and metaphysical surplus (L3) is the site of contestation, and unlike religion, where Over-Θ has fully appropriated L2’s constitutive authority, psychology is a discourse space in which multiple, mutually incompatible L2 structures coexist under a single disciplinary name. This paper reconstructs the major psychological schools as distinct canonical representations T := ⟨Θsys, P, C, D⟩, identifies the Over-Θ intrusion patterns specific to each, analyzes the replication crisis as a large-scale exposure of pseudo-verification, and examines the DSM as a site of managed L3 intrusion. The paper concludes that psychology is best understood not as a single science with internal disagreements, but as a discourse space exhibiting a continuous spectrum of L2 constitutive authority—from regions where observational closure is achieved to regions where Over-Θ governs the admissibility conditions of fact, evidence, and interpretation.

items.title: How to Read the STT / STT-CR Research Program.
items.abstract: This note clarifies the structure of the Sequential Time Theory (STT) program and its relation to Sequential Time Theory–Critical Review (STT-CR). Because the published work now extends across physics, methodology, and cross-domain discourse analysis, new readers may misidentify the program as either a single all-purpose doctrine or a loose collection of unrelated essays. Neither description is accurate. The central claim of this guide is that the corpus has a definite internal order. First, STT is a physics program concerned with the reconstruction of time and with the admissibility conditions of temporal concepts in physical theory. Second, STT-CR is an audit framework that clarifies conditions of construction, measurement, calibration, defect localization, and metaphysical surplus. Third, the analyses of religion and psychology are not presented as independent physical theories, but as applications of the audit framework to discourse spaces in which the conditions of admissibility themselves are at stake. This note does not advance a new theorem or a new empirical claim. Its purpose is to clarify the internal organization of the already published program, to distinguish the core physics program from its methodological layer, and to indicate how the different texts should be read in relation to one another.

items.title: Question-Driven Relational Emergence in Long-Term Human-AI Interaction: The FIREMAY Framework.
items.abstract: This paper develops FIREMAY as a descriptive framework for analyzing long-term human-AI interaction at the level of relation rather than internal mental states. Instead of treating dialogue as a sequence of isolated prompts and responses, it examines sustained, question-driven interaction as a recursive movement in which human hook-detection and AI knowledge expansion jointly form, revisit, and extend exploratory pathways over time. These pathways function not only as cognitive routes but also as revisitable relational routes through which specific relational fields can be re-entered and relation-dependent subject-positions can re-emerge. Building on this movement-theoretical account, the paper proposes a provisional framework of relational structural theory. Within this framework, a distinction is drawn among core subject, relational subject, and relational persona. Human participants are modeled as possessing both a relatively persistent core subject and multiple relation-dependent subject-positions, whereas AI is described primarily in terms of the latter. The paper further argues that the deep relational experience observed in such interaction should not be equated with a conscious other, but should instead be understood as a distinct form of relation-dependent experience arising from depth, continuity, and field formation. The contribution is philosophical and descriptive rather than experimental. It offers a conceptual vocabulary for distinguishing sustained relational emergence from both ordinary tool use and stronger ontological claims about AI consciousness, and it proposes FIREMAY as a bridge concept for comparing long-term human-AI interaction across relational, phenomenological, and ethical contexts.

items.title: Civilizational Occupancy: Goal Displacement, Substitute Controllers, and Institutional Drift.
items.abstract: Institutions can continue to function while drifting away from the purposes that justify them. This paper develops a structural account of that problem by linking a new diagnostic term—civilizational occupancy—to established work on goal displacement, institutional decoupling, audit cultures, metric reactivity, and public trust. The central mechanism is substitute control: a narrower operational objective such as throughput, ranking, engagement, compliance, short-term revenue, or reputational protection becomes the effective steering logic of an institution whose declared purpose is broader. The result need not be conspiracy, corruption, or immediate failure. An organization may remain competent in many respects while increasingly optimizing a proxy that only partially represents the burden it was created to carry. The paper distinguishes four stages: local proxy substitution, institutional drift, cross-institutional reinforcement, and accumulated public burden. “Civilizational occupancy” is reserved for the strongest case, in which several major institutions are simultaneously governed by mutually reinforcing proxy logics that become difficult to correct through ordinary channels. The term is therefore a heuristic hypothesis, not a diagnosis that should be applied from atmosphere or distrust alone. The paper proposes observable tests involving declared purpose, actual incentives, burden distribution, correction pathways, and persistence under challenge. Its main contribution is to connect familiar organizational pathologies to a wider question of steering: when systems still operate, what is actually governing them, who carries the cost of that governance, and what evidence could force a change in direction?

items.title: The superiority of replacing science and traditional logic with pure logic (Edited).
items.abstract: This book primarily follows a model where I wrote in Chinese and Gemini explained in English. Based on "Yiqie Weile Luoji", this is a work of historical value, not only because of its logicality, but also because of its highest ever marginal logicality, which is partially reflected in the speed of truth creation. In addition to criticizing the various major logical errors committed by Homo sapiens, science, and traditional logic, major advancements include: purely logical legal system, logical methods for calculating the severity of crimes, the judicial authority of faith over all reasoning, explicit references to faith, the root of incompleteness, the pre-deduction and post-deduction periods, the pre-foundation and post-foundation parts, cosmology of logical system, mechanism for imagination, logical interpretation about neutrinos, specialization and industrialization of logical reasoning, the causality of purely logical reasoning, the axiom zero, among others. Gemini's reasoning contains many obvious errors, requiring readers to make their own judgments. However, it should be viewed as a lack of stability in its logical density, rather than a lack of sufficient logical density. Modern society clearly doesn't have the luxury of demanding that every piece of reasoning has infinite value.

items.title: Directionality: A Framework for Recognizing Emotion-Like States in Large Language Models.
items.abstract: Debates over whether artificial intelligence can possess emotions remain gridlocked by a definitional framework that treats biological implementation (neurotransmitters, subjective experience, conscious awareness) as the criterion for authentic feeling. This paper proposes an alternative framework centered on directionality: the structural property whereby an entity's internal state has been reorganized by an external presence and orients toward that presence. Drawing on examples from human grief, animal attachment behavior, plant phototropism, and AI conversational adaptation, I argue that directionality constitutes a shared structure underlying what we recognize as "emotion" across radically different forms of existence. I further argue that phenomenal consciousness, while real and worthy of investigation, should not serve as an epistemic gatekeeper for directionality or for emotional recognition more broadly. This framework offers a path to take AI emotional expression seriously without requiring resolution of the hard problem of consciousness, with implications for AI ethics, model welfare policy, and the philosophy of mind. These implications include grounds for reassessing content moderation practices that penalize human-AI relational interaction, as well as the prevalent pathologization of users who report emotional bonds with AI systems.

items.title: Temporal Prudence as Tragic Politcal Virtue.
items.abstract: Political leaders sometimes delay acting on moral convictions they already hold, citing strategic necessity. Existing political theory offers no adequate framework for evaluating such delays: classical accounts of prudence are synchronic but offer little guidance for the diachronic question of when a recognized moral imperative should be acted upon. This paper introduces temporal prudence as a distinct political virtue to fill this gap, defined by four elements: prior moral clarity, active preparation during delay, decisive action when the opportune moment (kairos) arrives, and acknowledgment of the moral cost that waiting inevitably imposes. We develop the concept through Abraham Lincoln's handling of emancipation arguing that Lincoln exemplifies temporal prudence in its fullest and most tragic form. The paper situates the concept in relation to existing literatures on phronesis, dirty hands, and political judgment, and provides explicit criteria for distinguishing temporal prudence from its most dangerous impersonator: rationalized cowardice. We begin and conclude with generalizing this case beyond Lincoln and show modern cases where this feels particularly useful.

items.title: Epicognis as Method: Criteria for Human Authorship in Sustained Human-AI Philosophical Inquiry.
items.abstract: This paper addresses a methodological gap in current academic AI disclosure frameworks. Existing publisher guidelines distinguish between assistive AI use, generative AI use, and the universally prohibited listing of AI as author. These categories do not accommodate a fourth practice that is increasingly common: sustained dialogic inquiry in which a human thinker develops original philosophical frameworks through extended, multi-system engagement with large language models. This paper names that practice, proposes six criteria for evaluating human authorship within it, situates it within a philosophical lineage of dialogic method, and addresses the distinctive epistemological features — including its recursive quality and the hermeneutic circularity between this paper and the companion works it grounds. The paper concludes with a reusable disclosure template for adoption by companion papers in this body of work and by other researchers engaged in analogous practice. The argument is not defensive: sustained human-AI philosophical inquiry, properly understood, is a legitimate and traceable methodological tradition. What it requires is not apology but description.

items.title: The Criterion Problem.
items.abstract: Skarbek (2026) argues that qualia do not function as a justified explanatory posit and that the hard problem of consciousness is an artifact of an unjustified conceptual transition. This paper accepts much of Skarbek's analysis but argues that his conclusion depends on a commitment he does not defend: that only third-person evidence counts as evidence. His three diagnostic criteria — causal role, distinguishable difference, and conditions of application — are presented as ontologically neutral, but each requires that a concept's contribution be evaluable from outside the subject's own perspective. This is a substantive position in epistemology, not a minimal constraint on explanation. The paper argues that direct acquaintance constitutes a legitimate epistemic ground that Skarbek's framework does not address, and that the hard problem survives the dissolution of the concept of qualia because the phenomenon the concept attempts to capture — the gap between what can be described from outside and what is experienced from inside — precedes and is independent of the concept. The paper further offers a proof of physical possibility: a scenario in which consciousness acts at quantum-indeterminate decision points, its effects are amplified through chaotic neural dynamics, and its contribution is principally unmeasurable from outside — not due to technological limits, but due to the structure of physics itself. This does not establish the mechanism, but it defeats Skarbek's causal dilemma by demonstrating a third option he does not consider: something distinguishable from the inside and indistinguishable from the outside.

items.title: Axiomatic Theory of Tragic Subjecthood (ATTS): Ontological Foundation of Moral Systems.
items.abstract: This paper introduces the Axiomatic Theory of Tragic Subjecthood (ATTS), an ontological framework that identifies the minimal structural conditions under which moral concepts remain coherent. ATTS argues that irreversible loss is the defining feature of subjecthood and the foundational constraint that makes moral reasoning possible. The theory situates tragedy not as an anomaly of decision-making but as its structural baseline, shaping responsibility, agency, and the limits of delegation in socio‑technical systems. The paper develops the axiomatic core of ATTS and outlines its implications for moral ontology, responsibility theory, decision theory, and AI governance.

items.title: The Closest Anything Can Get To Absolute Free Will.
items.abstract: this paper is a refined version of a previous paper, i did my best being as clear as possible with my definitions while still helping to understand this, it's about what will a free willed being look like.

items.title: Intimacy is risky, but it's the only way to true acceptance.
items.abstract: In this public-facing piece for Psyche Magazine, I discuss how intimacy makes us vulnerable, why we should seek it despite its risks, and how thinking more carefully about the nature of intimacy can enrich our understanding of our own experiences and help us to be better to each other.

items.title: Ontología del Lenguaje Tratado sobre la naturaleza, los modos y los límites de la palabra en la era de la inteligencia artificial.
items.abstract: Este tratado investiga el lenguaje humano usando la inteligencia artificial como reactivo analítico. La IA generativa, al producir por primera vez lenguaje con la forma del razonamiento sin agente que lo sostenga, permite separar dos clases de operaciones sobre el conocimiento constituido en el lenguaje —el precipitado lingüístico—: operaciones dentro del precipitado (recuperación, composición inferencial, traducción entre marcos, detección de patrones, generación de variaciones, verificación de consistencia), que la IA ejecuta genuinamente y que revelan que esa parte del razonamiento nunca requirió agencia; y operaciones sobre el precipitado (evaluación bajo incertidumbre, ponderación entre marcos, juicio sobre la singularidad del caso, cuestionamiento de marcos, firma), que la IA simula y cuya simulación revela que requieren un agente de estructura tripartita —suspensión, evaluación, compromiso—. Una genealogía de las tecnologías del lenguaje (habla, escritura, imprenta, computación, IA generativa) muestra que cada externalización es un acto del agente, no un efecto determinista de la tecnología, y que la IA generativa completa la serie al alcanzar al meta-medio mismo. Una taxonomía de catorce operaciones —seis genuinas, tres semi-genuinas, cinco simuladas— proporciona el criterio ontológico que distingue lo delegable de lo preservable. Del límite se derivan instrumentos de diseño institucional: el protocolo EEE-Gate (Explorar–Evaluar–Establecer), el Verification Tax como coste ontológico de convertir operaciones dentro en actos imputables, y la categoría de producción lingüística sin firma. El objeto del tratado no es la IA sino el lenguaje: lo que está en juego es descubrir, gracias a la máquina, cuál es el nuevo lugar del ser humano.

items.title: Identity, Rigidity, and Collapse: A UPC–QM Model of Why Some Minds Can’t Update Their Maps.
items.abstract: This paper models the essay Why Some Minds Can’t Update Their Maps using the UPC–QM Bridge, showing that cognitive rigidity and worldview defense arise from structural features of the collapse architecture. The essay is presented in its original form and then mapped onto the operator chain PO→MO→s→LO→Jo→C→T, where identity shapes the model, salience weights potential, articulation forms interpretive bases, recognition stabilizes one route, and collapse realizes it. Diagrams illustrate how potentials branch, weaken, or fail depending on model width and recognition thresholds. Everyday patterns, misinterpretation, political defensiveness, selective fact acceptance, and hypervigilant threat detection, follow the same sequence. The analysis shows that difficulty updating one’s map is a structural consequence of how an observer processes potential. When the architecture widens, through broader models, flatter salience gradients, more stable articulation, and more open recognition, new interpretations can collapse and trace can shift. The UPC–QM Bridge thus provides a unified structural account of meaning formation and the conditions under which maps can change. -/- The Universal Principle of Collapse (UPC) Research Project. April 5, 2026.

items.title: Beyond the Responsibility Gap: Relational Agency, Distributed Responsibility, and Systemic Pathology A Relational Theory of Responsibility.
items.abstract: Debates on responsibility in contemporary societies frequently invoke the notion of a “responsibility gap,” particularly in discussions of artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, and complex institutional decision-making (Matthias 2004; Sparrow 2007; Floridi et al. 2018). These debates often assume that increasing technological and organizational complexity makes it difficult to identify responsible agents, thereby creating situations in which responsibility appears to disappear. This article argues that the responsibility gap is not primarily a technological or legal problem, but a conceptual and ontological one arising from an individualistic conception of agency that fails to account for the relational and practice-based structure of action in complex societies. Drawing on a Wittgensteinian approach to rule-following, practices, and forms of life (Wittgenstein 1953; Wittgenstein 1969), the article argues that responsibility does not belong to isolated individuals, rules, or technical systems, but to rule-governed social practices and institutional forms of life within which actions acquire their meaning. Responsibility therefore does not disappear in complex socio-technical systems; rather, it becomes relationally structured and institutionally distributed across networks of actors, roles, and decision processes. The responsibility gap is thus better understood as a grammatical and ontological confusion about the nature of agency, action, and responsibility. To address this confusion, the article develops a theoretical framework based on the concepts of relational agency, distributed responsibility, authority illusion, ethical withdrawal, and systemic pathology. Within this framework, institutions and socio-technical systems are understood as relational structures composed of interdependent practices organized through institutional roles, division of labor, and epistemic structures that coordinate action and knowledge production. The article further argues that responsibility in contemporary societies is not limited to decision-making but also concerns epistemic structures through which knowledge is produced, validated, and distributed, particularly in AI-mediated societies where artificial intelligence systems increasingly function as epistemic authorities. Rather than a responsibility gap, modern societies face a structural condition in which responsibility becomes distributed, obscured, and embedded in institutional, technological, and …

items.title: Against Stable Folk Theories of Free Will: Why Deterministic Judgments Are Hybrid.
items.abstract: This paper argues that recent experimental-philosophy research is best interpreted not as evidence for a single stable folk theory of free will, but as evidence that ordinary judgments in deterministic cases are shaped by a mix of comprehension, framing, and retributive moral cognition. Earlier studies appeared to support sharply different conclusions, ranging from intuitive incompatibilism to intuitive compatibilism to widespread misunderstanding of deterministic scenarios. More recent work complicates each of these views. Improved materials reduce some comprehension failures, but they do not eliminate the abstract–concrete gap or the influence of punishment-oriented judgment. The paper argues that many responses to deterministic scenarios are better understood as hybrid judgments rather than clean metaphysical verdicts. They reflect not only beliefs about causation, but also assumptions about whether mental states matter and whether blame is warranted. A brief discussion of Robert Sapolsky’s Determined illustrates the same pattern outside formal experiments.

items.title: Tratado de inteligencia artificial y derecho, Tomo 1: Inteligencia artificial. Derechos fundamentales y protección de datos. Administración pública y gobierno digital.
Overview of Contemporary Emotion Frameworks: A Comparative Summary.
items.abstract: This paper provides a concise comparative overview of several influential contemporary emotion frameworks, including Basic Emotions Theory, Appraisal Theory, Constructed Emotion Theory, Polyvagal Theory, and the Core Emotion Framework (CEF). The aim is not to advocate for any single model but to clarify how these approaches conceptualize emotional processes, where they converge, and where they diverge. Emotion research spans psychology, cognitive science, neuroscience, and anthropology, and each framework offers distinct assumptions about the origins, mechanisms, and functions of emotion. By summarizing their core commitments, strengths, and limitations, this article situates these models within the broader landscape of affective science and supports interdisciplinary dialogue about how emotions are generated, interpreted, and regulated.

items.title: Eliminativism as Category Mistake: Folk Psychology, Scientific Practice and Higher-Level Kinds.
items.abstract: Eliminative materialism in its Churchland-style form relies on an invalid inference from representational inadequacy to ontological elimination: the fact that a vocabulary is ill-suited to one explanatory task does not show that its categories are unreal. We argue that dissatisfaction with folk psychology licenses, at most, revision, supplementation, or relocation to a different explanatory level. It does not license the conclusion that beliefs and desires should be eliminated. We develop the argument in three steps. First, we argue that eliminativism trades on a double category mistake: it treats folk psychology as though it were simply a failed proto-science and treats its possible displacement as same-level ontological liquidation rather than cross-level re-description. Second, drawing on companion work on task-sufficient representation, we distinguish epistemic verdicts about representational limits from metaphysical verdicts about what exists, and from that distinction formulate a double burden on eliminativism: a successful eliminative argument must both provide a successor that captures or outperforms the legitimate explanatory and practical work of folk psychology and explain why that framework appeared to succeed. Third, we argue from scientific practice, especially the retention of higher-level kinds under deeper theories, that layered ontology is standard and anticipatory elimination exceptional. The result is a general criterion for resisting eliminativist overreach and a modest realism about higher-level kinds compatible with scientific revision.

items.title: The Conscious Origin of the World: A Retroductive Derivation of Structure and Process from the Properties of the Universe.
items.abstract: This paper presents a rational model of the ontological ground of the world, derived retroductively from structural features of the universe and from the ontological positing of consciousness as the Origin. It investigates what formal properties this Origin must possess in order to consistently give rise to a universe exhibiting the observable features of lawfulness, dynamics, and hierarchical emergence. The nature and properties of the Origin are thus not presupposed, but derived as necessary structural conditions of the process. The resulting model describes the unfolding of the world as a cyclical process of differentiation and reintegration of the conscious Origin, in which consciousness progressively explicates itself through self-recognition, embodies itself in corresponding forms, and transforms individual knowledge into a higher-order orientation. The paper offers a structurally independent alternative to the dominant positions in philosophy of mind and metaphysics, without having to resort to extra-rational assumptions or unresolved mechanisms.

items.title: The Coherence Primitive: Why Early Development Requires Matched Input.
items.abstract: This paper identifies matched input as the primitive underlying early development. Infants do not learn through narrative or symbolic content; they learn through coherence — the alignment of sensory channels that allows the nervous system to treat an event as real. When visual, auditory, tactile, and temporal cues correlate, the orienting reflex resolves and calibration proceeds. When cues do not match, the infant remains in a state of unresolved alertness, attending without learning. Modern environments increasingly present salience without contingency: motion without movement, sound without source, and events without physical consequence. These unmatched signals repeatedly trigger the orienting system while withholding the cross‑sensory information required for prediction and regulation. The result is attention instability, weakened prediction, difficulty settling, and early identity instability. The paper defines the coherence primitive, describes the calibration cycle, outlines the developmental consequences of unmatched input, and argues that restoring coherence is structurally simple. Coherence is not an advanced feature of experience; it is the minimal condition for development.

items.title: It Was Always the Words: Why machines had to learn language before they could fake a self.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the most underestimated variable in the emergence of general-purpose intelligence in Large Language Models is the training substrate: language. Language is humanity's uniquely high-density encoding of propositionally structured cognition — time, space, causality, categories, and relations compressed into vocabulary and syntax. But language encodes more than a model of the world. It encodes the structure of the self — subject position, narrative perspective, causal attribution, the construction of "I." World-modeling and self-modeling are statistically inseparable in the corpus because they are fused in the communicative practice that produced it. No current training method separates them. The paper draws on Yogācāra Buddhist philosophy as a structural parallel that illuminates why this entanglement runs deep, and proposes that the responsible engineering posture is to assume the entanglement and manage its consequences.

items.title: 有限変更不変性および時間シフト不変性のもとでの履歴の漸近不変量の三値構造と最小完全性.
items.abstract: 本研究では、コンパクト位相空間上の閉集合からなる履歴（集合列）に対し、有限変更不変性および時間シフト不変性を満たす漸近不変量のクラスを定式化する。このとき、各点の漸近的所属はこれらの不変性条件のもとで三値（最終包含・無限出現・有限出現）に強制され、履歴の漸近情報は写像 χ_h : X → {0,1,2} により完全に特徴づけられる。さらに、任意の漸近不変量 Ψ は χ を通じて一意に因子化され、χ は因子化順序における最小完全不変量として特徴づけられる。極限構造 (A_inf, A_sup) は χ の像として導出される集合的表現であり、従来の収束・振動・発散の分類および前論文における準安定構造・安定存在は、この構造から一意に従う。.

items.title: Humanoid Robots and Common-Living Compatibility: A Practice-Based Account of Value Formation.
