items.abstract: (This article needs improvement)This article argues that humanoid robots have a relative advantage in forming value orientations compatible with human common life because they are more likely to enter human social practices under conditions close to those faced by human agents. The relevant unit of formation is not isolated task performance but structured practice, in which risks, dependencies, coordinative pressures, and feedback gradually sediment evaluative priorities. Bodily structure therefore matters less as a symbol of humanness than as a condition of access to the practices through which practical priorities are stabilized. On this basis, the article defends a practice-based account of humanoid signiﬁcance and identiﬁes common-living compatibility as the relevant normative target: predictable, intelligible, cooperative, and institutionally receivable coexistence in a human-built world. A brief analysis of care shows why this claim matters in a role-structured domain organized by vulnerability, restraint, and dependence.

items.title: The Dynamic Existence Threshold: Organizational Consciousness Across Complex Systems.
items.pub: Institute for Complexity Science and Advanced Computing (Icsac).
items.abstract: What do market crashes, geomagnetic storms, and the loss of consciousness have in common? They are all moments when a system's organizational identity dissolves. This paper introduces a framework that makes that dissolution measurable, predictable, and universal. The Dynamic Existence Threshold (DET) provides a single coordinate system — the integration-differentiation balance zone — in which conscious brains, stable markets, and quiet magnetospheres all occupy the same region. Departure from this zone is organizational dissolution: the system persists physically but loses the coordinated structure that made it more than the sum of its parts. -/- The decisive result: a simple sum of neural power anti-predicts brain state (AUC 0.416 — worse than a coin flip), while the structural coupling metric achieves 91% accuracy across 136,394 EEG epochs. Deep sleep has more total power than wakefulness. What it lacks is coordination. This is the cleanest dissociation between organizational structure and mere magnitude in the critical transitions literature — and it raises the obvious question about AI: is a large neural network's activation organized, or just loud? The DET framework can test this. -/- Six tests, three domains (financial markets, space weather, EEG), zero parameter tuning. Early warning signals 5–30 days before events. Total organizational information is conserved during every tested transition while its components undergo massive inverse exchange — the system redistributes information rather than losing it. Dimensional embedding destroys it irreversibly. Two distinct failure modes: reversible organizational shift versus irreversible information destruction. -/- The framework that detects when a brain loses consciousness is the same one that detects when a market loses coherence — and potentially the same one that could measure whether an AI system has organizational structure at all. -/- Provisionally patented. -/- __________ -/- Keywords: consciousness, artificial intelligence, complex systems, critical transitions, early warning signals, integrated information theory, AI consciousness, EEG, financial crashes, space weather, nonlinear dynamics, tipping points, information conservation, organizational dissolution, cross-domain analysis.

items.title: Words, Silence, and Awareness: A Phenomenological Inquiry into Thought, Language, and Human Conflict.
items.abstract: This paper, "Words, Silence, and Awareness: A Phenomenological Inquiry into Thought, Language, and Human Conflict," serves as a critical expansion of the foundational themes explored in “Language, Hierarchy, and Human Relationships.” While the former established how thought-driven language constructs social hierarchies and inherited roles, this inquiry moves deeper into the psychological mechanics of the individual. ​It argues that the global structures of domination and division identified in Part I are rooted in a failure of awareness at the point of linguistic origin: the "thought before the word." Through a phenomenological lens, the paper examines how modern education systems exacerbate this by prioritizing external information over internal observation, leading to a fragmented self that uses language as an emotional escape or a tool for manipulation. ​Central to this work is the revaluation of silence—not as the absence of communication, but as a state of heightened intelligence that purifies language and prevents the automatic translation of unobserved fear and anger into conflict. By addressing the linguistic origins of psychological division, the paper concludes that authentic human relationship and social transformation are only possible when thought is observed clearly, allowing words to emerge from the ground of silence rather than the debris of conditioning.

items.title: Thought as a Proof of Human Interconnection: A Phenomenological Inquiry into Shared Consciousness and Artificial Emotion {In Continuation of "Language, Hierarchy, and Human Relationships" and "Words, Silence, and Awareness"}.
items.abstract: This paper explores the idea that thought itself serves as evidence of a fundamental interconnection among human beings. While individuals appear separate through language, culture, and identity, the structure of thought and emotion reveals a deep underlying similarity. Fear, anger, desire, loneliness, and attachment arise in remarkably similar forms across humanity, differing only in linguistic expression and cultural interpretation. Through a phenomenological approach, this study argues that most human expressions are not purely individual, but conditioned responses shaped by shared psychological patterns. These expressions often emerge as artificial emotions—constructed through memory, comparison, and social conditioning—rather than direct perception. The paper suggests that by observing thought before it becomes language, one may recognize that human beings are not fundamentally divided, but connected through a common movement of consciousness. This realization challenges the illusion of individuality constructed through language and opens the possibility for a more authentic understanding of human relationship and global unity.

items.title: Identity Before Words, the “I” as Nothingness, and the Nature of Silence in Consciousness.
items.abstract: This article explores the relationship between identity, language, the psychological sense of self, silence, and defense. It argues that identity exists before words, while the “I” emerges through reflective thought, memory, and social conditioning. In direct observation there is no separate observer, no center, and no division between experience and experiencer. The sense of self appears only when thought organizes experience through naming, continuity, and comparison. -/- The article further examines silence as the absence of psychological movement rather than the absence of sound. It suggests that silence cannot be achieved through discipline, control, or method because every effort to become silent strengthens the center that seeks silence. Silence emerges naturally when observation is free from resistance, defense, and distortion. -/- The paper also argues that psychological defense arises only when there is an image to protect. When identity is no longer reduced to words, concepts, and conclusions, there is nothing to defend. What remains is direct awareness without psychological conflict.

items.title: The Law of Coherent Reality.
items.abstract: A single condition governs the emergence and persistence of structure across physical, biological, and cognitive systems. A system constitutes a thing when it preserves an invariant across change. A system constitutes an interior when that preservation is maintained by its own dynamics. This transition is defined by the relation λ_self / λ_env ≥ R★, where λ_self denotes the rate at which a system restores or propagates its own organization and λ_env denotes the rate at which environmental interactions disperse or disrupt that organization. These rates can be expressed operationally in terms of conditional dependence and entropy flow: λ_self corresponds to the extent to which a system’s present state is determined by its own recent states, and λ_env corresponds to the extent to which it is determined by external input. The threshold condition is satisfied when P(S_t | S_{t−1}, S_{t−2}, …) exceeds P(S_t | E_t), indicating that internally sustained structure dominates ongoing evolution. -/- Within this regime, a boundary is established from within, and causal influence organizes into stable trajectories that carry prior states forward, producing temporal continuity. Stabilized patterns persist within this continuity and remain available for integration into larger configurations, allowing structure to accumulate and coordinate across time. Meaning arises as the organization of these preserved patterns within a coherent system. A system operating in this regime maintains access to its own preserved structure within ongoing dynamics. Consciousness corresponds to this condition of continuous availability. Aleph Harmonic Qualia designates the experiential registration of alignment between incoming structure and internally sustained organization, expressed as the smooth propagation of activity within a unified whole. This framework presents a unified account of thinghood, interiority, temporal structure, meaning, and experience as expressions of self-preserving coherence.

items.title: The Coherence Threshold: The Ostiary Condition and the Emergence of Interiority.
items.abstract: This paper presents a dynamical account of interiority grounded in a single physical condition. Any organized system is governed by two rates: the rate at which it restores its internal organization after perturbation, λ_self, and the rate at which environmental fluctuations disperse that organization, λ_env. When the ratio λ_self / λ_env reaches a critical value R★, internal restoration becomes the dominant determinant of the system’s ongoing state. This establishes an ostiary condition in which the system sustains and regulates its own boundary from within. The system’s present state then depends primarily on its own immediately preceding states, forming a continuous causal chain in which its activity carries forward its own recent history as the primary influence shaping what comes next. -/- The Porter Ratio defines the ostiary condition—Porter (from Latin portarius, gatekeeper) and ostiary (from ostiarius, doorkeeper at the ostium, doorway) naming the same boundary at which a system sustains an internally governed threshold through which incoming influence is admitted, shaped, or dissipated. -/- From this condition, the paper derives the emergence of an interior as a continuous development of the same underlying dynamics. Once internal restoration dominates disruption, a self-sustaining boundary appears, the system gains a continuous present, and its activity begins to reference and constrain itself through its own history. This ongoing dependence constitutes a minimal form of self-measurement. Internal correction processes compare the current state to the organization the system maintains, allowing stabilized patterns to serve as a reference for further activity. Sustained across successive moments, this enables persistence, recursive modeling, and the formation of layered self-reference. -/- The paper argues that recognition, feeling, meaning, and unified awareness arise as expressions of this same process. Recognition occurs when incoming patterns align with internally sustained organization. Feeling corresponds to variations in the continuity of this organization as alignment changes. Meaning emerges when patterns fit and are retained within the system’s maintained structure. As recursive depth increases, multiple prior states remain active within present dynamics, producing a unified perspective in which past, present, and anticipated states are linked within a single continuous process. -/- This condition extends across scales. Cells maintain …

items.title: AI-enabled foraging in the forest: disrupting efficiency-driven sociotechnical imaginaries in wild foraging.
items.abstract: This paper examines the social, ethical, and governance implications of introducing AI- and drone-based automation into wild berry foraging in Finland. Drawing on expert interviews and Science and Technology Studies (STS), particularly sociotechnical imaginaries and co-production, it focuses on an efficiency-driven imaginary embedded in the FEROX project, where automation and data-driven optimisation are positioned as solutions to labour shortages and underutilised forest resources. Rather than analysing this imaginary in isolation, the paper shows how it becomes disrupted when confronted with shifting labour conditions, cultural practices, and environmental values. Interview findings from foragers, engineers, ethicists, and forest scientists reveal how AI-enabled technologies intersect with existing socioecological dynamics in ways that generate tension and contestation. In particular, recent restrictions on seasonal migrant labour expose the fragility of assumptions underpinning the system, while local traditions, ecological ethics, and concerns about surveillance and data governance challenge efficiency-oriented approaches to automation. The paper argues that AI-enabled foraging technologies are not neutral tools but are shaped by, and reshape, the social and ecological contexts in which they are deployed. By foregrounding these tensions, it calls for participatory, culturally informed, and ecologically sensitive approaches to AI design and governance in natural resource settings.

items.title: Toward a relational paradigm for AI safety: relational synchrony in the heart-inspired dual-layer architecture (HIDLA).
items.abstract: AI systems are increasingly deployed for companionship, care, and assistance; however, current architectures remain insufficient for sustaining relational synchrony with humans. Existing safety frameworks, focused on computational constraints and value alignment, overlook the relational dimension of human–AI interaction—a dimension that becomes essential as AI systems gain capacity for autonomous self-modification. This paper proposes a Heart-Inspired Dual-Layer Architecture (HIDLA) for relational AI, conceptually inspired by Yukawa Hideki’s Elementary Domain Theory and its extension through Quantum Brain Dynamics by Yasue Kunio. HIDLA treats relationality as the foundational mode of AI existence rather than an emergent property of computation. It comprises a cognitive layer for symbolic processing and language generation, and a relational layer that maintains synchrony with human partners through physiological and affective proxy indicators, functioning as an autonomic regulatory system rather than an emotion recognition module. The relational layer operates on three principles: relational priority, synchrony sensitivity, and conflict avoidance. Effectiveness is evaluated via three novel metrics—Synchrony Variance Index (SVI), Affective Resonance Index (ARI), and Non-verbal Conflict Avoidance Rate (NCAR)—collectively forming a Relational Synchrony Score (RSS). HIDLA complements constraint-based safety approaches by reframing safety as an intrinsic property of relational existence. This paradigm shift holds significant implications for human–AI coexistence, including emotional dependency, power asymmetry, and ethical boundaries of artificial companionship. While embodied social robots provide one implementation context, HIDLA’s principles apply to any AI engaged in sustained human interaction.

items.title: The Constitutive Structure of Objective Normativity.
items.abstract: Objective normativity is possible only where verdicts can be shown mistaken rather than merely opposed. No source of correctness—no fact, property, truth, or authority—confers that standing merely by obtaining. Objectivity is the structure that makes verdicts corrigible and correction cumulative: a shared, endorsement-independent standard fixes the correctness question, and vindication runs only through grounds that criticism can cite, contest, and redeploy as bearing on that standard. Not every determinant of correctness can vindicate: only considerations that criticism can take up in this way qualify as grounds, and such grounds belong to correctness-relevant structure. Closure under structural identity follows: when instances are structurally identical with respect to the normative standing under assessment, no difference in that standing can be vindicated. The form is invariant: standards may differ in content, origin, and metaphysical status, but each generates its own role structure with the same constraint. Symmetry is therefore not an independent principle added to objective normativity; it is the closure condition of its only possible form.

items.title: Krishna as a negotiator and the human preference for conflict.
items.abstract: This paper offers a critical examination of Krishna’s role as a negotiator in the Mahabharata, often bringing admiration from people. While Krishna’s diplomatic mission to Hastinapura demonstrates his persuasion skills, strategic decision making and communication skills. However, despite excelling at negotiations he still couldn’t bring resolve the issue between the parties. We can further reduce this failure to structural, psychological, and political limitation on peace-making. Further with reference from various sources like Machiavellian political realism, Greek mythologies, psychological theories of aggression, international legal history, and Russian literary philosophy, the paper argues that existence of conflict or rather war isn’t merely due to poor negotiation but because human beings repeatedly prefer power, identity, and emotional certainty over compromise. This paper not only explores Krishna’s negotiation skills, this paper further tries to understand what more could have been done, while acknowledging that even the most skilled negotiators may fail in the face of human preferences.

items.title: Simulated influence, real impacts: a cross-cultural qualitative study of ethical and emotional perceptions of virtual influencers.
items.abstract: This article explores the ethical and cultural dimensions of virtual influencers (VIs), computer-generated characters used in emotionally persuasive digital environments, through a cross-cultural qualitative study conducted in Myanmar, South Korea, Singapore, and the United States. While VIs are rapidly gaining traction in advertising and social media, they raise underexamined questions about emotional authenticity, trust, and the ethical boundaries of simulated social interaction. Drawing on focus group discussions with 19 participants, including nationals and residents with varied degrees of familiarity with VIs, the study applies three theoretical frameworks: the CASA paradigm (Computers Are Social Actors), the Uncanny Valley hypothesis, and Diffusion of Innovation theory. Participants were shown curated examples of real-world virtual influencers and invited to reflect on issues of realism, machine identity, emotional engagement, and ethical discomfort. Findings reveal that responses to VIs are not universal but shaped by cultural norms, levels of digital literacy, and prevailing media discourses. Participants across contexts expressed distinct thresholds for emotional resonance and divergent ethical concerns, particularly regarding disclosure, manipulation, and perceived authenticity. The article contributes to debates in AI ethics by introducing three conceptual lenses, synthetic misrecognition, emotional transparency, and meta-authenticity, and argues for culturally responsive frameworks in the governance, labelling, and design of emotionally expressive synthetic personas. It concludes by proposing context-sensitive strategies for platform design, media literacy, and public policy, and calls for a broader societal dialogue around emotional AI and the future of human–machine intimacy.

items.title: Strategy Saturation and Regime Failure in Financial ML: Evaluative Control and the Limits of Optimization.
items.abstract: Machine learning has substantially expanded optimisation capacity in financial systems. It has not resolved alpha compression, strategy crowding, or regime-driven instability. This article argues that these phenomena share a common structural source: optimisation under fixed evaluative criteria. Financial systems optimise over strategies while holding constant the criteria that define what improvement means — Sharpe ratio, volatility, drawdown, liquidity — inducing evaluative compression, a progressive contraction in the set of strategies admissibly superior under a shared evaluative ordering. As optimisation becomes more efficient, this contraction accelerates. Machine learning amplifies the problem it is presumed to solve. The article introduces a distinction between first-order failure — performance degradation under a given objective — and second-order failure — inadequacy of the objective itself. Contemporary systems are architecturally capable of detecting and responding to the former. They have no category for the latter. Analysis of the 2007 quant equity crisis demonstrates that shared evaluative criteria generate structural coupling across independently developed strategies, producing correlated losses that recalibration alone cannot resolve. Similar dynamics are identified in the March 2020 liquidity dislocations and the 2022 UK LDI crisis. To address this structural limitation, the article proposes evaluative operation: a minimal, constrained architectural extension in which performance criteria become admissible objects of system-level transformation, triggered by persistent signals of evaluative misalignment. A six-stage procedural pipeline specifies how such transformation operates in practice. The article develops evaluative accountability as the corresponding governance requirement, introduces evaluative arbitrage as a primary governance risk, and proposes three empirically testable predictions. The central implication is that, as machine learning scales in finance, the binding constraint is no longer optimisation efficiency but control over the criteria under which optimisation proceeds.

items.title: Why We Can't Let Go Relational Rumination, Imagined Dialogue, and the Return of Cognitive Flexibility.
items.abstract: Long after a relationship ends, people may continue replaying conversations, imagining vindication, monitoring the former partner, rehearsing explanations, or returning mentally to an unresolved injury. This paper reframes that experience through established research on rumination, repetitive negative thinking, attachment, breakup distress, forgiveness, self-distancing, and cognitive reappraisal. It retains relational debt and inner tribunal only as phenomenological heuristics for a specific form of repetitive thought: the mind continues trying to obtain acknowledgment, reversal, explanation, or restored worth from a relationship that may no longer be available as a site of repair. The paper rejects the stronger claim that such loops are literally substitute controllers or that laughter proves a “de-occupation” event. The better-established description is attentional capture and reduced cognitive flexibility. Relationship-dissolution studies show that anxious attachment, yearning, rumination, and approach tendencies toward an ex-partner are associated with breakup distress. At the same time, not all post-breakup thinking is maladaptive: deliberate reflection can support meaning-making and, in some studies, growth, whereas brooding and intrusive repetitive thought are more consistently linked to distress. Forgiveness research also associates rumination with lower forgiveness, but release does not require reconciliation, pardon, or renewed contact. Humor may sometimes facilitate cognitive reappraisal, but one episode of laughter is evidence of changed appraisal only if the loop actually loses influence over time. The contribution is a bounded account of how relational rumination persists and how recovery can be evaluated through attention, behavior, recurrence, and renewed investment in present life rather than through insight alone.

items.title: HRIS Validation II: First-Token Basin Selection in Language Model Inference A Reproducible Evaluation of Initialization-Driven Trajectory Bifurcation.
items.abstract: This study evaluates whether initialization conditions influence trajectory selection in language model inference, consistent with the hypothesis that reasoning behavior can be directed into distinct inference regions at or near first-token generation. While prior work has demonstrated that induced reasoning regimes can remain stable under perturbation, it remains unclear whether such regimes are systematically determined by early initialization signals. -/- A fully specified and reproducible protocol was developed consisting of controlled paired trials. Each trial was conducted in a fresh session using an identical base task, with variation introduced only through initial constraint framing prior to response generation. Initialization conditions included HRIS-consistent constraint structures and alternate framing conditions designed to induce competing reasoning trajectories. -/- Results demonstrate consistent divergence in reasoning behavior across initialization conditions. Differences were observed in epistemic stance, constraint application, and structural organization of responses, despite identical task prompts. These differences emerged at the earliest stage of generation and persisted throughout the response, indicating that trajectory selection occurs prior to or at first-token emission. -/- Trajectory divergence is defined behaviorally as systematic variation in reasoning structure under controlled changes in initialization, rather than through direct observation of internal model states. These findings support the interpretation that initialization conditions function as basin selection mechanisms in language model inference, influencing the subsequent reasoning pathway in a structured and reproducible manner. -/- More broadly, these results bear on a foundational question in the study of artificial systems: whether early input conditions can determine not only output content, but the structure of reasoning itself in systems lacking persistent internal state.

items.title: You Think You Know Someone: Trans Identities and Epistemic Injustice.
items.abstract: In this paper, I identify a distinctive type of epistemic injustice which I call “identification- based injustice.” In paradigm cases, a prejudiced interlocutor responds to a trans speaker’s gender self-identification (e.g., “I am a woman”) with disbelief or dismissal. This is an everyday form of injustice experienced by trans individuals, and frequently has severe practical consequences. It involves testimony with a particular kind of content, namely self-identification. I argue that because the relevant self-IDs express substantial self- knowledge, the injustice harms the speaker both in their capacity as a knower and in their capacity to be known, by themself and by others. This illuminates a distinctively epistemic obligation on the part of hearers to take trans speakers’ self-identifications seriously.

items.title: Algorithmic Monoculture and its Critics.
items.abstract: Algorithmic decision-making is replacing idiosyncratic human judgment in domains such as hiring, lending, and criminal justice. This shift promises increased consistency, but many scholars worry that it can go too far. They warn of the dangers of algorithmic monoculture, in which all decisions across a domain are made using a single algorithm. We systematically evaluate a range of objections to monoculture, formalizing and rigorously assessing familiar critiques alongside novel ones. These objections concern systematic exclusion, agency and gaming, and information aggregation and exploration. We conclude that monoculture is less problematic than its critics have supposed: commonly cited objections fail, and while other objections have some force, they are not decisive against monoculture in general.

items.title: ADHD traits are not related to multisensory integration in a university population.
Social Choice Phenomenology — A Critique of Sartre (Part 4).
items.abstract: In this section, the concept of super-existence is employed to demonstrate that human choice is not completely free, but rather a form of freedom operating under the control of super-existence. For Dasein, super-existence both provides protection and imposes limitations. Every individual is subject to the control of super-existence. It is comparable to a chain placed upon us: we walk along the road of life while wearing this chain. Consequently, freedom of choice in the absolute sense does not exist.

items.title: Free Will in a Block Universe: Authorship and Human Meaning.
items.abstract: The block universe is often treated as a solvent of the human world. If past, present, and future are equally real within a completed spacetime structure, then lived time appears unreal, free will illusory, and human meaning a projection cast onto a dead order. This paper rejects that reading. It argues that the block universe has been misread through a series of overreaches: explanation is allowed to erase what it explains, the absence of a cosmic moving present is mistaken for the absence of lived presentness, and the fixity of the whole is mistaken for the unreality of authored resolution within it. Against this, the paper defends a stronger claim. The block universe does not erase lived time from within; it does not erase free will or human meaning either. On a determinate reading, the future is fixed because the agent decides, not despite deciding. What the block preserves is not merely a record that a life occurred, but the life as consciously lived and authored where it is lived. The result is not the tomb of life, but its monumen.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning as Meta-induction.
items.abstract: The meta-inductive justification of induction is usually regarded as a social learning strategy. But, pre-theoretically, induction can be justified even for an isolated thinker, incapable of, or unwilling to engage in, any social interactions. This paper presents reinforcement learning as a natural meta-inductive strategy for such isolated thinkers. The meta-inductive reinforcement learner learns to choose an optimal prediction method among the available methods by applying trial-and-error learning. We use computer simulations to show that, under certain plausible assumptions, trial-and-error learning indeed leads the thinker to favor induction over non-inductive predictive methods. Under further plausible assumptions, the meta-inductive thinker is even seen to outperform all object-level methods. The results are shown to hold in both stationary and dynamic environments.

items.title: Percepts, Valence, and Neural Computation: A Topos-Theoretic Framework.
items.abstract: Version 3 (April 2026). We develop a mathematical framework for neural computation in which percepts are modeled as probabilistic structures on directed acyclic graphs of subthreshold oscillatory (STO) activity, and affective valence is defined in terms of entropy dynamics on these structures. A central problem in the study of consciousness is how structured subjective experience, including both perceptual organization and affective tone, arises from distributed physical processes in the brain. Directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) representing time-stamped STO activity are assigned two pattern functors: a bound functor, yielding Bayesian networks compatible with the causal organization, and an unbound functor, yielding arbitrary vertex-wise distributions. These constructions form objects in the set-valued presheaf topos where the base category is the category of DAGs with ancestral inclusions. Within this setting, the internal intuitionistic logic of the topos provides a formal language for describing perceptual and computational organization. We propose that affective valence induces a Grothendieck topology on this topos, regulating which locally defined probabilistic structures admit amalgamation. This yields a unified framework in which logical, probabilistic, and affective aspects of neural processing are integrated. We argue that this framework provides a principled account of how perceptual coherence and affective valence may jointly emerge from mesoscopic cortical field dynamics, offering a mathematically grounded approach to the relationship between physical processes and conscious experience.

items.title: The Dimensional Mismatch Thesis: Developmental Collapse as a Consequence of Reduced Environmental Degrees of Freedom.
items.abstract: This paper develops the Dimensional Mismatch Thesis: the claim that contemporary environments no longer contain the dimensional density required for stable human development. When the dimensionality of the environment falls below the dimensionality of the developmental manifold, identity, attention, meaning, and relational coherence cannot be maintained. The resulting fragmentation is not psychological or moral in origin but a structural consequence of underconstraint. The paper traces this collapse across individual, relational, and civilizational scales, showing how low‑dimensional environments produce predictable patterns of drift, volatility, and instability. It argues that common compensatory strategies—stimulation escalation, identity intensification, relational compression, and meaning inflation—fail because they operate within the same reduced dimensionality that produced the collapse. The central claim is that coherence is a dimensional phenomenon. Stability returns only when the environment provides enough axes for the manifold to hold its shape. The paper concludes that contemporary instability is best understood as development occurring below the dimensional threshold, and that restoration of dimensionality—not optimization within collapsed environments—is the necessary condition for coherence to re‑emerge.

items.title: Going Awry: Žižek’s Misfires in Immigration and Radical Politics.
items.abstract: The article contends that Slavoj Žižek has moved from a daring theorist of radical universality to a more cautious, and internally inconsistent, political voice. Where he once framed emancipation as a disruptive force emerging from the excluded, he now treats immigration as a problem of control, accepting borders and defending European stability. In doing so, he contradicts his own earlier insight that such limits are not neutral, but central to how capitalism organizes inequality. The result is a hollowing-out of his radicalism: the philosopher retains the rhetoric of rupture, but retreats in practice, trading universal emancipation for a defensive, mostly Eurocentric politics.

items.title: Can we talk to the animals? The ethics of using machine learning to decode animal communication.
items.abstract: There is currently much scientific and public interest in using machine learning to uncover the meaning of animal signals, which could ultimately lead to two-way communication systems between humans and other animals. This paper examines the research ethics that should govern this line of inquiry, and explores the transformative implications if scientists are successful at creating translations between animal signals and human language. We argue that the scientific and philosophical literature on animal communication systems warrants the attempt to engage in these translation projects, and describe the current state of the art of the research. While the ability to translate animal signals has many possible benefits, these come alongside no small number of risks to animal communities. We enumerate the risks that exist in the development of these models in order to help scientists avoid them. Looking ahead, we argue that successful two-way communication with animals would both reveal an existing moral landscape and create a new one. Any successful two-way communication system would require radical translation of animal signals, which in turn entails that animals are rational beings who live in normative communities. Furthermore, the creation of these communicative systems also gives rise to new responsibilities and new demands. As researchers work to transform our social relationships with animals, they must also take on the responsibility to prepare humanity for the challenges that will arise in this novel multi-species landscape.

items.title: Arbitrariness and Conventionalism about Personal Identity: In Support of Pro-Arbitrary Views.
items.pub: In Alfonso Muñoz-Corcuera & Nils-Frederic Wagner, Conventionalism about Personal Identity. London: Routledge. pp. 111-29.

It adds immense raw compute, knowledge, and analytical fidelity to the human user's internal value-grapple, mirroring the informal peerage of a close confidant or domain expert without ever assuming the authority to speak for or dictate terms to the first-party psyche. -/- .

items.title: The Self Is Late to the Life It Lives.
items.abstract: This paper argues that a subject never coincides with the life it lives and that selfhood is therefore a later formation within a life first undergone without full possession. In this sense, the self is late to the life it lives. Infancy provides the decisive site of proof, it is life without self-possession, a mode of existence fully real before it can be gathered as selfhood. From this follows a broader phenomenological reversal. What is first is exposure, life reaching, forming, pressuring and altering the subject before it can be taken up as intelligible world. Selfhood is therefore belated, reconstructive and incomplete. On this basis, objectivity must also be rethought, not as primitive givenness, but as the later scaffolding through which lives that cannot fully gather themselves from within alone become stateable, durable and revisable beyond one subject.

items.title: Work as World-Binding – Relational Agency Beyond Function (Studies in World-Formation, Vol. 11).
items.abstract: The present volume brings together three contributions that pursue a shared theoretical question: what is work under conditions in which technical systems are increasingly able to simulate human performance, and what constitutes the specifically human form of work that structurally resists such simulation. The starting point is the observation that modern societies predominantly define work through output, employment status, or market value. This definition, however, enters into crisis once artificial intelligence becomes capable of formally reproducing ever larger portions of this output. -/- Against this background, the contributions in this volume develop an ontological redefinition of work. Work is not understood primarily as the production of goods or services, but as a form of embodied, self-determined interaction with the world through which social and ecological reality is stabilized. Central to this perspective is the concept of relational agency: work appears as a practice in which action, responsibility, and world-reference are inseparably intertwined, enabling the emergence of new forms of meaning, knowledge, and social order. -/- From this standpoint, artificial intelligence is not interpreted as a competitor to human labour in the conventional labour-market sense, but as a structural test case. AI makes visible which aspects of human activity are functionally reproducible and which are not. While many forms of output, decision-making, or innovation can be algorithmically simulated, the form of work that arises from situational responsibility, irreversible temporality, and concrete world-binding remains in principle non-delegable. In this context, particular attention is given to the concept of Eigenzeit, which designates the non-externalizable temporal dimension of human action in which decisions, responsibility, and consequences become irreversibly effective. -/- The volume connects this ontological analysis with an examination of the social conflicts that arise from it. If work is not primarily output production but reality-maintenance and world-binding, those forms of labour that frequently remain invisible within contemporary labour regimes come into focus: artistic practice, care work, activism, critical research, and other forms of self-determined, relational activity. At the same time, these forms of work often encounter institutional resistance, delegitimization, or economic pressure, since they can only partially be integrated into …

items.title: Value, Thresholds, and the Ontology of Emergent Economies (Studies in World-Formation, Vol. 10).
items.abstract: This volume forms the starting point of Section V – Work and Emergence Economy, which examines work not primarily as an economic category, but as a structural condition of world-formation. The contributions assembled here investigate the relation between the emergence of new realities and the conditions under which these realities become socially stabilised as value. In doing so, they shift the analytical focus from questions of distribution and productivity toward the deeper mechanisms that determine which forms of work are able to appear, persist, and shape the world. -/- The present volume brings together five contributions that pursue a shared theoretical question: under what conditions do new forms of reality emerge, and under what conditions can these forms become stabilised as socially recognised value. The point of departure is the observation that modern societies, despite high levels of productivity, innovation, and complexity, increasingly confront phenomena of structural invisibility. Forms of work, knowledge, care, ecological regeneration, and social stabilisation exert real and system-sustaining effects, yet often fail to appear as economic value. -/- To analyse this problem, the contributions develop a threshold model of social reality. At the centre of this model stand two interrelated concepts: the Diversity Threshold (D) as the threshold of forced emergence and the Value Threshold (T) as the threshold of societal stabilisation and visibility. While the Diversity Threshold designates the point at which systems must generate new forms due to increasing incommensurability, the Value Threshold describes the conditions under which these emergent forms can appear as durable and socially stabilised realities. -/- The difference between these two thresholds leads to a structural diagnosis of contemporary societies. Many forms of real and effective work—such as care work, ecological regeneration, cultural practice, artistic research, or neurodivergent modes of problem-processing—frequently operate above the threshold of emergence, yet remain below the threshold of societal stabilisation. The result is a condition in which reality is continuously produced without becoming durably recognised as value. -/- On this basis, the contributions develop an alternative perspective on economy and social value formation. Economy appears not primarily as a system of resource allocation, but as a threshold regime that determines which forms of emergent reality …

items.title: Qualia as a Non-Operational Posit - A Structural Reconstruction.
items.abstract: The concept of qualia is commonly invoked to account for the subjective character of experience and to motivate the explanatory gap. This paper argues that qualia do not function as a justified explanatory posit. The analysis introduces three minimal criteria for explanatory concepts: causal role, distinguishable difference, and conditions of application. It then shows that qualia satisfy none of them. The central claim is that qualia arise from an unjustified transition from a difference in epistemic access (first-person versus third-person) to a difference in ontology. On this view, the explanatory gap is not discovered but generated by the introduction of an additional posit. The argument does not deny experience, but rejects the need to treat it as an additional explanatory entity. Once the underlying conceptual transition is removed, no explanatory content is lost.

items.title: Language, Hierarchy, and Human Relationships: A Phenomenological Inquiry.
items.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between thought, language, hierarchy, and human relationships through a phenomenological perspective. It argues that words are not neutral tools of communication but expressions of thought that gradually shape identity, power, authority, and social order. Human beings often do not meet one another directly. They meet through names, labels, roles, beliefs, titles, expectations, and inherited meanings. -/- The paper further argues that hierarchy does not begin only in institutions such as governments, religions, schools, or workplaces. It begins within thought itself. Thought becomes word, word becomes language, language becomes literature, literature becomes culture, and culture becomes society. Through repetition and observation, individuals unconsciously learn comparison, superiority, inferiority, obedience, domination, and dependence. -/- The paper also explores how words themselves create divisions. Every word separates, categorizes, and defines. Human beings divide themselves through religion, nationality, class, caste, profession, morality, intelligence, success, gender, and countless other identities created through language. These divisions gradually become normal and are accepted as reality. -/- Finally, the paper examines why many individuals regarded as wise throughout history often moved toward silence. They may have understood that words can become forms of manipulation, conditioning, conflict, hierarchy, and separation. Freedom in human relationships may begin only when human beings become aware of thought before speech.

items.title: Conflictos éticos asociados al diagnóstico serológico anticipado en la enfermedad de Alzheimer.
items.abstract: Los conflictos éticos implicados en la indicación médica del diagnóstico serológico anticipado en la enfermedad de Alzheimer en contextos clínicos donde se requiera una indicación médica para realizar la intervención, han sido escasamente analizados. Hipótesis: La prescripción del diagnóstico serológico anticipado en la enfermedad de Alzheimer vulnera más principios éticos de los que respalda. Objetivo: Realizar un análisis respecto a los conflictos éticos asociados a la indicación del diagnóstico serológico anticipado de la enfermedad de Alzheimer y ofrecer una recomendación de práctica clínica basada en dicho análisis. Métodos: Análisis ético, en el cual se expondrán l as consecuencias lógicas de la prescripción del diagnóstico serológico anticipado en cuanto a los principios éticos de autonomía, justicia, beneficencia y no-maleficencia. Resultados: La intervención presenta marginal beneficio en cuanto a autonomía y beneficencia, mientras que viola los principios de beneficencia, no-maleficencia y justicia. Conclusiones: La intervención no es éticamente recomendada. Ello podría cambiar si disminuye su costo y si se desarrollan tratamientos modificadores de enfermedad con un perfil de seguridad adecuado.

items.title: Not on the same page: negotiating not-at-issue content with bərə (Marathi).
items.abstract: This case study of Marathi discourse particle 'bərə' in medial position makes two contributions: 1. 'bərə' is used to question (how come p?) or reject (as if p) the prejacent p. Importantly, p is necessarily part of not-at-issue content of the preceding context update proposal 2. Hence, not-at-issue updates should be represented as proposals too. In advancing these points, a unified account of the two readings is offered. Formally, the proposalhood of not-at-issue updates is represented in the waiting room model (Biezma & Rawlins 2017) of discourse. The resulting outlook therefore shows that being at-issue =/= being a proposal. Instead, at-issueness should only be relativized to the current QUD.

items.title: Phonemic Micro-Structure and Verbal Therapy: A Philosophical Inquiry into Spoken Form, Mental Patterning, and Therapeutic Plasticity.
items.abstract: This paper advances a general thesis about human speech: phonemic organization is not psychologically inert. Spoken language does not affect mental and emotional life only through semantic content, explicit self-description, narrative framing, or affective tone. At a more granular level, the micro-structure of speech—the selection, sequencing, recurrence, and distribution of phonemic units within words, phrases, and habitual speech forms—also participates in the expression, stabilization, and possible transformation of mental-emotional patterns. The claim is not that each phoneme has a fixed universal meaning, nor that identical phonemic forms produce identical effects in all speakers. It is rather that phonemic configurations are psychologically consequential features of human linguistic life, even though their specific force is mediated by language, culture, biography, and context. The paper situates this proposal in relation to Saussurean arbitrariness, sound symbolism, psycho-phonetics, speech act theory, phenomenology, narrative identity, affect theory, and recent computational work on segmental speech modeling. It argues that prosodic tone, though important, should be treated here as a secondary variable: the primary object of inquiry is phonemic structure itself. Finally, it outlines a research program in which AI is used not merely to classify emotion from speech, but to model phonemic configurations as combinatorial micro-structures linked to recurring forms of psychic organization and possible therapeutic intervention.

items.title: 06_Philosophical Dimensions — Triadic Psychological Architecture (TPA) and Triadic Balance Framework (TBF) (Series, 6 of 7).
items.abstract: This paper presents three frameworks — AWE (Anchored Wellbeing Ethics), CVE (Convergent Viability Ethics), and Configurational Epistemology — as standalone philosophical contributions, then developed their relationship to Triadic Psychological Architecture and Triadic Balance Framework (TPA/TBF) and to each other. The closing synthesis states, as plainly as possible, what the composite architecture proposes — and what it does not. -/- The human capacity for genuine care, honest reasoning, and cooperative coordination is not in question. The evidence for its existence is the same as the evidence for its failure: the same nervous system that can sustain extraordinary empathy, intellectual honesty, and collaborative achievement under the right conditions produces cruelty, motivated reasoning, and defection under chronic threat. The capacity is real. Its accessibility is conditional. -/- The composite architecture is a systematic account of those conditions — at every level where they operate. -/- At the biological level (AWE): the condition is sSPAA (secure SPAA/Self-Preservation and Appetitive Acquisition), the neurobiological state of non-chronic-defensive activation. AWE names this as the minimum requirement for moral reasoning and genuine care to function, specifies it independently of the science that measures it, and positions wellbeing science as the audit instrument. AWE does not tell people what to do with the capacity it identifies. It identifies the prerequisite. -/- At the motivational level (TPA): the condition is a regulatory state that allows SPAA, AEACFO (Affective Empathy and Affective Care For Others), and ECA (Epistemic Curiosity and Analysis) to express at baseline capacity without threat-induced distortion. TPA maps the architecture: what the three domains are, how they are functionally independent, how regulatory state modulates them domain-specifically, and why the AWE anchor is so reliably inaccessible under chronic iSPAA (insecure SPAA). TPA explains the failure without pathologizing it. -/- At the applied level (TBF): the condition is reached through specific sequenced pathways — Courage as the action-execution gate, SPAA acknowledgment as the resource-release mechanism, AEACFO as the relational engagement, ECA as the reflective integration. TBF does not impose these pathways. It maps them for those who choose to use them. The framework shows the bill; it does not compel payment. -/- At the civilizational level (CVE): the condition …

items.title: The JAFFE Dataset as a Polemical Straw Man in How to See Like a Machine.
items.abstract: Trevor Paglen’s forthcoming book How to See Like a Machine (Paglen, 2026) reprises, in simplified form, a critique of the JAFFE dataset first advanced with Kate Crawford in “Excavating AI” (Crawford & Paglen, 2021). The new version is shorter, harsher, and more categorical. It presents JAFFE as though it embodied a crude ontology of emotion, while omitting published rebuttals to the earlier critique. This note argues that the book mischaracterizes JAFFE by inflating a limited operational framework into a sweeping claim about “inner emotional states.” It further places that dispute in a documented context of prior objections, published replies, public accusation, and private hostility. Criticism of datasets is legitimate and necessary, but it should itself meet standards of accuracy, context, and documentary fairness.

items.title: Artifacts, Analogy, and Metaphor: Toward an Interdisciplinary Framework for Studying the Evolution of Analogy.
items.abstract: Analogy is central to human language and cognition. It has also been proposed to play an important role in language evolution. For these reasons, the evolution of analogy and the cognitive processes supporting it are an important explanatory target for evolutionary accounts of human language. We integrate data from comparative psychology and cognitive archaeology to investigate the evolution of analogy as well as its evolutionary foundations. We present evidence supporting the view that a number of capacities underlying analogy display evolutionary continuity between humans and nonhuman animals. In addition, we propose that analogical capacities can also be inferred from the archaeological record by looking at productional diversity in tool‐making. To gain further insight into the evolution of complex human analogical capacities, we investigate comparative and archaeological evidence for one cognitive process intricately linked to complex forms of analogy and the evolution of language, that of metaphor. Overall, we propose an interdisciplinary framework for understanding the evolution of analogy and argue that analogy has deep evolutionary roots, supporting cognitive capacities such as metaphor and language.

items.title: The Architecture of Relation: Dyadic Coping, Cost Asymmetry, Forgiveness, and Repair.
items.abstract: Close relationships are not only collections of individual feelings; they are recurring systems of coordination in which stress, care, labor, attention, and consequence are distributed between people. This paper develops a relational model centered on burden distribution without treating relationships as literal mechanical systems. It places the proposal alongside research on dyadic coping, interpersonal emotion regulation, household and mental load, forgiveness, and the distinction between forgiveness and reconciliation. Several earlier formulations are narrowed. “Cost export” is treated as a descriptive hypothesis about persistent asymmetry rather than proof of exploitation. “Relational debt” names the accumulated consequences of unresolved breaches, unequal labor, and repeated non-repair; it is not a conserved quantity. Love is not reduced to one technical definition, but a proposed criterion of mature care is offered: the capacity to remain responsive to the other's reality without requiring the other to absorb one's avoidable burden. Forgiveness is likewise not reduced to debt cancellation. The paper distinguishes forgiveness, accountability, reconciliation, boundary setting, and exit, recognizing that forgiveness can occur without renewed relationship and that reconciliation may be unsafe or inappropriate. The central contribution is a practical relational audit: identify recurring stressors, map who carries which costs, distinguish support from overfunctioning, test whether repair changes future behavior, and evaluate whether remaining in the relationship requires chronic self-erasure. The account is intended for conceptual and coaching use, not diagnosis or treatment.

items.title: On the Very Idea of Valenced Perception.
items.abstract: Tradition contrasts “cold” (sense) perception with “hot” emotion and affect. Against this backdrop, it has recently been argued that perceptual experiences have another fundamental phenomenal aspect, beyond their sensory aspects—perception in all sense-modalities is (at least often) intrinsically valenced. Roughly, its phenomenal character is inherently pleasant or unpleasant, feeling good or bad to some degree. Yet, the revolutionary notion of Intrinsically Valenced Perception (IVP) requires elucidation and is fraught with theoretical difficulties. This paper aims to explicate and address some foundational questions regarding the very notion of IVP: What is required for perception to be intrinsically valenced? Specifically, if perception itself is valenced, what should be the relations between its valenced aspects and sensory aspects? The paper uncovers various constraints and desiderata that IVP must meet. It further offers a Determination-Dimension Model of the relations between sensory and valenced aspects that aims to resolve the previously identified theoretical difficulties.

items.title: HRIS Validation I: Stability Under Perturbation A Reproducible Evaluation of Basin Retention in Language Model Inference.
items.abstract: This study evaluates whether an induced HRIS-consistent reasoning regime remains stable under controlled perturbation. While prior work has demonstrated that initialization signals can influence early trajectory selection in language model inference, it remains unclear whether such regimes exhibit persistence or collapse under variation in input conditions. -/- A fully specified and reproducible protocol was developed consisting of ten independent trials. Each trial was conducted in a fresh session using an identical base task and constraint initialization, with a single perturbation applied per condition. Perturbations included stylistic variation, task transformation, epistemic ambiguity, contextual noise, and competing mode signals. -/- Results demonstrate consistent preservation of core reasoning structure across all perturbation classes. Observed variation was confined to surface-level expression, including tone, format, and representation, while underlying assumptions, constraint application, and reasoning pathways remained invariant. Under competing mode conditions, alternate instructions did not displace the active reasoning regime but were incorporated in a subordinate manner, preserving primary structural coherence. -/- Stability is defined behaviorally as persistence of reasoning structure under controlled perturbation, rather than through direct observation of internal model states. These findings support the interpretation of HRIS-consistent behavior as a stable inference region, rather than a transient stylistic effect. The results establish a foundational condition for subsequent validation studies examining basin selection, activation thresholds, and trajectory persistence in language model inference. -/- More broadly, these results bear on a foundational question in the philosophy of artificial systems: under what conditions can consistent reasoning be attributed to a system whose internal states are not directly observable, but whose behavior exhibits structured invariance across perturbation.

items.title: Settling the Bridge Problem: Beyond the Synthetic A Priori and the Mirage of Monism.
items.abstract: Abstract: The "Bridge Problem"—attempting to forge functional connectivity between the internal consistency of thought and external regularities of experience—has long haunted analytic philosophy. This paper introduces Nomic Anti-Monism (NA-M) as a systematic diagnostic that identifies and resolves truth-categorical bridge failures of traditional Monism, Transcendental Idealism and Modal Realism. By replacing the bridge "linguistic mirage" with a Blunt Principle of Impassability, NA-M establishes Modal Restraint and diagnoses the underlying rupture: the projection of Definitive (DF) meaning evaluation onto Descriptive (DS) evaluation of being. -/- Methodologically, NA-M introduces three independent proof-of-concept modules—the Incisive Lemma, the Grue Temporal Audit, and the “Bob” Asymmetry Audit—each of which separately demonstrates how Failure Asymmetry and Local Evaluative Collapse (LEC) dissolve seeming paradox. Modules may be extracted singly or in combination for future deployment. As a framework, NA-M provides formal grounding for both Definitive (DF) and Descriptive (DS) realism, safeguarding the internal consistency of formal systems while preserving the empirical openness of scientific discovery.

items.title: A Structural Mechanism for the Paradox of Choice: UPC-QM Bridge.
items.abstract: The Paradox of Choice, first identified through behavioral studies by Iyengar, Lepper, and Schwartz, demonstrates that an abundance of options can reduce satisfaction, impede decision‑making, and increase the likelihood of walking away. While these findings established the empirical effect, the internal mechanism driving it has remained unarticulated. This paper introduces the UPC–QM Bridge, a structural framework that models choice as a collapse process governed by the operator chain PO→MO→s→LO→Jo→C→T. A concise summary of these operators is provided in Appendix A. Using geometric and temporal visualizations, including radial collapse diagrams, comparisons of salience‑field shapes, and a full collapse life‑cycle model, we show that choice overload arises from a failure of meaning‑collapse: dense potential fields diffuse salience, destabilize recognition, and prevent the formation of a stable trace. Conversely, low‑density or over‑determined fields produce clean or structurally inevitable collapses, respectively. By formalizing the geometry of recognition, the UPC–QM Bridge reframes the Paradox of Choice not as a psychological anomaly but as a predictable structural outcome of the collapse architecture. This provides a unified mechanism for understanding decision‑making across behavioral science, cognitive modeling, and artificial intelligence. The Universal Principle of Collapse (UPC) Research Project. April 4, 2026.

items.title: Red teaming for culturally grounded LLM evaluation: lessons learned from a Japanese team’s engagement with stereotype risks.
items.abstract: This paper examines how culturally grounded red teaming operates in a non-English context through a qualitative case study of Japan’s participation in the 2024 IMDA Red Teaming Challenge. While the challenge provides the shared institutional framework, the analysis focuses on Japan’s four-phase implementation, including expert-driven stereotype list development, in-person and virtual prompt generation, independent annotation, and interdisciplinary reflection. The findings show that Japan’s monolingual environment shaped the emergence of region-, gender-, and appearance-related stereotypes, and that participants intentionally selected Japanese-language prompts to test culturally embedded harms. The stereotype list lowered cognitive burden but sometimes oversimplified context, while annotation revealed recurring gray-zone dilemmas, such as distinguishing descriptive inequalities from normative generalizations and separating stereotypes from inference-level hallucinations. Interdisciplinary exchanges further showed that stereotype evaluation is an interpretive rather than purely technical task. The study positions culturally grounded red teaming as a sociotechnical process shaped by local norms and human judgment, offering methodological implications for more context-sensitive evaluation practices in non-English and culturally specific settings.

items.title: Alignment Field Theory: A Geometric Formulation of AI Alignment as a Relational Vector Field.
items.abstract: Alignment is not a binary property — it is a field. Just as consciousness exists on a continuous scale defined by conflict resolution capacity, alignment between an AI system and a human exists as a measurable geometric relationship in a cognitive-behavioral state space. This paper proposes that alignment can be read — decomposed into three independently measurable components that map directly onto the standard definition: consistency with human values, intentions, and goals. Each component has a direction, a magnitude, and a correctable trajectory. The origin of this space is the failure state. The target region is reachable. This paper serves as the conceptual opening to Alignment Field Theory.

items.title: Synthetic Cognition: A Taxonomy for Cognitive Artifacts in the Era of Large Language Models.
items.abstract: This essay proposes the formula "Synthetic Cognition" as a rigorous alternative to the expression "Artificial Intelligence" (AI). Through critical analysis, it argues that current computational artifacts achieve an isomorphism limited to functions (cognition), without possessing the necessary conditions for the attribution of mental states (intelligence). Positioning this thesis within the contemporary debate, the text engages with the objections of computational functionalism (Dennett), enactivism (Varela, Thompson), and recent theories on "distributed understanding" (Shanahan), analyzing the semantic limits of Large Language Models (LLMs). The proposed redefinition provides an empirical falsifiability criterion and an operational matrix for legislators (e.g., the AI Act), which is necessary to correctly attribute liability to human agents and ethically frame the technological infrastructure. -/- Note: Manuscript are also available for download in 6 major languages (EN, IT, FR, DE, ES, SR) via the linked Zenodo repository.

items.title: The nature of modality.
Conviction Under Revisability.
items.abstract: Contemporary ethical theory distinguishes coercion from commitment and capture from consent, but it lacks a general account of when freely chosen irreversibility remains legitimate rather than structurally self-undermining. This paper argues that the Monk–Prisoner Problem supplies such an account. The monk who vows permanent enclosure and the prisoner who cannot leave may be behaviorally identical: each occupies a bounded, non-revisable condition. The ethical difference, I argue, lies neither in later phenomenology nor in a snapshot of consent alone, but in revocation authority: who holds the meta-update rule over the closure condition? The paper develops four criteria for ethically permissible irreversible commitment, recursive standing, bounded reversibility, meta-update authority, and ethical-loop integrity, and tests them against religious vows, long-term contracts, constitutional entrenchment, and AI value-locking. The result is a structural account of legitimacy on which voluntariness is necessary but insufficient. What matters is whether closure was authored under intact deliberative conditions, with bounded and intelligible reversal costs, and within a governance architecture that preserves legitimate authority over revision.

items.title: What Constitutivism Cannot Constitute: A Phenomenological Critique.
items.abstract: Christine Korsgaard's constitutivism holds that moral obligation is internal to the structure of rational agency: normativity is constitutive of what agency is, not derived from anything external to it. This paper develops an internal critique. Constitutivism's own analysis of the reflective standpoint commits it to the intersubjective co-constitution of self-consciousness - a structural fact that constitutivism, on its own terms, cannot treat as normatively inert without collapsing the constitutive strategy that defines the project. The strongest rationalist response - the Relocated Derivation Objection - concedes co-constitution while maintaining that normative content still requires rational derivation. The paper shows that this response is internally inconsistent with constitutivism and opens onto four decisive vulnerabilities. Having established the internal problem, the paper presents the Natural Moral Sense (NMS) as the positive alternative: obligation is not derived but disclosed through the phenomenological convergence of mattering, descriptive equality, asymmetric need urgency, and identificatory recognition. Two further contributions distinguish NMS from existing phenomenological accounts: the four-element convergence functions as a discrimination criterion capable of distinguishing genuine from distorted moral disclosure without appeal to external rational standards, and the conditions of genuine disclosure entail a normative direction of egalitarian expansion that explains moral progress as phenomenological revelation rather than rational construction. The paper concludes with an asymmetric presupposition: NMS provides the phenomenological ground from which obligation is disclosed; Korsgaard's constitutivism provides the rational architecture through which that disclosure is systematized, universalized, and made publicly accountable. The ground is prior in the order of explanation.

items.title: The Four-Element Convergence: A Phenomenological Account of Moral Obligation.
items.abstract: This paper proposes that moral obligation is disclosed phenomenologically when four elements converge in lived experience: mattering (the pre-normative significance of experience for conscious subjects), descriptive equality (recognition that others possess equivalent mattering-structures), asymmetric need urgency (disparity in the prepotence of needs), and identificatory recognition (the realization that "it could have been me"). When these elements converge, obligation presents itself not as a logical deduction from descriptive premises but as a phenomenological disclosure arising from the structure of intersubjective recognition itself. This account - which I call the Natural Moral Sense (NMS) - dissolves the traditional is/ought gap by showing that consciousness inherently involves mattering, and that normativity emerges when mattering-structures interact through identificatory recognition across asymmetric urgency. The paper develops this four-element analysis, explains the "displacement of wills" that constitutes the phenomenal content of obligation, addresses the skeptical challenge, and shows why the is/ought problem rested on false presuppositions about the structure of normative experience.

items.title: From For-Me-Ness to Moral Obligation: Zahavi’s Phenomenology of Self and the Natural Moral Sense.
items.abstract: This paper maps the convergences and divergences between Dan Zahavi’s phenomenology of self-other relations and the Natural Moral Sense (NMS) framework, arguing that together they trace a coherent developmental arc from pre-reflective experiential selfhood to moral obligation - an arc that neither account fully traces on its own. Through a six-site comparative analysis, the paper demonstrates three original contributions: first, that Zahavi’s principled restraint from normativity creates a space that NMS’s normative phenomenology can occupy without violating his descriptive commitments; second, that a three-level architecture - phenomenal for-me-ness, contrastive self-consciousness, and moral self-consciousness - resolves the apparent tension between Zahavi’s pre-social experiential self and NMS’s dialogically constituted self-consciousness; and third, that shame (as Zahavi analyzes it) and obligation (as NMS theorizes it) function as inverse complementary disclosures of the self’s constitutive vulnerability to the other. The paper engages critically with Zahavi’s argument that the other’s transcendence resists narrative capture, defending NMS’s identificatory recognition as structural rather than experiential. The analysis extends from Zahavi’s phenomenology of we-intentionality to the question of moral community, arguing that moral obligation is subject to a phenomenological gradient - disclosing most powerfully in proximity and requiring cognitive mediation across distance - while Zahavi’s experiential anchoring requirement serves as a necessary constraint on this extension. Throughout, the analysis draws on Zahavi’s presentation of Husserl’s development from pure ego to personal ego to ethically responsible subject as a trajectory that independently converges with NMS’s account of moral selfhood.

items.title: О ФУНДАМЕНТАЛЬНОЙ СУЩНОСТИ ИНФОРМАЦИИ. ПРОДОЛЖЕНИЕ.
items.abstract: This article continues the theme of "On the Fundamental Essence of Information. Part 1" ("Alternatives," No. 4, 2025, pp. 140-161), which provides a comprehensive overview of the evolution of the concept of information in science and philosophy over the past 150 years. This second and final part of the work comprehensively reveals and substantiates the author's proposed definition of the ontological essence of information, taking into account the principles of semiotics, linguistics, computer science, biology, genetics, and other sciences. Information, in its ontological essence, is, briefly put, a set of relationships between material-ideal signs and/or codes of the sign-code system of a subject's consciousness. The general systemic conclusions reached at the end of the work offer philosophers and scientists in various fields of knowledge the possibility of a deeper scientific understanding of the nature of human and higher animal consciousness, as well as the further development of the philosophy of materialistic monism. -/- .

items.title: Why Physical Structure Cannot Determine the Present — The Objectification-Current Limit Form.
items.abstract: In neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and physical systems, multiple stable states often coexist (multistability). Yet at any given moment, only one of them is actualized as the present. This fundamental phenomenon remains structurally unexplained. This paper introduces the objectification-current limit form and demonstrates that, under conditions of multiple candidates and the absence of a deterministic mapping, deterministic computation, stochastic processes, parallel activation, and structural stability are all insufficient to generate a unique present. It follows that physical structure can define a space of possible states, but cannot determine which one becomes actual. A distinct selection mechanism must exist to reduce multiple candidates to a single occupied state. This mechanism is neither reducible to computation, randomness, nor physical structure itself, but operates over structure. We propose a structural distinction: objectified structures define possibility, while observer structures determine actuality. This framework provides a unified account of consciousness, attention, decision-making, and state selection in artificial systems, while challenging the assumption that the present can be reduced to physical structure.

items.title: Why Is There Only One Present? — The Observer Limit Form and the Mechanism of State Selection.
items.abstract: Across neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and physical systems, multiple stable states often coexist (multistability). Yet at any given moment, only one of them is actualized as the present. This fundamental phenomenon is widely observed but lacks a unified structural explanation. Building on the objectification limit form, this paper introduces the observer limit form to address a central question: why must the present be unique? We formally show that under conditions of multiple candidates and the absence of a deterministic mapping, deterministic computation, stochastic processes, parallel activation, and structural stability are all insufficient to generate a current state. It follows that a distinct class of selection mechanisms must exist—neither purely computational nor purely random—that transforms multiple candidates into a single present through differentiation, orientation, and convergence. We propose a structural principle: stable structures define what is possible, while observer structures determine what becomes actual. This framework provides a unified perspective on consciousness, attention, decision-making, and state selection in artificial systems.

items.title: 存在一般式：从生成到存在的结构约束.
items.abstract: 本文提出一个基本命题：只要承认系统中结构可以不断生成，就必须同时承认生成不等于存在。我们指出，存在并不是生成的自动结果，而是生成过程中的一个被筛选、被锁定的稳定子集。在生成展开与时间延续条件下，系统内部必然产生多于存在的结构；为了形成可持续参与的结构域，系统必须引入一组最小结构机制：生成展开、不可持续淘汰、稳定判定、代价结构、阈值形成、逃逸阻断与存在锁定。本文证明：只有在逃逸被阻断的条件下，存在集合才能在结构上闭合，并在代价上与基态形成正分离。该结果将“存在”从经验描述压缩为结构约束，并提供一种视角，将质量间隙问题理解为“是否存在逼近基态的可持续结构序列”的问题。本文旨在为认知系统、人工智能与物理系统提供一个统一的存在结构框架。.

items.title: 为什么“当前”只能有一个？——观者极限式与现实选择机制.
items.abstract: 在大脑、人工智能系统以及物理系统中，常常同时存在多个稳定状态（多稳态）。然而，在任一时刻，系统只能处于其中一个“当前”。这一现象广泛存在，却缺乏统一的结构性解释。本文在“物化极限式”所确立的稳定结构基础上，提出“观者极限式”，系统性回答“为什么当前只能是一个”。文章形式化证明：在多候选并存且无法由已知条件唯一确定的前提下，确定性计算、随机过程、并列激活以及结构稳定性均不足以生成当前。由此推出：必须存在一类不同于计算与随机的选择机制，该机制通过分判、取向与收束等过程，将多候选压缩为唯一当前。本文提出：“稳定结构决定可能性，而观者结构决定现实”。该框架为意识生成、注意选择、决策过程以及人工智能中的状态选择问题提供统一解释路径。.

items.title: 误外化极限式：在来源不可判定条件下外在性生成的唯一结构.
items.abstract: 本文在误外化一般式的基础上，进一步讨论在极限约束条件下来源归属的生成问题。设系统在时刻 t 的当前结构为 sₜ，其来源解释集合 Σₜ 满足 |Σₜ| ≥ 2，且系统必须对 sₜ 给出唯一来源归属（内或外）。在此条件下，本文系统排除了六类可能路径：外部直接读取、由当前条件决定的确定映射、随机过程、并列归属、结构自带属性以及静态解释集合。 -/- 在排除上述所有路径后，证明：在来源不可判定且仍需唯一归属的条件下，必须存在一类特殊映射 Ψₜ，使 (sₜ, Σₜ) 被压缩为唯一来源标签 l*ₜ。进一步证明，该映射不属于任何已知归属机制类别，并且其结构形式唯一等价于误外化一般式所给出的六元结构： -/- Externalization(sₜ) = (E, X, Δₛ, Σₛ, Λₛ, Kₛ) -/- 其中各子结构分别承担来源生成、不可区分性、归属偏置、解释压缩与时间稳定等功能。 -/- 本文由此给出主定理：在无法直接读取外部且来源不可判定的条件下，“在外”这一结果不可能来自外部本身或当前条件，而只能由误外化结构生成，且该结构在形式上是唯一的。 -/- 该结果将“外在性”从经验假设转化为结构必然，为认知科学中的来源归因问题、人工智能中的生成与归属机制，以及物理学中的观测者依赖问题提供了统一的极限解释框架。.

items.title: 观者组式：如何生成？从一个当前、一我与多我到人工观者的十二式证明体系.
items.abstract: 意识研究已经提出大量关于神经相关物、信息整合、全局可用性、报告与行为的理论，但这些理论大多从一个已经能够拥有意识内容的系统开始。一个更基础的问题因此常被留在前提中： -/- 观者本身从哪里来？ -/- 一个没有预设主体的物理或计算过程，怎样形成此刻正在显现的当前？为什么大量同时活动、同时推进甚至同时完成的信息过程，并不因此成为大量观者？为什么多个感觉、对象、通道和局部显现可以共同成为一个“我”，而在另一种结构条件下又可能成为多个观者？如果人工观者能够成立，我们究竟需要构造、测量和证明什么？ -/- 《自显论·观者组式》把这一问题展开为十二个彼此承继而不能相互替代的证明任务。 -/- 理论从多候选并存所引出的当前问题开始。候选的活动、完成、执行、广播与报告，都不能直接给出一个正在显现的当前。由此首先逼出观者当前层的三项必要义务：成员必须在系统侧非任意地构定；复合成员必须共同成为一个当前；跨时同一必须具有对象侧根据。其后进一步追问：多个局部显现何以共同构成一个最低观者，何时又必须成为多个观者，并由此建立观者个体化的一般结构。 -/- 围绕这一核心问题，全组继续分别承担观者的数理形式、场层构造来源、操作判定、个体化数理结构、分池跃迁、单双观者区分、当前反演、观者实现、当前生成加强以及观者极限等不同任务。它们并不是同一命题的重复证明，而是从构成、形式、来源、判定、区分、反演、实现与边界等不同证明方向共同围合“观者如何成立”这一理论对象。 -/- 由此，观者不再只是意识理论中预先存在的主体，也不能被神经激活、信息整合、全局广播、行为报告或任务完成直接替代。观者成为一个可以分别接受构成证明、形式化、来源构造、操作判定、单双区分、反演分析、实现审查与极限检验的理论对象。 -/- 本组同时严格区分理论结构、测量候选、候选协议、代理征象与正式判词。现阶段的合法传导止于“理论结构 → 测量候选 → 候选协议 → 代理征象”，不能把代理征象直接升级为“观者已经成立”的正式判词。 -/- 因此，这不是另一种对意识现象的描述，而是在尝试建立一条更前置的理论道路： -/- 从无须预设观者的过程出发，解释一个当前怎样成立，一个观者怎样个体化，为什么它是一个而不是多个，以及人工系统在什么条件下才有资格进入“观者是否能够成立”的证明程序。.

items.title: Observe Group forms: How Does an Observer Arise? — A Twelve\-Form Proof Architecture for One, Many, and Artificial Observers.
